Interactive lecture notes · condensed-matter theory

Electrons, phonons and photons in crystals

A guided path from the first-principles electron–phonon theory reviewed by Giustino (2017) to the electron–phonon–photon (EPP) formalism. EPP puts the full electromagnetic field, transverse photons included, on the same footing as the lattice. Every section pairs the theory with figures you can drive.

Part A

Electron–phonon interactions from first principles

Part A follows F. Giustino, “Electron-phonon interactions from first principles,” Rev. Mod. Phys. 89, 015003 (2017), cited below as Giustino, with his equations tagged (G.n). The review is organized around one object, the canonical electron–phonon Hamiltonian of his Eq. (1), displayed and read term by term in §A.2.

Its parameters are the band energies $\varepsilon_{n\bk}$, the phonon energies $\hbar\omega_{\bq\nu}$ and the coupling matrix elements $g_{mn\nu}(\bk,\bq)$, plus the second-order $g^{\rm DW}$. Part A builds the lattice that defines $\omega_{\bq\nu}$ (A.1), reads the coupling term (A.2), shows how density-functional perturbation theory computes $g$ as a statically screened vertex (A.3) and what polar crystals add (A.4). It then rebuilds the theory from many-body perturbation theory, where the phonons appear as a second contribution to the screened interaction $W$ and the parameters of Eq. (G.1) acquire precise definitions (A.5). With that machinery it dresses phonons (A.6) and electrons (A.7) with self-energies, and it ends with what is measured: temperature-dependent gaps and lifetimes, transport and superconductivity (A.8, A.9).

One thread runs through all of it. Every interaction in Part A is the instantaneous, longitudinal Coulomb interaction $v(\br-\br')\,\delta(t-t')$, screened by the electrons and, through the phonons, by the ions. There is no vector potential and no photon: light enters only as an external classical field that drives electronic transitions (Giustino §IX.B, Eq. G.200). The Bridge asks what changes when that Coulomb line becomes the longitudinal part of the full photon propagator, whose transverse part travels at the finite speed of light, and Part B develops the resulting electron–phonon–photon theory.

A.1Giustino §III.A, App. B · EPP §1

Lattice dynamics and phonons

How force constants become a dynamical matrix, how its eigenvectors become normal modes, and how quantizing those modes gives phonons whose zero-point amplitude is a few hundredths of an ångström. This is the phonon line of Eq. (G.1) and the displacement operator from which every coupling on this page is built.

Two approximations: slow nuclei, parabolic wells

Nuclei are heavier than electrons by factors from about 1800 (hydrogen) to about $3.8\times10^5$ (lead). In the Born–Oppenheimer picture the electrons adjust instantaneously and stay in their ground state, so the nuclei move on a potential-energy surface $U(\{\boldsymbol\tau_{\kappa p}\})$: the total energy of the electrons plus classical nuclei clamped at positions $\boldsymbol\tau_{\kappa p}$, a standard output of every DFT code. Giustino works in a Born–von Kármán (BvK) supercell of $N_p$ unit cells with lattice vectors $\bR_p$. Nucleus $\kappa$ of cell $p$ sits at $\boldsymbol\tau_{\kappa p}=\bR_p+\boldsymbol\tau_\kappa$, and the $N_p$ allowed wavevectors $\bq$ form a uniform grid with (Giustino App. A)

$$\sum_{\bq}\exp(i\bq\cdot\bR_p)=N_p\,\delta_{p0},\qquad \sum_{p}\exp(i\bq\cdot\bR_p)=N_p\,\delta_{\bq\mathbf 0}. \tag{G.A1}$$

The harmonic approximation keeps $U$ to second order in the displacements $\Delta\tau_{\kappa\alpha p}$ from equilibrium. The linear term vanishes because the forces are zero there, and the second derivatives define the interatomic force constants:

$$U=U_0+\frac12\sum_{\substack{\kappa\alpha p\\ \kappa'\alpha'p'}}\frac{\partial^2U}{\partial\tau_{\kappa\alpha p}\,\partial\tau_{\kappa'\alpha'p'}}\,\Delta\tau_{\kappa\alpha p}\,\Delta\tau_{\kappa'\alpha'p'}, \tag{G.12}$$
$$C_{\kappa\alpha p,\kappa'\alpha'p'}=\partial^2U/\partial\tau_{\kappa\alpha p}\,\partial\tau_{\kappa'\alpha'p'}. \tag{G.13}$$

$C$ is real and symmetric, depends only on $\bR_{p'}-\bR_p$, and obeys the acoustic sum rule

$$\sum_{\kappa'p'}C_{\kappa\alpha p,\kappa'\alpha'p'}=0\qquad\text{for all }\kappa,\alpha,p,\alpha',$$

because a rigid translation of the whole crystal costs no energy. Section III.A uses it only implicitly, when the zero-frequency modes are discarded; its many-body form returns as Eq. (G.120) in §A.5. Treating the nuclei as quantum particles gives the lattice Hamiltonian

$$\hat H_{\rm p}=\frac12\sum_{\substack{\kappa\alpha p\\ \kappa'\alpha'p'}}C_{\kappa\alpha p,\kappa'\alpha'p'}\,\Delta\tau_{\kappa\alpha p}\,\Delta\tau_{\kappa'\alpha'p'}-\sum_{\kappa\alpha p}\frac{\hbar^2}{2M_\kappa}\frac{\partial^2}{\partial\tau^2_{\kappa\alpha p}}, \tag{G.19}$$

which, as Giustino stresses, rests on (i) the harmonic truncation of (G.12) and (ii) the Born–Oppenheimer adiabatic approximation, since $C$ is computed with the electrons in their ground state for each frozen configuration. This section needs no electromagnetic units. Numbers are in eV, Å, amu and meV, and a spring $K$ (eV/Å²) on a mass $M$ (amu) vibrates at $\hbar\omega=64.654\,\text{meV}\times\sqrt{K/M}$.

What the two approximations hide

Born–Oppenheimer force constants already contain the static screening of the ion–ion interaction by the electrons: DFT phonons are dressed by the electrons at $\omega=0$. When the electrons cannot follow (doped graphene, Kohn anomalies) nonadiabatic corrections appear, the subject of §A.6. The harmonic expansion fails for light atoms such as H, near soft-mode or charge-density-wave instabilities, and at high temperature when displacements approach a tenth of a bond length.

In polar crystals the force constants also carry a long-range dipole–dipole tail $\propto|\bR_p|^{-3}$. Its Fourier transform is non-analytic at $\bq\to0$, which is the LO–TO splitting of §A.4. The short-range chain used below cannot show it.

From force constants to the dynamical matrix

A crystal of $N_p$ cells has $3MN_p$ coupled coordinates, but translational invariance makes $C$ depend only on cell differences, so lattice plane waves $e^{i\bq\cdot\bR_p}$ decouple different $\bq$. Dividing by $\sqrt{M_\kappa M_{\kappa'}}$ then turns Newton's generalized eigenproblem into a standard Hermitian one. Giustino follows the convention of Maradudin and Vosko:

$$D^{\rm dm}_{\kappa\alpha,\kappa'\alpha'}(\bq)=(M_\kappa M_{\kappa'})^{-1/2}\sum_p C_{\kappa\alpha0,\kappa'\alpha'p}\exp(i\bq\cdot\bR_p), \tag{G.14}$$
$$\sum_{\kappa'\alpha'}D^{\rm dm}_{\kappa\alpha,\kappa'\alpha'}(\bq)\,e_{\kappa'\alpha',\nu}(\bq)=\omega^2_{\bq\nu}\,e_{\kappa\alpha,\nu}(\bq). \tag{G.15}$$

For each $\bq$ this is a $3M\times3M$ problem. Its eigenvalues $\omega^2_{\bq\nu}$ are the squared frequencies of independent classical oscillators, real because $D^{\rm dm}$ is Hermitian and non-negative for a stable lattice. Hermiticity also makes the polarization vectors complete and orthonormal,

$$\sum_\nu e^*_{\kappa'\alpha',\nu}(\bq)\,e_{\kappa\alpha,\nu}(\bq)=\delta_{\kappa\kappa'}\delta_{\alpha\alpha'}, \tag{G.16}$$
$$\sum_{\kappa\alpha}e^*_{\kappa\alpha,\nu}(\bq)\,e_{\kappa\alpha,\nu'}(\bq)=\delta_{\nu\nu'}, \tag{G.17}$$

and because $C$ is real, $D^{\rm dm}(-\bq)=D^{\rm dm}(\bq)^*$, which permits the phase choice

$$\omega^2_{-\bq\nu}=\omega^2_{\bq\nu},\qquad e_{\kappa\alpha,\nu}(-\bq)=e^*_{\kappa\alpha,\nu}(\bq). \tag{G.18}$$

The eigenvectors are mass-weighted: atom $\kappa$ moves with an amplitude proportional to $e_{\kappa\alpha,\nu}(\bq)/\sqrt{M_\kappa}$. Of the $3M$ branches, three are acoustic. The sum rule forces $\omega\to0$ as $\bq\to0$, where all atoms of a cell move together, $e_\kappa\propto\sqrt{M_\kappa}$. The other $3M-3$ are optical: at $\bq=0$ the sublattices move against each other with the centre of mass fixed, $\sum_\kappa\sqrt{M_\kappa}\,e_\kappa=0$. In a polar crystal that antiphase motion carries an oscillating dipole, which is the hook for the Fröhlich coupling of §A.4 and for the photons of Part B.

Derivation: why lattice plane waves decouple, from (G.12) to (G.15)

From (G.19) the classical equation of motion is $M_\kappa\Delta\ddot\tau_{\kappa\alpha p}=-\sum_{\kappa'\alpha'p'}C_{\kappa\alpha p,\kappa'\alpha'p'}\Delta\tau_{\kappa'\alpha'p'}$. Insert the trial solution $\Delta\tau_{\kappa\alpha p}(t)=M_\kappa^{-1/2}\,e_{\kappa\alpha}\,e^{i(\bq\cdot\bR_p-\omega t)}$ and use translational invariance, $C_{\kappa\alpha p,\kappa'\alpha'p'}=C_{\kappa\alpha0,\kappa'\alpha',p'-p}$. Relabelling $\bR_{p'}-\bR_p\to\bR_{p''}$ gives

$$\omega^2 M_\kappa^{1/2}\,e_{\kappa\alpha}\,e^{i\bq\cdot\bR_p}=\sum_{\kappa'\alpha'p''}C_{\kappa\alpha0,\kappa'\alpha'p''}\,M_{\kappa'}^{-1/2}\,e_{\kappa'\alpha'}\,e^{i\bq\cdot(\bR_p+\bR_{p''})}.$$

The factor $e^{i\bq\cdot\bR_p}$ cancels, and dividing by $M_\kappa^{1/2}$ leaves (G.15) with $D^{\rm dm}$ of (G.14). The cell index has disappeared: there is one $3M\times3M$ problem per $\bq$, $N_p$ of them in all. Note that the phase $e^{+i\bq\cdot\bR_p}$ in (G.14) belongs to the cell of the second atom. That is what a displacement pattern $\propto e^{+i\bq\cdot\bR_p}$, as in (G.20) below, requires. The EPP manuscript's Eq. (E.15) uses the opposite assignment (see the end of this section).

A worked example: the diatomic chain

Take one dimension and two atoms per cell: mass $M_1$ at the cell origin, mass $M_2$ inside the cell, an intracell spring $K_1$, and an intercell spring $K_2$ that ties atom 2 of cell $p$ to atom 1 of cell $p+1$. Seen from atom 1 of cell 0, the nonzero force constants are $C_{10,10}=K_1+K_2$ (fixed by the sum rule), $C_{10,20}=-K_1$ and $C_{10,2(-1)}=-K_2$, because the $K_2$ partner of atom 1 sits in cell $-1$, at $R_p=-a$. Equation (G.14) then gives

$$D^{\rm dm}(q)=\begin{pmatrix}\dfrac{K_1+K_2}{M_1} & -\dfrac{K_1+K_2\,e^{-iqa}}{\sqrt{M_1M_2}}\\[3mm] -\dfrac{K_1+K_2\,e^{iqa}}{\sqrt{M_1M_2}} & \dfrac{K_1+K_2}{M_2}\end{pmatrix},$$
$$\begin{gathered}\omega^2_\pm(q)=\frac{A+C}{2}\pm\sqrt{\Big(\frac{A-C}{2}\Big)^2+|B|^2},\\ A=D^{\rm dm}_{11},\quad C=D^{\rm dm}_{22},\quad |B|^2=\big|D^{\rm dm}_{12}\big|^2=\frac{K_1^2+K_2^2+2K_1K_2\cos qa}{M_1M_2}.\end{gathered}$$

Three limits carry most of the physics. At $q=0$, $\omega_-=0$ and $\omega_+^2=(K_1+K_2)(1/M_1+1/M_2)$. For small $q$ the acoustic branch is linear, $\omega_-\simeq v_s|q|$ with $v_s=a\,\{K_1K_2/[(K_1+K_2)(M_1+M_2)]\}^{1/2}$. At the zone edge $q=\pi/a$, $|B|=|K_1-K_2|/\sqrt{M_1M_2}$. With equal springs $D^{\rm dm}$ becomes diagonal, the branches sit at $\sqrt{2K/M_1}$ and $\sqrt{2K/M_2}$, and only one sublattice moves in each: the heavy one in the acoustic mode, the light one in the optical mode. With equal masses they sit at $\sqrt{2K_1/M}$ and $\sqrt{2K_2/M}$. A gap opens whenever the two atoms differ in mass or in bonding. When they do not, the two branches are one monatomic branch folded into a doubled cell.

Derivation: eigenvectors, phase convention and sound velocity

For an eigenvalue $\lambda$ of $D^{\rm dm}(q)$, the first row of $(D^{\rm dm}-\lambda)\,e=0$ gives $e\propto(D^{\rm dm}_{12},\ \lambda-D^{\rm dm}_{11})$. The figure normalizes this vector and multiplies it by the phase that makes $e_1$ real and positive (if $e_1=0$, $e_2$ is made real and positive instead). Since $D^{\rm dm}(-q)=D^{\rm dm}(q)^*$, this gauge satisfies $e(-q)=e(q)^*$, which is (G.18). At $q=0$ it gives $e_-\propto(\sqrt{M_1},\sqrt{M_2})$ and $e_+\propto(\sqrt{M_2},-\sqrt{M_1})$, so that the physical displacements of the optical mode obey $M_1u_1=-M_2u_2$.

The product of the eigenvalues is $\det D^{\rm dm}=2K_1K_2(1-\cos qa)/(M_1M_2)$. Dividing by $\omega_+^2(0)$ gives $\omega_-^2\simeq K_1K_2\,q^2a^2/[(K_1+K_2)(M_1+M_2)]$, the sound velocity quoted above. With $K$ in eV/Å² and $M$ in amu, $\omega^2$ comes out in eV Å⁻² amu⁻¹, and $\hbar\omega=64.654\,\text{meV}\times\sqrt{\omega^2}$ because $\hbar^2/(\text{amu}\cdot\text{Å}^2)=4.1803$ meV.

Quantization: phonons and the zero-point length

Each normal mode is a harmonic oscillator, so quantization is the ladder-operator construction of a single oscillator applied mode by mode. Giustino's Appendix B does it with care, because a complex normal coordinate at $\bq$ and its partner at $-\bq$ describe the same pair of real oscillators (details below). The result is

$$\Delta\tau_{\kappa\alpha p}=\left(\frac{M_0}{N_pM_\kappa}\right)^{1/2}\sum_{\bq\nu}e^{i\bq\cdot\bR_p}\,e_{\kappa\alpha,\nu}(\bq)\,l_{\bq\nu}\left(\hat a_{\bq\nu}+\hat a^\dagger_{-\bq\nu}\right), \tag{G.20}$$
$$l_{\bq\nu}=[\hbar/(2M_0\omega_{\bq\nu})]^{1/2}, \tag{G.21}$$
$$\hat H_{\rm p}=\sum_{\bq\nu}\hbar\omega_{\bq\nu}\left(\hat a^\dagger_{\bq\nu}\hat a_{\bq\nu}+1/2\right). \tag{G.22}$$

Here $M_0$ is an arbitrary reference mass, typically the proton mass, introduced only so that $l_{\bq\nu}$ is a length. It cancels in every physical quantity, since $(M_0/M_\kappa)^{1/2}l_{\bq\nu}=[\hbar/(2M_\kappa\omega_{\bq\nu})]^{1/2}$. Equation (G.22) is the phonon line of (G.1): $3MN_p$ independent oscillators, of which the three $\bq=0$ translations have $\omega=0$ and an undefined $l_{\bq\nu}$; they are skipped in every sum that contains $l_{\bq\nu}$. The commutators $[\hat a_{\bq\nu},\hat a^\dagger_{\bq'\nu'}]=\delta_{\nu\nu'}\delta_{\bq\bq'}$ make phonons bosons.

The combination $\hat a_{\bq\nu}+\hat a^\dagger_{-\bq\nu}$ deserves a second look. A displacement wave $\propto e^{i\bq\cdot\bR_p}$ either absorbs a phonon of momentum $\bq$ or emits one of momentum $-\bq$; both transfer $\bq$ to whatever the displacement acts on. This is the operator that multiplies $g_{mn\nu}(\bk,\bq)$ in (G.1), and $(M_0/M_\kappa)^{1/2}l_{\bq\nu}\,e_{\kappa\alpha,\nu}(\bq)$ is the length that multiplies the potential gradient inside $g$ (§A.2).

Thermal averages need only the occupation $n_{\bq\nu}$ of each mode,

$$\big\langle(\hat a_{\bq\nu}+\hat a^\dagger_{-\bq\nu})(\hat a_{-\bq\nu}+\hat a^\dagger_{\bq\nu})\big\rangle=2n_{\bq\nu}+1=\coth\frac{\hbar\omega_{\bq\nu}}{2k_BT},$$

Inserted in the square of (G.20), the thermal average keeps only the pairs $\bq'=-\bq$, $\nu'=\nu$, and with (G.18) gives the mean-square displacement

$$\big\langle\Delta\tau^2_{\kappa\alpha p}\big\rangle=\frac1{N_p}\sum_{\bq\nu}\frac{\hbar}{2M_\kappa\omega_{\bq\nu}}\,\big|e_{\kappa\alpha,\nu}(\bq)\big|^2\coth\frac{\hbar\omega_{\bq\nu}}{2k_BT}.$$

Each mode contributes $1/N_p$ times its squared zero-point amplitude, enhanced by the coth: a plateau for $k_BT\ll\hbar\omega$ and the classical $k_BT/(M_\kappa\omega^2)$ for $k_BT\gg\hbar\omega$. In numbers, $\hbar/(2M\omega)=2.0901\,\text{Å}^2/(M[\text{amu}]\cdot\hbar\omega[\text{meV}])$. An Si optical phonon (28.09 amu, about 64 meV) gives an amplitude of 0.034 Å and a graphene optical phonon (12.01 amu, about 196 meV) 0.030 Å, against bond lengths of 1.4 to 2.5 Å (phonon energies are literature values, illustrative). This smallness is what justifies both the harmonic expansion and the linear coupling of (G.1).

Derivation: Giustino's Appendix B in a few lines

Define complex normal coordinates

$$z_{\bq\nu}=N_p^{-1/2}\sum_{\kappa\alpha p}e^{-i\bq\cdot\bR_p}(M_\kappa/M_0)^{1/2}e^*_{\kappa\alpha,\nu}(\bq)\,\Delta\tau_{\kappa\alpha p}. \tag{G.B1}$$

With (G.18) they obey

$$z_{-\bq\nu}=z^*_{\bq\nu}, \tag{G.B2}$$

and (G.16), (G.A1) invert (G.B1) into

$$\Delta\tau_{\kappa\alpha p}=N_p^{-1/2}(M_0/M_\kappa)^{1/2}\sum_{\bq\nu}e^{i\bq\cdot\bR_p}e_{\kappa\alpha,\nu}(\bq)\,z_{\bq\nu}. \tag{G.B3}$$

Because of (G.B2), $z_{\bq\nu}$ and $z_{-\bq\nu}$ are not independent. Giustino splits the grid into the set $\mathcal A$ of inversion-invariant points ($-\bq=\bq+\bG$, such as Γ and the zone-face centres), where $z_{\bq\nu}$ is real, and the sets $\mathcal B$ and $\mathcal C=-\mathcal B$ of pairs. Writing $z_{\bq\nu}=x_{\bq\nu}+iy_{\bq\nu}$ for $\bq\in\mathcal B$ leaves exactly $3MN_p$ real coordinates, and (G.19) becomes a sum of real oscillators. Real ladder operators are kept on $\mathcal A$ (G.B13), and circular combinations assign a definite momentum to each quantum on $\mathcal B$ and $\mathcal C$:

$$\hat a_{\bq\nu}=(\hat a_{\bq\nu,x}+i\hat a_{\bq\nu,y})/\sqrt2\qquad\text{for }\bq\text{ in }\mathcal B,\mathcal C. \tag{G.B14}$$

In this basis

$$z_{\bq\nu}=l_{\bq\nu}\left(\hat a_{\bq\nu}+\hat a^\dagger_{-\bq\nu}\right), \tag{G.B15}$$

and inserting (G.B15) into (G.B3) gives (G.20). The EPP manuscript takes the compact complex route instead: its (E.72) pairs $a_{\bk\alpha}$ with $a^+_{-\bk\alpha}$ from the start, and the anomalous terms $a_{\bk\alpha}a_{-\bk\alpha}$ and $a^+_{-\bk\alpha}a^+_{\bk\alpha}$ cancel in the Hamiltonian because $\omega_\alpha(-\bk)=\omega_\alpha(\bk)$.

Physical picture: a phonon is not an oscillating atom

In a state with a definite number of phonons $n_{\bq\nu}$ the mean displacement vanishes, $\langle\Delta\tau\rangle=0$; only the fluctuations $\langle\Delta\tau^2\rangle\propto2n_{\bq\nu}+1$ survive. The classical running wave animated below is the mean displacement in a coherent state, which is a superposition of many phonon numbers. Zero-point motion is not a bookkeeping constant: it is what the Fan–Migdal and Debye–Waller self-energies of §A.7 turn into the zero-point renormalization of band gaps (§A.8).

The same lattice in the EPP manuscript

Section 1 of the EPP manuscript derives the same theory in what it calls three steps: a lattice Fourier transform (E Eqs. 7–17), a mass scaling followed by a unitary rotation onto the polarization vectors (E Eqs. 18–45), and quantization with ladder operators (E Eqs. 46–91). Its force constants come from a pair potential with the electronic degrees of freedom frozen. The notation differs: cell $i$, atom ${\rm a}$ with physical mass $m_{\rm a}$ and no reference mass, Cartesian index $\mu$, branch $\alpha$, and a phonon wavevector called $\bk$ in §1 and $\bq$ from §2 on. Its dynamical matrix and its mass-scaled form are

$$\Omega^2_{{\rm a}\mu{\rm b}\nu}(\bk)=\sum_{\boldsymbol\delta}e^{i\bk\boldsymbol\delta}\,k_{{\rm a}\mu{\rm b}\nu}(\boldsymbol\delta), \tag{E.15}$$
$$\tilde\Omega^2_{{\rm a}\mu{\rm b}\nu}(\bk)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{m_{\rm a}m_{\rm b}}}\,\Omega^2_{{\rm a}\mu{\rm b}\nu}(\bk), \tag{E.24}$$

where $k$ is the elastic (force-constant) matrix and $\boldsymbol\delta=\bR^0_i-\bR^0_j$ points from the cell $j$ of atom ${\rm b}$ to the cell $i$ of atom ${\rm a}$ (E Eq. 16). The $\Omega^2$ of (E.15) has the units of a force constant; only $\tilde\Omega^2$ is a squared frequency, and neither has anything to do with the cell volume $\Omega$ used elsewhere on this page. The manuscript illustrates the unitary step with the matrix $\tilde\Omega^2=\left[\begin{smallmatrix}3&2\\2&3\end{smallmatrix}\right]$, whose eigenpairs are

$$\omega_1^2=1,\ \ \mathbf e_1=\frac1{\sqrt2}\begin{bmatrix}1\\-1\end{bmatrix};\qquad \omega_2^2=5,\ \ \mathbf e_2=\frac1{\sqrt2}\begin{bmatrix}1\\1\end{bmatrix}. \tag{E.30}$$

The manuscript calls this matrix hypothetical and attaches no model to it. Our reading: in units of eV Å⁻² amu⁻¹ it is exactly the zone-edge ($qa=\pi$) dynamical matrix of the chain above with $M_1=M_2=1$ amu, $K_1=0.5$ eV/Å² and $K_2=2.5$ eV/Å², which is how the third preset of the figure reproduces it. The soft mode $\mathbf e_1$ stretches only the weak intracell spring, the stiff mode $\mathbf e_2$ only the intercell one. Quantization with ladder operators (E.72–E.78) then gives the displacement operator (E.83), which is Giustino's (G.20) with $M_0$ cancelled, while (E.78) is (G.22); §B.1 displays it and follows EPP's three steps in detail.

Bridge to EPP: same phonons, different role

The algebra is identical, but the two papers feed it different force constants. Giustino's are Born–Oppenheimer derivatives of the DFT total energy, long-range dipole–dipole tail included. EPP's bare phonons may contain only the short-range (analytic) part, because photon exchange regenerates the rest, LO–TO splitting included: this is the double-counting rule of §B.1. The same three-step recipe later quantizes the transverse photon field (§B.4).

Dictionary: Giustino's cell $p$, atom $\kappa$, Cartesian $\alpha$ and branch $\nu$ are EPP's $i$, ${\rm a}$, $\mu$ and $\alpha$, so $\alpha$ is Cartesian in one paper and a branch label in the other. To avoid a later clash with EPP's photon propagator $D$, this page writes Giustino's phonon Green function as $\mathcal D$ (from §A.5); the dynamical matrix keeps its superscript, $D^{\rm dm}$.

Note on the source: phase convention and on-site term in EPP §1

With $\boldsymbol\delta=\bR^0_i-\bR^0_j$ as defined, the printed (E.15) equals Giustino's $D^{\rm dm}(-\bq)=D^{\rm dm}(\bq)^*$. On p. 9 the manuscript diagonalizes the potential energy using a claimed symmetry $\tilde\Omega^2_{{\rm b}\nu{\rm a}\mu}(\bk)=\tilde\Omega^2_{{\rm a}\mu{\rm b}\nu}(\bk)$, but the matrix is only Hermitian. The step holds where $\tilde\Omega^2$ is real (at Γ and at the other time-reversal-invariant points, such as the zone edge of the chain, which is why (E.30) is unaffected); elsewhere it needs $e^{-i\bk\boldsymbol\delta}$ in (E.15). Frequencies do not change, but eigenvectors of the printed matrix are the complex conjugates of those that solve the equations of motion with the $e^{+i\bk\bR^0_i}$ pattern of (E.83). The figure uses Giustino's convention, $D^{\rm dm}_{12}=-(K_1+K_2e^{-iqa})/\sqrt{M_1M_2}$.

Two smaller points. (E.4) gives the elastic matrix of a pair potential only for $i{\rm a}\neq j{\rm b}$; the on-site block, $k_{i{\rm a}\mu,i{\rm a}\nu}=-\sum_{j{\rm b}\neq i{\rm a}}k_{i{\rm a}\mu,j{\rm b}\nu}$, follows from the acoustic sum rule, which §1 never states. And (E.78) is said to describe $3\times N\times s$ oscillators, but the three $\bk=0$ acoustic modes have $\omega=0$ and must be left out of (E.72) and (E.83), as Giustino does. The manuscript also calls $\omega^2_\alpha(-\bk)=\omega^2_\alpha(\bk)$ an "isotropy property"; it follows from the reality of the force constants, i.e. time reversal.

A.2Giustino §I–II, §III.B · Eqs. 1–11, 38

The electron–phonon Hamiltonian and a century of $g$

Giustino's review is built around one model Hamiltonian with three sets of parameters. Read it term by term, see what it leaves out, and follow nearly nine decades of attempts to compute its coupling $g$, most of them lessons in how electrons screen a moving ion.

An electron moving through a crystal feels the periodic potential of the ions. If one ion is displaced by a small $\mathbf u$, the potential changes by about $-\mathbf u\cdot\nabla V$, and this perturbation can scatter the electron from $\bk$ to $\bk+\bq$ while a phonon of wavevector $\bq$ is absorbed or one of wavevector $-\bq$ is emitted. Every formula below refines that sentence in one of two ways: how large $\mathbf u$ is for a quantum oscillator, and which potential $V$ is differentiated, from the bare ionic potential to the one left after all other electrons have rearranged to screen it.

Reading Eq. (1) term by term

Giustino states the "standard form" of the coupled electron–phonon Hamiltonian at the start of his historical section (Giustino §II, Eq. (G.1)). Like all of Part A it is written in SI units, and every potential $V$ is the potential energy of an electron, so $g$ and $g^{\rm DW}$ have units of energy:

$$\begin{aligned} \hat H={}&\sum_{n\bk}\varepsilon_{n\bk}\hat c^\dagger_{n\bk}\hat c_{n\bk}+\sum_{\bq\nu}\hbar\omega_{\bq\nu}\big(\hat a^\dagger_{\bq\nu}\hat a_{\bq\nu}+1/2\big)\\ &+N_p^{-1/2}\sum_{\substack{\bk,\bq\\ mn\nu}}g_{mn\nu}(\bk,\bq)\,\hat c^\dagger_{m\bk+\bq}\hat c_{n\bk}\big(\hat a_{\bq\nu}+\hat a^\dagger_{-\bq\nu}\big)\\ &+\Big[N_p^{-1}\sum_{\substack{\bk,\bq,\bq'\\ mn\nu\nu'}}g^{\rm DW}_{mn\nu\nu'}(\bk,\bq,\bq')\,\hat c^\dagger_{m\bk+\bq+\bq'}\hat c_{n\bk}\\ &\qquad\times\big(\hat a_{\bq\nu}+\hat a^\dagger_{-\bq\nu}\big)\big(\hat a_{\bq'\nu'}+\hat a^\dagger_{-\bq'\nu'}\big)\Big] \end{aligned}\tag{G.1}$$
  • Line 1 holds two independent subsystems: band electrons with energies $\varepsilon_{n\bk}$ and fermion operators $\hat c^\dagger,\hat c$, and harmonic phonons with energies $\hbar\omega_{\bq\nu}$ and boson operators $\hat a^\dagger,\hat a$ (§A.1). $N_p$ is the number of unit cells in the Born–von Kármán supercell.
  • Line 2 is linear in the atomic displacements: $\hat a_{\bq\nu}+\hat a^\dagger_{-\bq\nu}$, times the zero-point length $l_{\bq\nu}$, is the normal coordinate of mode $\bq\nu$ (Eqs. (G.20)–(G.21)). An electron in $n\bk$ goes to $m\bk+\bq$ by absorbing a phonon $\bq\nu$ or emitting a phonon $-\bq\nu$, so crystal momentum is conserved up to a reciprocal-lattice vector.
  • Lines 3–4 are second order in the displacements, bracketed because this term "is rarely found in the early literature". To first order in perturbation theory only $\bq'=-\bq$, $\nu'=\nu$ survives, giving the static band shift $\Delta\varepsilon_{n\bk}=N_p^{-1}\sum_{\bq\nu}g^{\rm DW}_{nn\nu\nu}(\bk,\bq,-\bq)(2n_{\bq\nu}+1)$ (Giustino p. 10, unnumbered). It is finite at $T=0$ and essential for temperature-dependent band gaps (§A.8).

What Eq. (1) leaves out

Eq. (G.1) has no electron–electron interaction, no ion–ion interaction, no vector potential and no photons. Yet electrons and nuclei interact only through electromagnetic forces, so each Coulomb interaction must be hidden in one of the three parameter sets:

InteractionHidden inHow Giustino obtains it
electron–electronband energies $\varepsilon_{n\bk}$Hartree and xc potentials of Kohn–Sham theory (G.24–28), or quasiparticle corrections
ion–ion, screened by electronsphonon frequencies $\omega_{\bq\nu}$force constants of the clamped-ion electronic ground state (G.12–15), adiabatic; §A.1
electron–ioncouplings $g$, $g^{\rm DW}$screened first and second derivatives of $V^{\rm en}$ (G.38, G.40); §A.3
transverse field (photons)nowherelight appears later only as a classical external field; §A.9

Eq. (G.1) is therefore an effective model in which the Coulomb field has been integrated out, statically and longitudinally, into screened parameters. Giustino names its assumptions: well-defined quasiparticles, harmonic and adiabatic phonons, and no prescription for the parameters. In his words, "the history of the study of electron-phonon interactions is really the history of how to calculate the parameters entering Eq. (1) using procedures that can be at once rigorous, reliable, and practical." The many-body justification, with the lattice placed inside the screened interaction $W$, comes in §A.5.

Bridge to EPP · putting the field back

EPP §2 starts from the same first three terms, built from bare quantities, plus an explicit bare electron–electron Coulomb term (Eq. (E.109)). Its bare vertex $g^0$ (Eq. (E.107)) is the rigid-ion vertex of the derivation below, written for general Bloch states as a sum over $\bG$. EPP then puts the field back: Coulomb becomes the energy of the longitudinal field (EPP §4.4, Eq. (E.235)) and transverse photons couple to electronic and ionic currents. Its Lagrangian (Eq. (E.134)) contains no $g$. The polar coupling arises from exchanging a longitudinal or transverse photon between an electron and a Born-charge dipole, the short-range rigid-ion channel of §2 is left out, and there is no Debye–Waller vertex (the diamagnetic $A^2$ contact terms are only an analogue). Notation: EPP puts $N^{-1/2}$ inside $g$ and writes $c^\dagger_{n\bk}c_{m\bk-\bq}$, so $g^{\rm EPP}_{nm}(\bk,\bq)=N^{-1/2}g^{\rm G}_{nm}(\bk-\bq,\bq)$. See §X.1, §B.1, §B.2.

Anatomy of $g$: zero-point amplitude times a potential gradient

Giustino derives line 2 in §III.B.2. Expanding the Kohn–Sham potential to first order in the displacements and inserting the phonon expansion (G.20) yields the coupling Hamiltonian (G.37) with the matrix element

$$ g_{mn\nu}(\bk,\bq)=\langle u_{m\bk+\bq}|\Delta_{\bq\nu}v^{\rm KS}|u_{n\bk}\rangle_{\rm uc}, \tag{G.38}$$

an integral over one unit cell between the lattice-periodic Bloch parts $u_{n\bk}$. The scattering potential is

$$ \Delta_{\bq\nu}v^{\rm KS}=l_{\bq\nu}\sum_{\kappa\alpha}(M_0/M_\kappa)^{1/2}e_{\kappa\alpha,\nu}(\bq)\,\partial_{\kappa\alpha,\bq}v^{\rm KS}, \tag{G.34}$$

where $\partial_{\kappa\alpha,\bq}v^{\rm KS}$ (G.35) is the lattice-periodic part of the response to displacing atom $\kappa$ along $\alpha$ in every cell with phase $e^{i\bq\cdot\bR_p}$, and $l_{\bq\nu}=[\hbar/(2M_0\omega_{\bq\nu})]^{1/2}$ is the zero-point length (G.21). Because $l_{\bq\nu}(M_0/M_\kappa)^{1/2}=(\hbar/2M_\kappa\omega_{\bq\nu})^{1/2}$, the reference mass $M_0$ cancels and, schematically,

$$ g\;\sim\;\underbrace{\Big(\frac{\hbar}{2M_\kappa\omega_{\bq\nu}}\Big)^{1/2}}_{\text{zero-point amplitude (Å)}}\times\underbrace{\mathbf e_{\kappa\nu}\cdot\Big\langle\frac{\partial V}{\partial\boldsymbol\tau_\kappa}\Big\rangle}_{\text{potential gradient (eV/Å)}}.$$

With the zero-point amplitudes of §A.1 (0.034 Å for a silicon optical phonon, against a 2.35 Å Si–Si bond; literature values, illustrative) the linear expansion is safe, and a gradient of a few eV/Å gives $|g|\sim0.1$ eV.

The physics sits in the choice of $\partial V$. In the rigid-ion approximation $V^{\rm KS}\to V^{\rm en}$: each displaced ion carries its bare potential with it, and $\partial_{\kappa\alpha,\bq}v^{\rm en}$ is known analytically (G.43). In the self-consistent picture the other electrons respond, and the induced Hartree and xc terms of $\partial v^{\rm KS}=\partial v^{\rm en}+\partial v^{\rm H}+\partial v^{xc}$ (G.42) largely cancel the bare change. §A.3 shows that the result is $\partial v^{\rm KS}=(\epsilon^{{\rm H}xc})^{-1}\partial v^{\rm en}$ (G.53): the bare vertex screened by a static RPA+xc dielectric matrix. The history below is the slow discovery of that statement.

Note on the source · where $N_p$ goes

Eqs. (G.1) and (G.37) put $N_p^{-1/2}$ in front of the coupling, and (G.38) defines $g$ as an $N_p$-independent unit-cell integral. Eqs. (G.2), (G.57), (G.58), (G.61) and (G.180) nevertheless carry $N_p$ inside the square root, $(\hbar/2N_pM_\kappa\omega_{\bq\nu})^{1/2}$; inserted into (G.1) they would count $N_p^{-1/2}$ twice. Part A follows the (G.38) convention and drops $N_p$ from those formulas; EPP makes the other consistent choice, $N^{-1/2}$ inside $g$.

Derivation: Bloch, Nordheim and Bardeen from (G.38) (Giustino §III.B.5)

Take the rigid-ion potential, one atom per cell at $\boldsymbol\tau_\kappa=0$, and free-electron Bloch parts $u_{n\bk}=\Omega^{-1/2}e^{i\bG_n\cdot\br}$. The bare perturbation is

$$ \partial_{\kappa\alpha,\bq}v^{\rm en}(\bG)=-i(\bq+\bG)_\alpha V_\kappa(\bq+\bG)\,e^{-i(\bq+\bG)\cdot\boldsymbol\tau_\kappa}. \tag{G.43}$$

With Giustino's Fourier convention, $f(\br)=\sum_\bG f(\bG)e^{i\bG\cdot\br}$, the unit-cell integral picks a single component, $\langle u_{m\bk+\bq}|f|u_{n\bk}\rangle_{\rm uc}=f(\bG_m-\bG_n)$. Inserting this and (G.34) into (G.38) gives

$$ g_{mn\nu}(\bk,\bq)=-i\Big(\frac{\hbar}{2M_\kappa\omega_{\bq\nu}}\Big)^{1/2}V_\kappa(\bq+\bG_m-\bG_n)\,(\bq+\bG_m-\bG_n)\cdot\mathbf e_{\kappa\nu}(\bq),$$

which is Eq. (G.57) without the $N_p$. Without umklapp ($\bG_m=\bG_n$) it reduces to $-i(\hbar/2M_\kappa\omega_{\bq\nu})^{1/2}\,\bq\cdot\mathbf e_{\kappa\nu}(\bq)\,V_\kappa(\bq)$ (cf. G.58): Nordheim's matrix element, and Bloch's after $V_\kappa\to V_0$. For a Coulomb ion $|g|\propto q^{-1}\omega_{\bq}^{-1/2}\propto q^{-3/2}$ for acoustic phonons. Screening the perturbation with the free-electron Lindhard function (G.59–60, §A.3) replaces $V_\kappa(q)$ by $V_\kappa(q)/\epsilon(q)$ (cf. G.61), which is Bardeen's result. Its long-wavelength limit follows from $k_{\rm TF}^2=e^2N(\varepsilon_F)/\epsilon_0$, with $N(\varepsilon_F)=m_ek_F/(\pi^2\hbar^2)$ states per volume (both spins), and $n=Z/\Omega=k_F^3/3\pi^2$:

$$ \lim_{q\to0}\frac{V_\kappa(q)}{\epsilon(q)}=-\frac{Ze^2}{\epsilon_0\Omega k_{\rm TF}^2}=-\frac{n}{N(\varepsilon_F)}=-\frac{\hbar^2k_F^2}{3m_e}=-\frac23\varepsilon_F .$$

No factor of $N_p$ appears anywhere in this derivation, which confirms the source note above.

A century of $V_0$

Bloch (1929) wrote the first matrix element, for free electrons with $\varepsilon_{n\bk}=\hbar^2\bk^2/2m_e-\varepsilon_F$ scattered by Debye phonons with $\omega_{\bq\nu}=v_s|\bq|$. In modern notation, and with $N_p$ removed as explained above (cf. Eq. (G.2)), it reads

$$ g_{mn\nu}(\bk,\bq)=-i\left(\frac{\hbar}{2M_\kappa\omega_{\bq\nu}}\right)^{1/2}\bq\cdot\mathbf e_{\kappa\nu}(\bq)\,V_0 .$$

$V_0$ is the unit-cell average of the "effective" potential felt by the electrons. The polarization factor $\bq\cdot\mathbf e_{\kappa\nu}$ means that, without umklapp, only longitudinal sound waves scatter electrons. The rest of Giustino §II.A is a list of what to put in place of $V_0$.

For simple metals the ladder has four rungs:

  • Bloch argued from a deformable continuum that $V_0=\hbar^2/(16m_ea_0^2)\approx1.70$ eV, with $a_0$ the Bohr radius.
  • Nordheim (1931) replaced $V_0$ by the Fourier component of the bare ion, $V_\kappa(\bq)=-Z_\kappa e^2/(\epsilon_0\Omega|\bq|^2)$ in Giustino's per-cell convention. This rigid-ion model diverges as $q^{-2}$ and "leads to unrealistically strong EPIs".
  • Mott and Jones (1936) integrated $V_\kappa(\br)$ over one Wigner–Seitz cell only, "the first attempt at including the electronic screening of the nuclear potential in a rudimentary form". For a Wigner–Seitz sphere of radius $R_{\rm WS}$ this gives $V_\kappa(q)[1-\cos(qR_{\rm WS})]$ (our closed form; Giustino describes the model only in words). It is finite as $q\to0$, but its limit $-\tfrac32 Z_\kappa e^2/(4\pi\epsilon_0R_{\rm WS})$ is, for Al, Na and K, about five times deeper than the screened value found next.
  • Bardeen (1937) screened the ion with the static Lindhard function, computed self-consistently in linearized Hartree theory, a strategy "similar in spirit to modern DFPT calculations":
$$ V_0\to V_\kappa(\bq)/\epsilon(q), \tag{G.3}$$
$$ \epsilon(q)=1+(k_{\rm TF}/q)^2F(q/2k_{\rm F}), \tag{G.4}$$
$$ F(x)=\frac12+\frac{1-x^2}{4x}\ln\left|\frac{1+x}{1-x}\right| .$$

$k_{\rm F}$ is the Fermi wavevector and $k_{\rm TF}$ the Thomas–Fermi wavevector, $k_{\rm TF}^2=4k_{\rm F}/(\pi a_0)$ (the expression given after (G.60), rewritten with the Bohr radius $a_0$). $F(0)=1$ and $F(1)=\tfrac12$, but $dF/dx$ diverges logarithmically at $x=1$, that is at $q=2k_{\rm F}$.

Physical picture · why screening removes the divergence

As $q\to0$ the Lindhard function behaves as $\epsilon\to(k_{\rm TF}/q)^2$, which cancels the $1/q^2$ of the ion exactly. What is left is $V_\kappa/\epsilon\to-\tfrac23\varepsilon_F$: $-7.80$ eV in Al, $-2.16$ eV in Na, $-1.41$ eV in K. The Fermi sea screens a slowly varying potential perfectly, and only a local shift of the Fermi level survives. Indeed, for jellium $\Omega\,\partial\varepsilon_F/\partial\Omega=-\tfrac23\varepsilon_F$: Bardeen's long-wavelength screened ion is the free-electron deformation potential of Eq. (G.6) below (our check, not stated by Giustino). An insulator screens with a finite $\epsilon$, so a dipolar $1/q$ part can survive: the polar coupling of Eq. (G.7).

Bardeen–Pines: the first retarded vertex

Bardeen and Pines (1955), following Nakajima (1954), treated the electron–phonon problem field-theoretically for the first time. They found that the potential felt by an electron depends on how fast the ion moves, so the Lindhard function must be evaluated at the phonon frequency (Giustino §II.A.1):

$$ V_0\to V_\kappa(\bq)/\epsilon(q,\omega_{\bq\nu}). \tag{G.5}$$

This is the first retarded electron–phonon vertex, where "retarded" means, in Giustino's usage, a frequency-dependent electronic screening. Bardeen and Pines also included screened exchange. Giustino remarks: "Somewhat surprisingly, this development was not followed up in the literature on ab initio calculations of EPIs."

For acoustic phonons the static approximation is excellent. With $u=\omega/(qv_F)=v_s/v_F\approx3\times10^{-3}$, the dynamic Lindhard function has ${\rm Re}\,\epsilon(q,\omega)=\epsilon(q,0)+O(u^2)$ and ${\rm Im}\,\epsilon\approx\tfrac{\pi}{2}(k_{\rm TF}/q)^2u$ for $q<2k_{\rm F}$ (standard RPA, not printed by Giustino). The imaginary part is Landau damping by electron–hole pairs: a small phase of the vertex ($3\times10^{-3}$ at $q=k_{\rm F}$ in Al, see the readout) and a phonon linewidth. Dynamic screening matters only when $\omega\gtrsim qv_F$, as for optical phonons at small $q$ in doped semiconductors or graphene (§A.6).

Bridge to EPP · the electrostatic precursor

Eq. (G.5) is the scalar, longitudinal ancestor of what EPP does. EPP's bare and screened vertices $g^{\rm dyn,0}$ and $g^{\rm dyn}$ (EPP §7.2, Eqs. (E.415)–(E.416)) depend on frequency. For $c\to\infty$ the screened one reduces to the Verdi–Giustino vertex with $\epsilon^\infty$ replaced by a dynamic RPA tensor $\hat\epsilon^{\rm e}(\bq,\omega)$, and the bare one to the same vertex without electronic screening. The replacement $g(\omega)\to g(0)$ that Giustino later makes in the phonon self-energy (§A.6) discards exactly this dependence, and EPP keeps it (§B.8). In EPP "retardation" also has a second meaning, the finite speed of light in the photon propagator (§X.1).

Semiconductors and ionic crystals

In semiconductors the carriers sit near band extrema, so the dominant scattering involves long-wavelength phonons. Bardeen and Shockley (1950) considered long acoustic waves, which look locally like a uniform strain, and showed that $V_0$ can then be replaced by a deformation potential (Giustino §II.A.2):

$$ V_0\to E_{1,n\bk}=\Omega\,\partial\varepsilon_{n\bk}/\partial\Omega . \tag{G.6}$$

A local dilation $\Delta\Omega/\Omega$ shifts the band edge by $E_1\Delta\Omega/\Omega$, and with $\omega=v_sq$ this again gives $|g|\propto q^{1/2}$. $E_1$ was fitted to mobility data, so the method "lacks predictive power". In ionic crystals the displacements create long-range electric fields, and Fröhlich, Pelzer and Zienau (1950) found (Giustino §II.A.3)

$$ V_0\to-\left[\frac{e^2M_\kappa\omega^2_{\bq\nu}}{\epsilon_0\Omega}\left(\frac{1}{\epsilon^\infty}-\frac{1}{\epsilon^0}\right)\right]^{1/2}\frac{1}{|\bq|^2}, \tag{G.7}$$

with $\epsilon_0$ the vacuum permittivity and $\epsilon^0$, $\epsilon^\infty$ the static and high-frequency relative permittivities. For an LO mode ($\omega_{\bq\nu}=\omega_{\rm LO}$, $\bq\cdot\mathbf e=|\bq|$) the mass cancels against the Bloch prefactor:

$$ |g^{\rm Fr}(\bq)|=\frac{1}{|\bq|}\left[\frac{e^2\hbar\omega_{\rm LO}}{2\epsilon_0\Omega}\left(\frac{1}{\epsilon^\infty}-\frac{1}{\epsilon^0}\right)\right]^{1/2}.$$

The $1/q$ survives because an insulator screens with a finite $\epsilon^\infty$ rather than the metallic $(k_{\rm TF}/q)^2$, and $1/\epsilon^\infty-1/\epsilon^0$ is the ionic part of the screening; the singular coupling is what dresses carriers into Fröhlich polarons (§A.7, §A.8). §A.4 derives the general Born-charge form (G.180) and ties it to the LO–TO splitting.

Note on the source · Eq. (7)

Eq. (G.7) uses $\epsilon_0$ (subscript, vacuum permittivity) next to $\epsilon^0$ (superscript, static relative permittivity), and the sentence after it writes the divergence condition with subscripts, as $\epsilon_0>\epsilon_\infty$; it should read $\epsilon^0>\epsilon^\infty$. Since (G.2) is a one-atom formula, the factor $M_\kappa\omega^2_{\bq\nu}$ in (G.7) only cancels the mass; in a real diatomic crystal the masses enter through the LO eigenvector and still cancel, so the mass-free $|g^{\rm Fr}|$ is the form to use.

From Bardeen to DFPT

Pseudopotentials made the rigid-ion approach quantitative beyond the alkali metals: Phillips and Kleinman (1959) turned orthogonality to the cores into a repulsive potential, which Cohen and Heine (1961) showed largely cancels the nuclear attraction, and Sham (1961) showed how to obtain $g$ from local pseudopotentials moving rigidly with their cores, "an improved version of the rigid-ion approximation". Density-functional theory removed the rigid-ion assumption. Chang et al., Dacorogna, Cohen and Lam (1985–86) computed $g$ as Giustino's Eq. (G.11), identical to (G.38), from frozen phonons in a supercell, "ab initio since only information about the Al atom, i.e., the atomic number and atomic mass, is used as input." The self-consistent $\Delta_{\bq\nu}v^{\rm KS}$ includes the rearrangement of the electronic charge. Density-functional perturbation theory (1987–1992) then delivered it at any $\bq$ from a single unit cell, a saving of order $N_p^2$ (§A.3). Put free electrons back into (G.38) and Bloch, Nordheim and Bardeen reappear (see the derivation above): the century of models is contained in one formula.

What is still static and electrostatic

Apart from (G.5), every vertex here, DFPT included, uses static screening: $\partial v^{\rm en}$ is frequency independent and phonons are quasistatic (Giustino p. 12). And the screening field is always the instantaneous, longitudinal Coulomb interaction, with no transverse field and no ionic current. Giustino §IV (§A.5) lifts the first restriction; the EPP formalism (Part B) lifts the second.

A.3Giustino §III.B.2–B.5 · Eqs. 23–61

DFPT: the vertex is screened

When an ion moves, the electrons move with it. Density-functional perturbation theory computes the self-consistent result one wavevector at a time, and the answer is the bare electron–ion perturbation screened by a static dielectric matrix: the same $\epsilon=1-v\chi^0$ that a GW or BSE code builds, plus exchange and correlation.

Displace sublattice $\kappa$ by a small wave, $\Delta\tau_{\kappa\alpha p}\propto e^{i\bq\cdot\bR_p}$. Each ion carries its bare potential along, and that change alone, $\partial V^{\rm en}$, would scatter electrons far too strongly (Nordheim's model, §A.2). But the electrons respond: charge flows toward the regions the ions have made more attractive, and the Hartree and exchange–correlation potential of the induced charge cancels most of the bare change. What an electron finally feels, and what enters $g_{mn\nu}(\bk,\bq)$, is the self-consistent remainder. Giustino §III.B builds it from Kohn–Sham theory and condenses it into one line, $\partial v^{\rm KS}=(\epsilon^{{\rm H}xc})^{-1}\partial v^{\rm en}$ (G.53). As in all of Part A, units are SI and every $V$ or $v$ is the potential energy of an electron of charge $-e$.

A self-consistent potential, one wavevector at a time

The electrons obey the Kohn–Sham equation with $\hat H^{\rm KS}=-\hbar^2\nabla^2/2m_e+V^{\rm KS}$ (G.23), whose potential has three parts:

$$ V^{\rm KS}=V^{\rm en}+V^{\rm H}+V^{xc}. \tag{G.24}$$

$V^{\rm en}$ sums ionic potentials with the Coulomb tail $-(e^2/4\pi\epsilon_0)Z_\kappa/|\br|$ (G.25–26), $V^{\rm H}$ is the instantaneous Coulomb potential of the density (G.27) and $V^{xc}=\delta E^{xc}/\delta n$ (G.28). There is no vector potential anywhere: the electrons see the nuclei only through electrostatics. To first order in the displacements,

$$ V^{\rm KS}(\{\boldsymbol\tau_{\kappa p}\})=V^{\rm KS}(\{\boldsymbol\tau^0_{\kappa p}\})+\sum_{\kappa\alpha p}\frac{\partial V^{\rm KS}}{\partial\tau_{\kappa\alpha p}}\Delta\tau_{\kappa\alpha p}, \tag{G.31}$$

where the derivative is the self-consistent one: $V^{\rm H}$ and $V^{xc}$ change because the density changes. For a displacement wave with phases $e^{i\bq\cdot\bR_p}$ the summed response is $e^{i\bq\cdot\br}$ times a lattice-periodic function,

$$ \partial_{\kappa\alpha,\bq}v^{\rm KS}=\sum_p e^{-i\bq\cdot(\br-\bR_p)}\,\frac{\partial V^{\rm KS}}{\partial\tau_{\kappa\alpha}}\bigg|_{\br-\bR_p}, \tag{G.35}$$

which, weighted by the normal-mode amplitudes, becomes the $\Delta_{\bq\nu}v^{\rm KS}$ of (G.34) and the matrix element (G.38) of §A.2. Linear response does not mix wavevectors, so each $\bq$ is a separate calculation in one unit cell. Frozen phonons instead take finite differences (G.41) in a supercell commensurate with $\bq$, impractically large at long wavelengths; Giustino puts the DFPT saving at a factor proportional to $N_p^2$, typically more than $10^3$.

DFPT splits the perturbation like the potential,

$$\partial_{\kappa\alpha,\bq}v^{\rm KS}=\partial_{\kappa\alpha,\bq}v^{\rm en}+\partial_{\kappa\alpha,\bq}v^{\rm H}+\partial_{\kappa\alpha,\bq}v^{xc}. \tag{G.42}$$

The bare part is known in closed form in reciprocal space,

$$\partial_{\kappa\alpha,\bq}v^{\rm en}(\bG)=-i(\bq+\bG)_\alpha\,V_\kappa(\bq+\bG)\,e^{-i(\bq+\bG)\cdot\boldsymbol\tau_\kappa}, \tag{G.43}$$

a gradient (moving the ion by $\boldsymbol\tau$ shifts $V_\kappa(\br-\boldsymbol\tau)$) times a structure factor, with $f(\bG)=\Omega^{-1}\int_{\rm uc}d\br\,e^{-i\bG\cdot\br}f(\br)$. For a Coulomb ion $V_\kappa(\bq)\propto1/q^2$, so the $\bG=0$ term grows as $1/q$: it is the long-range field of a displaced charge, and only the displacement component along $\bq+\bG$ couples. The induced parts are linear in the induced density $\partial_{\kappa\alpha,\bq}n$,

$$\begin{align} \partial_{\kappa\alpha,\bq}v^{\rm H}(\bG)&=\Omega\,v^{\rm C}(\bq+\bG)\,\partial_{\kappa\alpha,\bq}n(\bG), \tag{G.44}\\ \partial_{\kappa\alpha,\bq}v^{xc}(\bG)&=\Omega\sum_{\bG'}f^{xc}(\bq+\bG,\bq+\bG')\,\partial_{\kappa\alpha,\bq}n(\bG'), \tag{G.45} \end{align}$$

with $v^{\rm C}(\bq)=e^2/(\epsilon_0\Omega q^2)$ the Coulomb kernel per cell and $f^{xc}=\delta^2E^{xc}/\delta n(\br)\delta n(\br')$ the xc kernel (G.46), local in the LDA.

The Sternheimer equation

The induced density needs the first-order change of the occupied orbitals. Translational symmetry fixes its form, $\partial u_{v\bk,\bq}e^{i\bq\cdot\br}$ with $\partial u$ lattice periodic, and first-order perturbation theory written as a linear system, rather than as a sum over states, is the Sternheimer equation:

$$(\hat H^{\rm KS}_{\bk+\bq}-\varepsilon_{v\bk})\,\partial u_{v\bk,\bq}=-\partial_{\kappa\alpha,\bq}v^{\rm KS}\,u_{v\bk}, \tag{G.47}$$

with $\hat H^{\rm KS}_{\bk+\bq}=e^{-i(\bk+\bq)\cdot\br}\hat H^{\rm KS}e^{i(\bk+\bq)\cdot\br}$. Only occupied states $v$ appear. There is no sum over empty bands, which Giustino names as the principal advantage over standard perturbation theory. (At $\bq=0$ the first-order eigenvalue shift $\langle u_{v\bk}|\partial_{\kappa\alpha,0}v|u_{v\bk}\rangle_{\rm uc}u_{v\bk}$ joins the right-hand side; the projectors below cancel it except in metals.) The operator on the left is ill conditioned whenever an occupied state at $\bk+\bq$ lies close to $\varepsilon_{v\bk}$, and singular at an exact degeneracy. Those directions are harmless, because rotating occupied states into each other leaves the density unchanged. Giannozzi et al. (1991) therefore keep only the component in the unoccupied manifold, $\partial\tilde u=(1-\hat P^{\rm occ}_{\bk+\bq})\partial u$:

$$(\hat H^{\rm KS}_{\bk+\bq}-\varepsilon_{v\bk})\,\partial\tilde u_{v\bk,\bq}=-(1-\hat P^{\rm occ}_{\bk+\bq})\,\partial_{\kappa\alpha,\bq}v^{\rm KS}\,u_{v\bk}. \tag{G.48}$$

Since $\hat P^{\rm occ}_{\bk+\bq}\partial\tilde u=0$, adding $\alpha\hat P^{\rm occ}_{\bk+\bq}$ to the operator leaves the solution unchanged but, with $\alpha$ larger than the valence bandwidth, removes every small eigenvalue. The density response is then

$$\partial n_{\kappa\alpha,\bq}(\br)=2N_p^{-1}\sum_{v\bk}u^*_{v\bk}\,\partial\tilde u_{v\bk,\bq}, \tag{G.49}$$

where the explicit 2 comes from time-reversal symmetry and the spin factor is already inside the $\bk$ sum. Closing the loop through (G.44) and (G.45) gives a cycle much like a ground-state SCF calculation:

  1. 1 · start
    bare ionic perturbation, $\partial v^{\rm KS}=\partial v^{\rm en}$ (G.43)
  2. 2 · Sternheimer
    solve for $\partial\tilde u_{v\bk,\bq}$, every occupied $v$ and every $\bk$ (G.48)
  3. 3 · response
    induced density $\partial n_{\kappa\alpha,\bq}$ (G.49)
  4. 4 · Hartree + xc
    $\partial v^{\rm H}$ and $\partial v^{xc}$ from $\partial n$ (G.44–45)
  5. 5 · update
    new $\partial v^{\rm KS}$ (G.42); mix and return to 2 until $\partial n$ stops changing

The converged $\partial v^{\rm KS}$ also yields the force constants (G.13) of §A.1, so every DFPT phonon code "already contains all the information necessary" for $g_{mn\nu}(\bk,\bq)$ (Giustino).

The loop sums a geometric series

To see what the loop computes, Giustino expands $\partial\tilde u$ over all Kohn–Sham states, occupied and empty, and inserts it into (G.48) and (G.49). The induced density is linear in the total perturbation,

$$\partial_{\kappa\alpha,\bq}n(\br)=\int_{\rm uc}d\br'\,\chi^0_{\bq}(\br,\br')\,\partial_{\kappa\alpha,\bq}v^{\rm KS}(\br'), \tag{G.50}$$
$$\begin{aligned}\chi^0_{\bq}(\br,\br')=N_p^{-1}\sum_{mn\bk}&\frac{f_{n\bk}-f_{m\bk+\bq}}{\varepsilon_{n\bk}-\varepsilon_{m\bk+\bq}}\\ &\times u^*_{n\bk}(\br)\,u_{m\bk+\bq}(\br)\,u^*_{m\bk+\bq}(\br')\,u_{n\bk}(\br').\end{aligned} \tag{G.51}$$

This is the independent-particle polarizability of Adler and Wiser, the $\chi^0$ that a GW or BSE code assembles from a sum over empty bands, here at $\omega=0$. Writing (G.50) symbolically as $\partial n=\chi^0\partial v^{\rm KS}$, the three pieces of (G.42) combine into a self-consistency condition and its solution:

$$\begin{align} \partial v^{\rm KS}&=\partial v^{\rm en}+(v^{\rm C}+f^{xc})\chi^0\,\partial v^{\rm KS}, \tag{G.52}\\ \partial v^{\rm KS}&=(\epsilon^{{\rm H}xc})^{-1}\partial v^{\rm en}, \tag{G.53}\\ \epsilon^{{\rm H}xc}&=1-(v^{\rm C}+f^{xc})\chi^0. \tag{G.54} \end{align}$$

Iterating (G.52) from $\partial v^{\rm KS}=\partial v^{\rm en}$, without mixing, generates the Neumann series of $(\epsilon^{{\rm H}xc})^{-1}$. With $K\equiv v^{\rm C}+f^{xc}$,

$$\partial v^{\rm KS}=\big[\,1+K\chi^0+K\chi^0K\chi^0+K\chi^0K\chi^0K\chi^0+\cdots\big]\,\partial v^{\rm en}.$$

Each power adds one bubble $\chi^0$ and one interaction line $K$. Read as diagrams, the dressed vertex is the bare vertex followed by a chain of bubbles:

= + + + ⋯

Zigzag: phonon $\bq\nu$. Solid lines: Kohn–Sham electrons; a closed pair is the bubble $\chi^0$ of (G.51). Dashed: $K=v^{\rm C}+f^{xc}$. Giustino's Fig. 1(d) draws the same resummation in Dyson form, $g=g^{\rm b}+vGG\Gamma g$, with the many-body polarization $P=GG\Gamma$ in place of $\chi^0$ (Giustino §V.A.3; §A.6).

Physical picture · rounds of response

Each term is one round of response: the bare field induces a density, the Hartree and xc potential of that density induces more, and so on. In a metal at long wavelength every round overcorrects, $|K\chi^0|\simeq(k_{\rm TF}/q)^2\gg1$, so the terms alternate in sign and grow. Yet the resummed answer $1/\epsilon$ is tiny, because the Fermi sea neutralizes a slowly varying perturbation almost perfectly. (G.53) is still the right answer, but the literal series diverges, and an algorithm has to reach it another way.

The usual way is mixing. With linear mixing (standard practice, not spelled out by Giustino) each cycle updates

$$\partial v_{n+1}=(1-\beta)\,\partial v_n+\beta\big[\partial v^{\rm en}+K\chi^0\,\partial v_n\big],$$

whose fixed point is (G.53) for any $\beta$. The error shrinks by $r=1-\beta\epsilon^{{\rm H}xc}$ per cycle, so the loop converges only if $0<\beta\epsilon<2$, and at $\beta=1$ the iterates are exactly the partial sums of the series. In jellium each Fourier component decouples and $v^{\rm C}\chi^0=-(k_{\rm TF}/q)^2F(q/2k_{\rm F})$, so the loop reduces to numbers. At long wavelength $\epsilon\to(k_{\rm TF}/q)^2$, and any fixed $\beta$ fails at small enough $q$: the induced charge overshoots back and forth, the "charge sloshing" familiar from ground-state SCF cycles in metals. Kerker's preconditioner (1981; literature, not in Giustino) uses $\beta(q)=\beta_0q^2/(q^2+q_0^2)$ with $q_0\approx k_{\rm TF}$. For Thomas–Fermi screening this makes $\beta\epsilon=\beta_0$ exactly; with the Lindhard function $\beta\epsilon$ stays between about $\beta_0/2$ and $\beta_0$ at every $q$, so any $\beta_0<2$ converges.

Test electron, test charge, and your $\epsilon=1-v\chi^0$

Giustino calls $\epsilon^{{\rm H}xc}$ the "test-electron" dielectric matrix, a name hinting that the density redistribution arises both from classical electrostatics ($v^{\rm C}\chi^0$) and from quantum exchange and correlation ($f^{xc}\chi^0$). The particle that feels the screened potential is itself an electron, so it also feels the xc potential of the induced density. Neglecting $f^{xc}$ gives the "test-charge" matrix, the random-phase approximation of Pines and Bohm (1952),

$$\epsilon^{\rm H}=1-v^{\rm C}\chi^0, \tag{G.55}$$

which in a plane-wave basis reads

$$\epsilon^{\rm H}_{\bG\bG'}(\bq)=\delta_{\bG\bG'}-\Omega^2\sum_{\bG''}\chi^0_{\bG''\bG'}(\bq)\,v^{\rm C}(\bq+\bG)\,\delta_{\bG\bG''}. \tag{G.56}$$

Its off-diagonal elements are the crystal local-field effects. Together with (G.38), Eq. (G.53) says that the DFPT matrix element is the bare electron–nucleus vertex screened at the "RPA + $xc$" level. For a reader who computes $\chi^0$ for 2D materials, the dictionary is short:

  • Same matrix. (G.56) is the $\epsilon_{\bG\bG'}(\bq,\omega=0)$ of a GW or BSE code, local fields included. The static $W=\epsilon^{-1}v$ of a BSE kernel uses exactly this object.
  • Different operand. $W$ screens the electron–electron interaction; DFPT screens the electron–ion perturbation, $g=\epsilon^{-1}g^{\rm b}$ in the notation of Giustino §V.A. The phonon self-energy contains one such screened vertex and the Fan–Migdal electron self-energy two (§A.6, §A.7).
  • Test electron. DFPT keeps $f^{xc}$; the usual GW $W$ is the test-charge RPA.
  • No inversion. DFPT never forms or inverts $\epsilon$. The loop solves (G.52) iteratively, one $\bq$ at a time, without empty states.
  • Two dimensions. A monolayer needs the same truncated Coulomb kernel in DFPT as in GW (implemented by Sohier, Calandra and Mauri, 2017; literature, not in either paper). For a semiconducting sheet the static screening takes the Rytova–Keldysh form $\epsilon_{\rm 2D}(q)\simeq1+r_0q$ familiar from 2D BSE (standard result, not printed in either paper). It tends to 1 as $q\to0$, so long-wavelength perturbations are barely screened, whereas in bulk $\epsilon\to\epsilon^\infty$ or $(k_{\rm TF}/q)^2$. Together with the 2D Coulomb kernel, which goes as $1/q$ instead of $1/q^2$, this shapes the 2D phonon results of §B.10, where the same $r_0$ appears.

Subtlety · what the labels mean

"Test charge" in (G.55) is shorthand for RPA. With xc present, a classical test charge would feel $\partial v^{\rm en}+v^{\rm C}\partial n$ with $\partial n$ computed including $f^{xc}$, that is $\epsilon^{-1}=1+v^{\rm C}\chi^0[1-(v^{\rm C}+f^{xc})\chi^0]^{-1}$ (standard linear-response result, not written by Giustino), which equals $(\epsilon^{\rm H})^{-1}$ only when $f^{xc}=0$. Separately, static density response is a ground-state property: with the exact functional, DFPT would give the exact static response and force constants. Using $\partial v^{\rm KS}$ as the vertex for quasiparticles is a further approximation, which Giustino makes explicit in §V.A (approximation (iii): the many-body dielectric matrix is replaced by its DFT "RPA + $xc$" counterpart; §A.6).

Jellium: Bardeen recovered

Free electrons make (G.51) analytic. With $\varepsilon_{n\bk}=\hbar^2(\bk+\bG_n)^2/2m_e-\varepsilon_{\rm F}$ in the extended-zone scheme the polarizability is diagonal,

$$\chi^0_{\bG\bG'}(\bq)=-\frac{m_ek_{\rm F}}{\pi^2\hbar^2\Omega}\,F(|\bq+\bG|/2k_{\rm F})\,\delta_{\bG\bG'}, \tag{G.59}$$

with $F$ the Lindhard function of (G.4) and $m_ek_{\rm F}/\pi^2\hbar^2$ the density of states per volume at $\varepsilon_{\rm F}$, both spins. Inserted in (G.56) without xc, it gives the Lindhard dielectric matrix,

$$\epsilon_{\bG\bG'}(\bq)=\delta_{\bG\bG'}\Big[1+\frac{k^2_{\rm TF}}{|\bq+\bG|^2}F(|\bq+\bG|/2k_{\rm F})\Big], \tag{G.60}$$

with $k_{\rm TF}=[4m_ee^2k_{\rm F}/(4\pi\epsilon_0\pi\hbar^2)]^{1/2}$. Screening the bare one-atom matrix element with its diagonal element, following (G.53), gives Bardeen's 1937 result (cf. G.61, with $N_p$ removed as explained in §A.2):

$$g_{mn\nu}(\bk,\bq)=-i\Big(\frac{\hbar}{2M_\kappa\omega_{\bq\nu}}\Big)^{1/2}\bq\cdot\mathbf e_{\kappa\nu}(\bq)\,\frac{V_\kappa(\bq)}{\epsilon(q)}.$$

Its long-wavelength limit, $V_\kappa/\epsilon\to-\tfrac23\varepsilon_{\rm F}$, is derived and plotted in §A.2. Here we look at the same screening in real space: displacing one ion along $z$ creates the bare dipole field $-\partial_zV_\kappa$, and screening multiplies each of its Fourier components by $1/\epsilon(q)$.

Derivation: the screened dipole field in real space

Use the continuum Fourier transform $V_\kappa(\bq)=-Ze^2/(\epsilon_0q^2)$; Giustino's $\Omega^{-1}$ normalization cancels in the ratio below. Displacing the ion by $\tau$ along $z$ changes the potential by $-\tau\,\partial_zV_\kappa$, whose Fourier components $-iq_zV_\kappa(\bq)$ are the $\bG=0$ term of (G.43). In jellium (G.53) divides each by $\epsilon(q)$, so the screened perturbation is $-\partial_z$ of the screened ion potential

$$V^{\rm scr}(r)=\int\!\frac{d\bq}{(2\pi)^3}\,\frac{V_\kappa(\bq)}{\epsilon(q)}\,e^{i\bq\cdot\br}=-\frac{Ze^2}{4\pi\epsilon_0}\,\frac{2}{\pi r}\int_0^\infty\!dq\,\frac{\sin qr}{q\,\epsilon(q)}.$$

For $\epsilon=1$ this is $-Ze^2/4\pi\epsilon_0r$. Along the displacement axis $\partial v/\partial\tau_z=-dV^{\rm scr}/dr$. Dividing by the bare value $-Ze^2/(4\pi\epsilon_0r^2)$ and writing $1/\epsilon=1+(1/\epsilon-1)$ gives the surviving fraction

$$S(r)=1+\frac{2}{\pi}\int_0^\infty\!dq\,\Big[\frac{1}{\epsilon(q)}-1\Big]\Big[\frac{\sin qr}{q}-r\cos qr\Big].$$

Thomas–Fermi screening, $\epsilon=1+k_{\rm TF}^2/q^2$, gives $S=(1+k_{\rm TF}r)\,e^{-k_{\rm TF}r}$ in closed form. For the Lindhard function the figure integrates numerically (trapezoid rule, $q\le12k_{\rm F}$). With the toy xc kernel, $1/\epsilon-1\to+k_{\rm TF}^2/3q^2$ at large $q$, a slowly decaying tail. The code subtracts $(k_{\rm TF}^2/3)/(q^2+4k_{\rm F}^2)$, which has the same tail, and integrates that term analytically.

Static means adiabatic

"So far we considered only the screening of static perturbations," Giustino stresses: $\partial v^{\rm en}$ was taken to be frequency independent. Physically the phonons are treated as quasistatic perturbations, "so that at each set of instantaneous atomic positions during a vibration cycle, the electrons have enough time to readjust and reach their ground state", which is the adiabatic approximation of Born and Oppenheimer. In the diagrams above, every bubble is $\chi^0$ at $\omega=0$ rather than at the phonon frequency. That is accurate when $\hbar\omega_{\bq\nu}$ is small against the electronic excitations that build $\chi^0$ (the gap of an insulator, or $\hbar qv_{\rm F}$ for intraband transitions in a metal), and it fails otherwise. Bardeen and Pines (1955) already screened the vertex with $\epsilon(q,\omega_{\bq\nu})$ (G.5, §A.2), but the first ab initio calculations of these effects came only much later (Lazzeri and Mauri, 2006, cited by Giustino; the doped-graphene case returns in his §VII and in §A.6). "Retardation" in Giustino's sense means exactly this frequency dependence of the screening. His formal framework is §IV (§A.5), and §A.6 splits the phonon self-energy into the adiabatic part that DFPT computes and a nonadiabatic remainder built from $\chi^0(\omega)-\chi^0(0)$.

Bridge to EPP · the same chain, kept dynamic

EPP resums the same bubble chain for its photon propagator, $D^{\rm e}=D^0+D^0\Pi^{\rm e,0}_{jj}D^{\rm e}$ (EPP §7, Eq. (E.388)), and its screened electron–phonon vertex has $D^{\rm e}$ where the bare one has $D^0$ (Eqs. (E.415)–(E.416), §B.8). Three things differ from DFPT. The screening is dynamic: the dielectric tensor $\hat\epsilon^{\rm e}(\bq,\omega)$ (Eqs. (E.431)–(E.432)) keeps the frequency dependence that DFPT drops and acts on transverse as well as longitudinal photons, so in EPP "retardation" also means the finite speed of light (§X.1). It is RPA without $f^{xc}$ and without crystal local fields (no $\bG,\bG'$ dependence from Eq. (E.380) on). For $c\to\infty$ its longitudinal projection becomes the scalar RPA function $1-v\Pi^{\rm e,0}_{\rho\rho}$, which at $\omega=0$ is (G.55) without local fields (§B.9). And EPP cannot take DFPT force constants as they come: which part of them may be combined with photon exchange is its double-counting rule, set out in §B.1.

Second order: the Debye–Waller matrix element

Expanding $V^{\rm KS}$ to first order while expanding the energy (G.12) to second order is "somewhat inconsistent" (Allen and Heine, 1976; Allen, 1978), so the Hamiltonian (G.1) also carries the second-order term (G.39), with

$$g^{\rm DW}_{mn\nu\nu'}(\bk,\bq,\bq')=\tfrac12\langle u_{m\bk+\bq+\bq'}|\Delta_{\bq\nu}\Delta_{\bq'\nu'}v^{\rm KS}|u_{n\bk}\rangle_{\rm uc}. \tag{G.40}$$

It needs the second derivative of the self-consistent potential, hence second-order Sternheimer equations (Gonze, 1995). Because these are involved, practical implementations express $g^{\rm DW}$ through products of the first-order $g_{mn\nu}(\bk,\bq)$, following Allen and Heine (1976) and Allen and Cardona (1981). According to Giustino, all recent DFPT calculations of electron–phonon effects use this approach (Giustino §IX.A.1; §A.7, §A.8).

Note on the source · notation in §III.B

Notational slips in (G.55), (G.56) and (G.60), the $\Omega$ normalization of $\chi^0_{\bG\bG'}$ that (G.56) implies, and the name "screening length" for $k_{\rm TF}$ are listed in Z.2; none changes the equations as displayed here. Two smaller points: (G.49) writes $\partial n_{\kappa\alpha,\bq}$ for the $\partial_{\kappa\alpha,\bq}n$ of (G.44)–(G.45), and $V_\kappa(\bq+\bG)$ in (G.43) needs an all-space integral with the $\Omega^{-1}$ prefactor. (G.57), (G.58) and (G.61) carry $N_p$ inside the square root; see §A.2.

A.4Giustino §II.A.3, §VI.A.3 · Eqs. 7, 175–180

Polar materials: Fröhlich, Verdi–Giustino and the LO–TO splitting

Why the electron–phonon vertex of a polar crystal diverges as $1/q$, how Born charges and $\epsilon^\infty$ fix its strength, why it must be removed before Wannier interpolation, and why the same electrostatic kernel splits LO from TO phonons.

In a polar crystal a displaced ion drags a net charge along. The dipole per cell created by displacing the sublattice of atom $\kappa$, at zero macroscopic electric field, defines the Born effective charge tensor $\bZ^*_\kappa$, dimensionless (in units of $e$) in Giustino's convention. A phonon that moves atom $\kappa$ by $\Delta\boldsymbol\tau_\kappa$ therefore puts a dipole $e\bZ^*_\kappa\cdot\Delta\boldsymbol\tau_\kappa$ in every cell, with phase $e^{i\bq\cdot\bR_p}$. Giustino §II.A.3 states the consequence: in ionic crystals "the atomic displacements can generate long-ranged electric fields; these fields provide a new scattering channel for electrons and holes." Notation: $\varepsilon_0$ is the vacuum permittivity, $\epsilon^\infty$ and $\epsilon^0$ are the high-frequency (clamped-ion) and static relative permittivities, and units are SI as in Giustino.

A wave of dipoles and its field

In a longitudinal wave the dipoles point along $\bq$. Their heads converge on some planes and diverge from others, so sheets of bound charge $-\nabla\cdot\bP$ appear half a wavelength apart (figure below). Their macroscopic potential solves Poisson's equation in a medium whose electrons screen with $\epsilon^\infty$, so $\phi(\bq)\propto\bq\cdot\bP/(\bq\cdot\boldsymbol\epsilon^\infty\cdot\bq)$, which grows as $1/q$. A transverse wave has $\bq\cdot\bP=0$: no bound charge and no electrostatic potential. In real space one displaced ion is a dipole whose potential falls off as $1/r^2$. In a nonpolar insulator the screened potential of a displaced atom is at least quadrupolar, $R^{-3}$ (Giustino §VI.A.2, citing Pick, Cohen and Martin 1970), and that one power of $R$ decides everything below. In a metal the Fermi sea screens even the dipole field and the coupling stays finite (§A.2).

Why polar crystals break Wannier interpolation

Converged Brillouin-zone integrals of electron–phonon quantities can need $10^6$ wave vectors, and every DFPT calculation is "roughly as expensive as one total energy minimization" (Giustino §VI). The way out is to rotate $g$ into maximally localized Wannier functions $\mathrm w_{mp}$ (G Eqs. 175–176) and represent it in real space:

$$ g_{mn\kappa\alpha}(\bR_p,\bR_{p'})=\Big\langle \mathrm w_{m0}(\br)\Big|\frac{\partial V^{\rm KS}}{\partial\tau_{\kappa\alpha}}(\br-\bR_{p'})\Big|\mathrm w_{n0}(\br-\bR_p)\Big\rangle_{\rm sc}, \tag{G.177}$$

the amplitude for an electron to hop from Wannier function $n$ in cell $p$ to $m$ in cell 0 when atom $\kappa$ of cell $p'$ moves along $\alpha$ ("sc" denotes an integral over the Born–von Kármán supercell). A generalized Fourier transform returns it to any $(\bk,\bq)$,

$$ g_{mn\nu}(\bk,\bq)=\sum_{pp'}e^{i(\bk\cdot\bR_p+\bq\cdot\bR_{p'})}\sum_{m'n'\kappa\alpha}U_{mm'\bk+\bq}\,g_{m'n'\kappa\alpha}(\bR_p,\bR_{p'})\,U^\dagger_{n'n\bk}\,\mathrm u_{\kappa\alpha,\bq\nu}, \tag{G.178}$$

with $U_{\bk}$ the unitary rotations that define the Wannier functions, $\mathrm u_{\kappa\alpha,\bq\nu}=(\hbar/2M_\kappa\omega_{\bq\nu})^{1/2}e_{\kappa\alpha,\nu}(\bq)$, and the inverse (G.179) evaluated on a coarse DFPT grid. This works if $g(\bR_p,\bR_{p'})$ has died off inside the Wigner–Seitz supercell of the coarse grid. In $\bR_p$ it decays like the Wannier functions, exponentially in insulators. In $\bR_{p'}$ it decays like the screened potential of the displaced atom, and in a polar material that is the dipole of the figure: $|g(0,\bR_{p'})|\sim|\bR_{p'}|^{-2}$. Then $g(\bk,\bq)\sim|\bq|^{-1}$ near Γ, and no finite real-space cutoff captures it. "Physically this singularity corresponds to the 'Fröhlich electron-phonon coupling'" (Giustino §VI.A.3).

The Verdi–Giustino long-range vertex

Verdi and Giustino (2015) and Sjakste et al. (2015) split $g=g^{\mathcal S}+g^{\mathcal L}$ and obtain the long-range part from electrostatics: the potential of all Born charges displaced according to mode $\nu$, screened by the electronic permittivity tensor,

$$ \begin{aligned} g^{\mathcal L}_{mn\nu}(\bk,\bq)=i\,\frac{4\pi}{\Omega}\frac{e^2}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\sum_\kappa\Big(\frac{\hbar}{2N_pM_\kappa\omega_{\bq\nu}}\Big)^{1/2} &\sum_{\bG\neq-\bq}\frac{(\bq+\bG)\cdot\bZ^*_\kappa\cdot\be_{\kappa\nu}(\bq)}{(\bq+\bG)\cdot\boldsymbol\epsilon^\infty\cdot(\bq+\bG)}\\ &\times\big\langle\psi_{m\bk+\bq}\big|e^{i(\bq+\bG)\cdot(\br-\boldsymbol\tau_\kappa)}\big|\psi_{n\bk}\big\rangle_{\rm sc}. \end{aligned} \tag{G.180}$$

Here $\Omega$ is the unit-cell volume and $\boldsymbol\tau_\kappa$ the position of atom $\kappa$ in the cell. Each factor has a plain meaning:

  • $\frac{4\pi}{\Omega}\frac{e^2}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\big[(\bq+\bG)\cdot\boldsymbol\epsilon^\infty\cdot(\bq+\bG)\big]^{-1}$ is the instantaneous, longitudinal Coulomb interaction per cell, screened by clamped-ion electrons: the long-wavelength, static limit of $W_{\rm e}$.
  • $(\bq+\bG)\cdot\bZ^*_\kappa\cdot\be_{\kappa\nu}$ projects the mode's dipole on the wave vector; only its longitudinal part makes a potential. For acoustic modes the acoustic sum rule $\sum_\kappa\bZ^*_\kappa=0$ cancels the leading term, so the basis phase $e^{-i(\bq+\bG)\cdot\boldsymbol\tau_\kappa}$ inside the matrix element matters there (Giustino footnote 7).
  • For small $\bq+\bG$ the matrix element is interpolated as $[U_{\bk+\bq}U^\dagger_{\bk}]_{mn}$, which tends to $\delta_{mn}$: the long-range coupling is intraband and forward-scattering.
  • $\bZ^*_\kappa$ and $\boldsymbol\epsilon^\infty$ are DFPT outputs, responses to a uniform electric field (§A.3). Eq. (G.180) has no free parameter.

In practice one subtracts (G.180) from the coarse-grid DFPT $g$, Wannier-interpolates the smooth remainder $g^{\mathcal S}$, and adds (G.180) back on the fine grid. The $\bG$ sum is damped by $e^{-a|\bq+\bG|^2}$, and "the results are independent of the choice of the cutoff parameter $a$", because what the cutoff removes is short-ranged and ends up in $g^{\mathcal S}$. Giustino's Fig. 7 shows anatase TiO2: the remainder is smooth and stays below about 150 meV, while the total diverges on both sides of Γ. The laboratory below reproduces this logic in one dimension.

Note on the source · $N_p$ in (G.180)

As printed, (G.180) carries $N_p$ inside the square root, like (G.2). This page drops it, for the reason given in the note of §A.2; the magnitudes in Giustino's Fig. 7 (hundreds of meV near Γ) confirm that choice.

From Born charges back to Fröhlich

Giustino writes that the 1950 Fröhlich replacement (G.7), shown in §A.2, "is derived in Sec. VI.A.3". That section gives only (G.180) and refers to Verdi and Giustino, so the reduction is written out here. Take a cubic diatomic crystal with one polar LO mode, $\bZ^*_1=-\bZ^*_2=Z^*$, $\boldsymbol\epsilon^\infty=\epsilon^\infty$, keep $\bG=0$ and the intraband term, and set $N_p\to1$. The sum over the two atoms gives $Z^*q/\sqrt\mu$, with $\mu$ the reduced mass, and

$$ |g^{\mathcal L}(q)|=\frac{4\pi}{\Omega}\frac{e^2}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\,\frac{Z^*}{\epsilon^\infty q}\Big(\frac{\hbar}{2\mu\omega_{\rm LO}}\Big)^{1/2}=\frac1q\Big[\frac{e^2}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\frac{4\pi}{\Omega}\frac{\hbar\omega_{\rm LO}}{2}\Big(\frac1{\epsilon^\infty}-\frac1{\epsilon^0}\Big)\Big]^{1/2}.$$

The second form follows from two relations between the same ingredients, the Born-charge LO–TO splitting and the Lyddane–Sachs–Teller (LST) relation (derivation below). It is exactly (G.2) with $V_0$ from (G.7), including the overall factor $i$.

Derivation: from (G.180) to the Fröhlich vertex

1. Keep $\bG=0$ and let $\bq\to0$ in the matrix element, which becomes $\delta_{mn}$. Insert the LO eigenvector of a cubic diatomic crystal, $\be_1=(M_2/M)^{1/2}\hat\bq$, $\be_2=-(M_1/M)^{1/2}\hat\bq$ with $M=M_1+M_2$:

$$\sum_\kappa\frac{\bq\cdot\bZ^*_\kappa\cdot\be_{\kappa}}{\sqrt{M_\kappa}}=Z^*q\Big(\sqrt{\frac{M_2}{MM_1}}+\sqrt{\frac{M_1}{MM_2}}\Big)=\frac{Z^*q}{\sqrt\mu},\qquad \mu=\frac{M_1M_2}{M},$$

so that, with $\frac{4\pi}{\Omega}\frac{e^2}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}=\frac{e^2}{\varepsilon_0\Omega}$,

$$g^{\mathcal L}=\frac{i}{q}\,\frac{e^2}{\varepsilon_0\Omega}\,\frac{Z^*}{\epsilon^\infty}\Big(\frac{\hbar}{2\mu\omega_{\rm LO}}\Big)^{1/2}\delta_{mn}.$$

2. The same eigenvector, projected on the nonanalytic force constants of the next subsection, gives $\omega_{\rm LO}^2-\omega_{\rm TO}^2=e^2Z^{*2}/(\varepsilon_0\Omega\mu\epsilon^\infty)$. Use it to eliminate $Z^{*2}/\mu$:

$$|g^{\mathcal L}|^2=\frac{e^2}{\varepsilon_0\Omega q^2}\,\frac{\hbar}{2\omega_{\rm LO}}\,\frac{\omega_{\rm LO}^2-\omega_{\rm TO}^2}{\epsilon^\infty}.$$

3. LST, $\omega_{\rm TO}^2/\omega_{\rm LO}^2=\epsilon^\infty/\epsilon^0$, turns the last factor into $\omega_{\rm LO}^2(1/\epsilon^\infty-1/\epsilon^0)$, which gives the Fröhlich form above.

4. Compare (G.2), $-i(\hbar/2M_\kappa\omega_{\bq\nu})^{1/2}\,\bq\cdot\be\,V_0$, with $V_0$ from (G.7): the mass cancels, $-i\times(-1)=+i$, and the magnitude is the same. With the GaAs inputs of the explorer below, the Fröhlich route gives $|g|q=0.0321$ eV Å$^{-1}$ and the Born-charge route 0.0305 eV Å$^{-1}$. The Born charge implied by LST is 2.19 (2.18 if the measured $\hbar\omega_{\rm TO}=33.3$ meV is used instead, the value quoted in §B.1 and §B.7), against the literature value 2.07 (illustrative), so the two input sets are slightly inconsistent.

The strength is set by $1/\epsilon^\infty-1/\epsilon^0$, the part of the screening that comes from the ions. Fast perturbations are screened by electrons alone, slow ones by electrons and ions, and the difference is what an electron feels from the LO phonon. The dimensionless polaron constant $\alpha=(1/\epsilon^\infty-1/\epsilon^0)(\mathrm{Ry}\,m^*/m_e\hbar\omega_{\rm LO})^{1/2}$ (standard, not printed in Giustino) is 0.07 for the GaAs preset of the explorer and about 5 for its LiF and NaCl presets, which assume $m^*=m_e$ (illustrative). Giustino calls the $1/q$ coupling "the physical basis for the phenomenon of electron self-trapping in polarons" (§II.A.3), and self-trapping is strongest at large $\alpha$.

Physical picture · the Fröhlich vertex is the ionic part of $W$

Square the vertex and attach the LO phonon propagator of Giustino's Eq. (132), written in energy units. With $v(q)=e^2/(\varepsilon_0\Omega q^2)$ and LST one finds (derived here)

$$\frac{v(q)}{\epsilon^\infty}+|g^{\mathcal L}(q)|^2\,\frac{2\hbar\omega_{\rm LO}}{(\hbar\omega)^2-(\hbar\omega_{\rm LO})^2}=\frac{v(q)}{\epsilon(\omega)},\qquad \epsilon(\omega)=\epsilon^\infty\,\frac{\omega_{\rm LO}^2-\omega^2}{\omega_{\rm TO}^2-\omega^2}.$$

The electronically screened Coulomb line plus one-phonon exchange is the fully screened interaction, with $v/\epsilon^0$ at $\omega=0$ and $v/\epsilon^\infty$ at high frequency. This is the polar case of $W=W_{\rm e}+W_{\rm ph}$, which §A.5 derives in general.

The same kernel splits LO from TO

Giustino does not write the phonon-side partner of (G.180). Section VI.A.3 only notes that the long-range split "is analogous to that in use for calculating the splitting between longitudinal-optical (LO) and transverse-optical (TO) phonons in polar materials (Gonze and Lee, 1997)". Here is that term for orientation, from Gonze and Lee; the review does not print it. The interatomic force constants of a polar crystal have a nonanalytic part at Γ,

$$ \widetilde C^{\rm NA}_{\kappa\alpha,\kappa'\beta}(\bq\to0)=\frac{4\pi}{\Omega}\frac{e^2}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\,\frac{(\bq\cdot\bZ^*_\kappa)_\alpha\,(\bq\cdot\bZ^*_{\kappa'})_\beta}{\bq\cdot\boldsymbol\epsilon^\infty\cdot\bq}, $$

with the same Born charges and the same screened Coulomb kernel as (G.180). It depends on the direction $\hat\bq$ but not on $|\bq|$, so the limit $\bq\to0$ depends on how Γ is approached. It is added to the analytic, short-range force constants before the dynamical matrix of §A.1 is diagonalized. For the cubic diatomic crystal the LO mode is pushed up and the TO mode, with $\bq\cdot\bZ^*\cdot\be=0$, is untouched:

$$ \omega_{\rm LO}^2-\omega_{\rm TO}^2=\frac{4\pi}{\Omega}\frac{e^2}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\,\frac{Z^{*2}}{\mu\,\epsilon^\infty},\qquad \frac{\omega_{\rm LO}^2}{\omega_{\rm TO}^2}=\frac{\epsilon^0}{\epsilon^\infty}\ \ (\text{LST}).$$

LST is the $\omega=0$ value of the $\epsilon(\omega)$ in the box above, whose pole is $\omega_{\rm TO}$ and whose zero is $\omega_{\rm LO}$, where a longitudinal polarization wave needs no external charge. Eliminating $Z^*$ gives a compact statement: $|g^{\mathcal L}|^2=\frac{v(q)}{\epsilon^\infty}\,\frac{\hbar(\omega_{\rm LO}^2-\omega_{\rm TO}^2)}{2\omega_{\rm LO}}$. The Fröhlich coupling and the LO–TO splitting are one number read off two objects, the vertex and the dynamical matrix. A crystal without LO–TO splitting has no Fröhlich coupling.

Where electrostatics stops being exact

Every factor in (G.180) is electrostatic. The kernel is the instantaneous Coulomb interaction and $\epsilon^\infty$ is a static electronic response, so neither meaning of "retardation" is present: not the frequency dependence of electronic screening (Giustino's sense, §A.2) and not the finite speed of light (EPP's sense). The second matters only inside the light cone, $q\lesssim q_c=\sqrt{\epsilon^\infty}\,\omega_{\rm LO}/c$. For GaAs $q_c\approx6\times10^{-5}$ Å$^{-1}$, four orders of magnitude below the zone boundary and well below the inverse polaron radius of 0.025 Å$^{-1}$. Inside the cone a TO phonon, dark for electrostatics, still carries a polarization current that radiates a transverse field. It mixes with light into a phonon-polariton, and whether LO and TO differ at $\bq=0$ depends on the order of the limits $\bq\to0$ and $c\to\infty$. §X.1 measures the light cone, and §B.7 recovers the splitting as a photon-mediated phonon self-energy.

Bridge to EPP · the static vertex (E.131)

EPP §3 derives the same vertex, (E.131), from the potential of Born-charge point dipoles in an anisotropic dielectric, and calls it "exactly equal" to Verdi and Giustino's. §B.1 displays it in EPP's notation and lists the bookkeeping differences.

The real difference is the status of $\epsilon^\infty$. EPP puts it in "only ad hoc and later we will remove it to avoid double-counting". In the full theory the bare dipole couples to the photon field, the RPA photon self-energy regenerates electronic screening (§B.5), and $\bq\cdot\epsilon^\infty\cdot\bq$ becomes $\bq\cdot\hat\epsilon^{\rm e}(\bq,\omega)\cdot\bq$, with a transverse channel added near the light cone (§B.8). Eq. (G.180) is the $c\to\infty$, statically screened limit of that vertex.

Note on the sources · basis phase and citation

Like Eq. (4) of Verdi and Giustino (2015), EPP's (E.131) lacks the basis phase $e^{-i(\bq+\bG)\cdot\mathbf r^0_a}$ that (G.180) restores (Giustino's footnote 7). EPP also cites the 2015 PRL as by Giustino alone. See the source note in §B.1.

Subtlety · what the reduction assumes

The Fröhlich form needs one polar LO mode, isotropic $\bZ^*$ and $\epsilon^\infty$, the $\bG=0$ term and intraband scattering. Eq. (G.180) needs none of these and sums over all modes, which matters in TiO2 with its several LO branches. The classic Fröhlich model adds parabolic bands and a dispersionless LO phonon. The multipole expansion behind (G.180) also has a next term: dynamical quadrupoles give a direction-dependent but finite long-range contribution, treated analytically in work after this review. In a two-dimensional crystal the dipole sheet gives a coupling that stays finite as $q\to0$ (§B.10).

A.5Giustino §IV · Eqs. 62–122, Table I

Hedin–Baym: the lattice inside $W$

The $W$ of a GW calculation is the Coulomb interaction screened by electrons around clamped nuclei. Letting the nuclei move adds a phonon-mediated piece, $W_{\rm ph}=W_{\rm e}\mathcal DW_{\rm e}$, whose vertex is the screened gradient of the nuclear potential. Together with a Dyson equation for the phonons, this closes into the Hedin–Baym equations, the exact framework from which Giustino derives the phonon and electron self-energies used in practice (§A.6–§A.8).

Sections A.2–A.4 took the Hamiltonian (G.1) as given and computed its parameters with DFT and DFPT. Giustino §IV asks which exact theory those numbers approximate. The answer is a field theory of electrons and nuclei that interact only through the Coulomb potential, built with Schwinger's functional derivatives exactly as in Hedin's derivation of GW. Units are SI with $\hbar$ explicit. All potentials ($V_{\rm tot}$, $\varphi$, $V_\kappa$) are potential energies of an electron, and densities are counted in units of the electron charge, so $\hat n_{\rm e}\ge0$ while the nuclear density $\hat n_{\rm n}\le0$. Giustino writes both the nuclear density correlator and the phonon Green function as $D$, and the phonon self-energy as $\Pi$. On this page they are $\mathcal D$ and $\Pi^{\rm ph}$, which keeps them apart from EPP's photon propagator $D$ and photon self-energy $\Pi_{jj}$.

Physical picture · two screening clouds

Place a test charge in a polar crystal. Within a femtosecond the electrons rearrange and reduce its field by a factor $\epsilon^\infty$; that reduced interaction is the $W$ of a GW calculation. If the charge stays put for longer than a phonon period, about 0.1 ps, the ions shift too and the field drops further, to $1/\epsilon^0$ of its bare value. A moving charge therefore carries a fast electronic cloud and a slow ionic one. Hedin–Baym theory puts both clouds into one screened interaction and treats the ionic cloud as a propagating quantum object: the phonon.

One Hamiltonian, one instantaneous interaction

Electrons are indistinguishable fermions with field operators $\hat\psi(\mathbf x)$, $\mathbf x=(\br,\sigma)$. Nuclei in a solid can be labelled individually, so they are treated in first quantization through their displacements $\Delta\hat{\boldsymbol\tau}_{\kappa p}$ from equilibrium positions $\boldsymbol\tau^0_{\kappa p}$, which are external parameters.
