Phonons appear later as quanta of these displacements. The most general nonrelativistic Hamiltonian is

$$\hat H=\hat T_{\rm e}+\hat T_{\rm n}+\hat U_{\rm ee}+\hat U_{\rm nn}+\hat U_{\rm en}, \tag{G.62}$$

with the kinetic energies $\hat T_{\rm e}$, $\hat T_{\rm n}$ and three Coulomb terms,

$$\hat U_{\rm ee}=\frac12\int d\br\int d\br'\,\hat n_{\rm e}(\br)\big[\hat n_{\rm e}(\br')-\delta(\br-\br')\big]v(\br,\br'), \tag{G.64}$$
$$\hat U_{\rm nn}=\frac12\sum_{\kappa'p'\neq\kappa p}Z_\kappa Z_{\kappa'}\,v\big(\boldsymbol\tau^0_{\kappa p}+\Delta\hat{\boldsymbol\tau}_{\kappa p},\,\boldsymbol\tau^0_{\kappa'p'}+\Delta\hat{\boldsymbol\tau}_{\kappa'p'}\big), \tag{G.65}$$

and $\hat U_{\rm en}=\int d\br\,d\br'\,\hat n_{\rm e}(\br)\hat n_{\rm n}(\br')v(\br,\br')$ (G Eq. 66), with point nuclei

$$\hat n_{\rm n}(\br)=-\sum_{\kappa p}Z_\kappa\,\delta\big(\br-\boldsymbol\tau^0_{\kappa p}-\Delta\hat{\boldsymbol\tau}_{\kappa p}\big). \tag{G.67}$$

Here $v(\br,\br')=e^2/(4\pi\varepsilon_0|\br-\br'|)$, $\hat n_{\rm e}=\sum_\sigma\hat\psi^\dagger\hat\psi$, and $Z_\kappa$ and $M_\kappa$ are the charge (in units of $e$) and mass of nucleus $\kappa$ in unit cell $p$. The $-\delta$ in (G.64) removes the self-interaction of the continuous electron charge, while the distinguishable nuclei in (G.65) are counted pair by pair. There is no vector potential, no current coupling and no photon. In the space-time notation used below, $1\equiv(\br_1\sigma_1t_1)$, $1^+$ is $1$ with $t_1+\eta$ ($\eta\to0^+$) and $\int d(34)\equiv\int d3\,d4$. The interaction is

$$v(12)=v(\br_1,\br_2)\,\delta(t_1-t_2),$$

so a charge moved at time $t_1$ is felt everywhere at $t_1$. Every bare interaction line in this section is this one. The screened lines $W_{\rm e}$ and $W$ are not instantaneous, because the screening clouds take time to form.

The electron Green function and its self-energy

The central object is the time-ordered Green function in the exact coupled electron–nuclear ground state $|0\rangle$, at zero temperature:

$$G(\mathbf xt,\mathbf x't')=-\frac{i}{\hbar}\langle0|\hat T\hat\psi(\mathbf xt)\hat\psi^\dagger(\mathbf x't')|0\rangle. \tag{G.70}$$

To derive its equation of motion, Giustino adds a fictitious scalar potential $\varphi(\br t)$ that couples to the total charge, $\hat H_1(t)=\int d\br\,\hat n(\br)\varphi(\br t)$ with $\hat n=\hat n_{\rm e}+\hat n_{\rm n}$, and sets it to zero at the end. Electrons feel electrons and nuclei through the same $v$, so the potential they move in, and its response to $\varphi$, involve all charges:

$$V_{\rm tot}(1)=\int d2\,v(12)\langle\hat n(2)\rangle+\varphi(1), \tag{G.79}$$
$$\epsilon^{-1}(12)=\delta V_{\rm tot}(1)/\delta\varphi(2). \tag{G.80}$$

Equation (G.80) is the most general dielectric response: because $\langle\hat n\rangle$ contains the nuclei, $\epsilon^{-1}$ includes electronic and lattice screening. With the vertex $\Gamma(123)=-\delta G^{-1}(12)/\delta V_{\rm tot}(3)$ (G Eq. 83), the equation of motion takes the Dyson form (G.84), listed in Table I below, with

$$\Sigma(12)=i\hbar\int d(34)\,G(13)\Gamma(324)W(41^+), \tag{G.85}$$
$$W(12)=\int d3\,\epsilon^{-1}(13)v(32)=\int d(3)\,v(13)\epsilon^{-1}(23). \tag{G.86}$$

The $\hbar$ in (G.85) appears because $G$ carries $1/\hbar$; with $\hbar=1$ it is the familiar $\Sigma=iGW\Gamma$. The vertex obeys Hedin's integral equation (G.87). The structure is that of GW, with one difference hidden in (G.80): $W$ is screened by the lattice as well as by the electrons.

Derivation: from the equation of motion to $\Sigma=i\hbar G\Gamma W$

The Heisenberg equation for $\hat\psi$ (G Eq. 73) contains $\int d\br'\,v(\br,\br')\hat n(\br't)\hat\psi$ with the total density, so the equation for $G$ acquires a two-particle term $-\frac{i}{\hbar}\int d3\,v(13)\langle\hat T\hat n(3)\hat\psi(1)\hat\psi^\dagger(2)\rangle$ (G Eq. 74). Schwinger's identity, $\delta\langle\hat T\hat a\hat b\rangle/\delta\varphi(3)=-\frac{i}{\hbar}\langle\hat T[\hat n(3)-\langle\hat n(3)\rangle]\hat a\hat b\rangle$ (G Eq. 75), splits it into a mean-field part, which builds the Hartree potential of electrons and nuclei inside $V_{\rm tot}$, and a fluctuation part:

$$\Big[i\hbar\frac{\partial}{\partial t_1}+\frac{\hbar^2}{2m_{\rm e}}\nabla^2(1)-V_{\rm tot}(1)-i\hbar\int d3\,v(1^+3)\frac{\delta}{\delta\varphi(3)}\Big]G(12)=\delta(12). \tag{G.78}$$

Now (G Eq. 81)

$$\frac{\delta G(12)}{\delta\varphi(3)}=-\int d(45)\,G(14)\,\frac{\delta G^{-1}(45)}{\delta\varphi(3)}\,G(52),$$

and the chain rule through $V_{\rm tot}$ (G Eq. 82) with (G.80) and (G.83) gives $\delta G^{-1}(45)/\delta\varphi(3)=-\int d6\,\Gamma(456)\epsilon^{-1}(63)$. The last term of (G.78) becomes

$$-i\hbar\int d(456)\,G(14)\Gamma(456)\Big[\int d3\,\epsilon^{-1}(63)v(31^+)\Big]G(52)=-\int d5\,\Sigma(15)G(52),$$

and the bracket is $W(61^+)$ by the first form of (G.86). Relabelling gives (G.85). The second form of (G.86), with $\epsilon^{-1}(23)$, is correct as printed: it uses $\delta\langle\hat n(1)\rangle/\delta\varphi(2)=\delta\langle\hat n(2)\rangle/\delta\varphi(1)$, so $W(12)=W(21)$. Inverting (G.84) and differentiating with respect to $V_{\rm tot}$ gives the vertex equation (G.87).

Screening by everything: $W=v+vPW$

Differentiating (G.79) with the chain rule through $\langle\hat n\rangle$ gives a Dyson equation for $W$ with the polarization propagator

$$P(12)=\frac{\delta\langle\hat n(1)\rangle}{\delta V_{\rm tot}(2)}, \tag{G.89}$$
$$W(12)=v(12)+\int d(34)\,v(13)P(34)W(42). \tag{G.90}$$

$P$ is irreducible with respect to $v$ because $V_{\rm tot}$ already contains the Hartree field, and $\epsilon=1-vP$ (G Eq. 91). Since $\hat n=\hat n_{\rm e}+\hat n_{\rm n}$, the polarization splits as $P=P_{\rm e}+P_{\rm n}$, with $P_{\rm n}\equiv\delta\langle\hat n_{\rm n}\rangle/\delta V_{\rm tot}$ (this page's notation). If the nuclei are classical point charges clamped at $\boldsymbol\tau^0_{\kappa p}$, only the electrons respond:

$$P_{\rm e}(12)=\frac{\delta\langle\hat n_{\rm e}(1)\rangle}{\delta V_{\rm tot}(2)}=-i\hbar\sum_{\sigma_1}\int d(34)\,G(13)G(41^+)\Gamma(342), \tag{G.92}$$
$$W_{\rm e}(12)=v(12)+\int d(34)\,v(13)P_{\rm e}(34)W_{\rm e}(42), \tag{G.94}$$

with $\langle\hat n_{\rm e}(1)\rangle=-i\hbar\sum_{\sigma_1}G(11^+)$ (G Eq. 93) and $\epsilon_{\rm e}=1-vP_{\rm e}$ (G Eq. 95). Equations (G.84)–(G.87) with $W\to W_{\rm e}$ are Hedin's equations (1965) for electrons in the field of clamped nuclei. With $\Gamma(123)=\delta(12)\delta(13)$ and $G$ replaced by the Kohn–Sham $G_0$, $P_{\rm e}=-i\hbar\sum_\sigma G(12)G(21^+)$ is the RPA $\chi^0$ and $W_{\rm e}$ is the $W$ of a GW or BSE calculation. In a gapped crystal at long wavelength and at phonon frequencies, $W_{\rm e}\simeq v/\epsilon^\infty$.

Bridge to EPP · your $W$ is $D^{\rm e}_{11}$ (§B.9)

EPP reaches $W_{\rm e}$ from the other side. At $c\to\infty$ only the Coulomb part of its electron-dressed photon propagator $D^{\rm e}$ (E.388) survives. Its scalar slot, written $D^{\rm e}_{11}$ (the index 1 labels that scalar, Coulomb slot, not the $x$ component), obeys (G.94) with $P_{\rm e}$ replaced by the RPA bubble without local fields or xc (E.435), and EPP names it $W^{\rm e}\equiv D^{\rm e}_{11}$ (E.437). So the $W$ of a GW code is one projection of EPP's photon propagator. §X.1 sets up the correspondence and §B.9 takes the limit step by step.

Letting the nuclei move: $W=W_{\rm e}+W_{\rm ph}$

Now treat the electronic part exactly and the nuclear part on top of it. Subtracting (G.94) from (G.90) gives $W=W_{\rm e}+W_{\rm e}P_{\rm n}W$, and since $P_{\rm n}\epsilon^{-1}=\delta\langle\hat n_{\rm n}\rangle/\delta\varphi$,

$$W(12)=W_{\rm e}(12)+\int d(34)\,W_{\rm e}(13)\frac{\delta\langle\hat n_{\rm n}(3)\rangle}{\delta\varphi(4)}v(42). \tag{G.96}$$

The remaining step, which Giustino calls "a delicate passage", needs the nuclear response to a probe of all charges. A second probe $J$ that couples only to the nuclei, $\hat H_2(t)=\int d\br\,\hat n_{\rm n}(\br t)J(\br t)$, gives the reciprocity relation $\delta\langle\hat n_{\rm n}(1)\rangle/\delta\varphi(2)=\delta\langle\hat n(2)\rangle/\delta J(1)$ (G Eq. 99): pushing on all charges and watching the nuclei is the same as pushing on the nuclei and watching all charges. When the nuclei move the electrons follow, so the total charge response is the nuclear response screened by $\epsilon_{\rm e}^{-1}$ (G Eq. 100). What is left is the nuclear density–density correlation function

$$\mathcal D(12)=-\frac{i}{\hbar}\big\langle\hat T[\hat n_{\rm n}(1)-\langle\hat n_{\rm n}(1)\rangle][\hat n_{\rm n}(2)-\langle\hat n_{\rm n}(2)\rangle]\big\rangle, \tag{G.103}$$

in which the nuclei already interact through $W_{\rm e}$. Assembling the pieces gives the main result of Giustino §IV.B, first derived by Hedin and Lundqvist (1969):

$$W(12)=W_{\rm e}(12)+W_{\rm ph}(12), \tag{G.104}$$
$$W_{\rm ph}(12)=\int d(34)\,W_{\rm e}(13)\,\mathcal D(34)\,W_{\rm e}(24). \tag{G.105}$$
Derivation: from (G.96) to (G.105), and the argument order in (G.100)

By reciprocity (G.99), $\delta\langle\hat n_{\rm n}(3)\rangle/\delta\varphi(4)=\delta\langle\hat n(4)\rangle/\delta J(3)$. The total density changes through the nuclei and through the electrons that respond to the nuclear potential $v\,\delta\langle\hat n_{\rm n}\rangle$. With $\chi_{\rm e}$ the reducible electronic density response,

$$\delta\langle\hat n(1)\rangle=\int d3\,\Big[\delta(13)+\int d5\,\chi_{\rm e}(15)v(53)\Big]\delta\langle\hat n_{\rm n}(3)\rangle=\int d3\,\epsilon_{\rm e}^{-1}(31)\,\delta\langle\hat n_{\rm n}(3)\rangle,$$

using $\epsilon_{\rm e}^{-1}(31)=\delta(31)+\int d5\,v(35)\chi_{\rm e}(51)$, which is (G.80) restricted to electrons, and the symmetry of $\chi_{\rm e}$ and $v$. With (G.102), $\delta\langle\hat n_{\rm n}(1)\rangle/\delta J(2)=\mathcal D(21)$, this gives $\delta\langle\hat n(4)\rangle/\delta J(3)=\int d5\,\epsilon_{\rm e}^{-1}(54)\mathcal D(35)$. Inserting it into (G.96) and using $\int d4\,\epsilon_{\rm e}^{-1}(54)v(42)=W_{\rm e}(52)$, the first form of (G.86) for electrons,

$$W(12)=W_{\rm e}(12)+\int d(35)\,W_{\rm e}(13)\,\mathcal D(35)\,W_{\rm e}(52),$$

which is (G.105) after relabelling and $W_{\rm e}(52)=W_{\rm e}(25)$. The argument order $\epsilon_{\rm e}^{-1}(31)$ is what makes the last step work; the printed (G.100) has $\epsilon_{\rm e}^{-1}(13)$. The two agree when $\epsilon_{\rm e}^{-1}$ is symmetric, and the final results (G.104)–(G.105) are correct as printed.

The vertex is a screened gradient of the nuclear potential

Phonons appear when the point-nucleus density (G.67) is expanded in the displacements. With $\delta(\br-\bu)=\delta(\br)-\bu\cdot\nabla\delta(\br)+\frac12\bu\cdot\nabla\nabla\delta(\br)\cdot\bu$ (G Eq. 106),

$$\begin{aligned}\hat n_{\rm n}(\br)=n^0_{\rm n}(\br)&+\sum_{\kappa p}Z_\kappa\Delta\hat{\boldsymbol\tau}_{\kappa p}\cdot\nabla\delta(\br-\boldsymbol\tau^0_{\kappa p})\\&-\frac12\sum_{\kappa p}Z_\kappa\Delta\hat{\boldsymbol\tau}_{\kappa p}\cdot\nabla\nabla\delta(\br-\boldsymbol\tau^0_{\kappa p})\cdot\Delta\hat{\boldsymbol\tau}_{\kappa p}.\end{aligned} \tag{G.107}$$

The first term is the static lattice of point charges. The second is a lattice of point dipoles $Z_\kappa\Delta\hat{\boldsymbol\tau}_{\kappa p}$, the seed of polar coupling (§A.4). The third smears each nucleus over its zero-point motion. Keeping the dipole term in each density fluctuation,

$$\mathcal D(12)=\sum_{\substack{\kappa\alpha p\\ \kappa'\alpha'p'}}Z_\kappa\nabla_{1,\alpha}\delta(\br_1-\boldsymbol\tau^0_{\kappa p})\,\mathcal D_{\kappa\alpha p,\kappa'\alpha'p'}(t_1t_2)\,Z_{\kappa'}\nabla_{2,\alpha'}\delta(\br_2-\boldsymbol\tau^0_{\kappa'p'}), \tag{G.108}$$

with the displacement–displacement correlation function, the phonon Green function of this page,

$$\mathcal D_{\kappa\alpha p,\kappa'\alpha'p'}(tt')=-\frac{i}{\hbar}\big\langle\hat T\Delta\hat\tau_{\kappa\alpha p}(t)\Delta\hat\tau_{\kappa'\alpha'p'}(t')\big\rangle. \tag{G.109}$$

Inserting (G.108) into (G.105), the delta-function gradients act on $W_{\rm e}=\epsilon_{\rm e}^{-1}v$, and $Z_\kappa v(\br,\boldsymbol\tau)=-V_\kappa(\br-\boldsymbol\tau)$ turns them into gradients of the nuclear potential:

$$\begin{aligned}W_{\rm ph}(12)=\sum_{\substack{\kappa\alpha p\\ \kappa'\alpha'p'}}\int d(34)\,&\epsilon_{\rm e}^{-1}(13)\nabla_{3,\alpha}V_\kappa(\br_3-\boldsymbol\tau^0_{\kappa p})\\&\times\mathcal D_{\kappa\alpha p,\kappa'\alpha'p'}(t_3t_4)\,\epsilon_{\rm e}^{-1}(24)\nabla_{4,\alpha'}V_{\kappa'}(\br_4-\boldsymbol\tau^0_{\kappa'p'}).\end{aligned} \tag{G.110}$$

$V_\kappa$ is the bare Coulomb potential of the nucleus, $-Z_\kappa e^2/(4\pi\varepsilon_0r)$, or its ionic pseudopotential. This is the central identification of Giustino §IV: the electron–phonon vertex is $\epsilon_{\rm e}^{-1}\nabla V_\kappa$, the field of a displaced nucleus screened by the full many-body dielectric matrix. The screening is dynamical, since $\epsilon_{\rm e}^{-1}(13)$ depends on $t_1-t_3$. Hedin and Lundqvist replaced it by its static limit, which is the Born–Oppenheimer approximation for the vertex. Giustino keeps the frequency dependence, following Bardeen and Pines (1955) and Baym (1961), and stresses that the harmonic truncation of (G.107) is the only approximation so far (but see the note on (G.108) at the end of this section).

In the mode basis of §A.6 the vertex becomes $g_{\bq\nu}(\br,\omega)=\int d\br'\,\epsilon_{\rm e}^{-1}(\br,\br',\omega)\,g^{\rm b}_{\bq\nu}(\br')$, with the bare coupling $g^{\rm b}_{\bq\nu}=\Delta_{\bq\nu}V^{\rm en}$, the change of the electron–nuclei potential per unit amplitude of phonon $\bq\nu$ (G Eqs. 142–143). The DFPT vertex (G.38) of §A.3 is its static RPA+xc approximation. Symbolically $W_{\rm ph}=g\,\mathcal D\,g^*$, with screened vertices at both ends; the phonon self-energy of §A.6 will instead carry one bare and one screened vertex.

Subtlety · which "retardation"

Here "retardation" means Giustino's frequency-dependent electronic screening; the speed of light is infinite throughout this section, because $v(12)$ is instantaneous. EPP's second meaning, the finite speed of light, is set out in §X.1.

A polar insulator: $W_{\rm ph}$ is the Fröhlich interaction

In a homogeneous polar insulator at long wavelength, (G.104) becomes scalar algebra. The electrons give $W_{\rm e}=v/\epsilon^\infty$, flat at phonon frequencies. The lattice adds a pole: $W=v/\epsilon(\omega)$ with $\epsilon(\omega)=\epsilon^\infty(\omega_{\rm LO}^2-\omega^2)/(\omega_{\rm TO}^2-\omega^2)$, the form EPP derives classically (E.159). With the Lyddane–Sachs–Teller relation $\epsilon^0/\epsilon^\infty=\omega_{\rm LO}^2/\omega_{\rm TO}^2$, the difference is

$$\begin{aligned}W_{\rm ph}(\bq,\omega)&=v(\bq)\Big(\frac1{\epsilon^\infty}-\frac1{\epsilon^0}\Big)\frac{\omega_{\rm LO}^2}{\omega^2-\omega_{\rm LO}^2}=\frac1\hbar\,|g(\bq)|^2\,\mathcal D^{\rm A}_{\rm LO}(\omega),\\ |g(\bq)|^2&=v(\bq)\,\frac{\hbar\omega_{\rm LO}}{2}\Big(\frac1{\epsilon^\infty}-\frac1{\epsilon^0}\Big),\qquad v(\bq)=\frac{e^2}{\varepsilon_0\Omega q^2},\end{aligned}$$

with $v(\bq)$ per unit cell of volume $\Omega$ and $\mathcal D^{\rm A}_{\rm LO}=2\omega_{\rm LO}/(\omega^2-\omega_{\rm LO}^2)$ the adiabatic LO propagator (G Eq. 132). $|g|^2$ is the square of Fröhlich's vertex (G.7) of §A.4, so the phonon part of the screened interaction is Fröhlich's coupling squared times the LO propagator: the long-wavelength content of (G.110). The model is not printed in Giustino; it follows from (G.104) and the LST relation. The figure evaluates it with damping.

Jellium with mobile ions: where the attraction comes from

In a simple metal the same algebra gives the effective interaction of Bardeen and Pines (1955), the work Giustino follows in keeping the frequency dependence of the screening. Treat the ions as a classical plasma of charge $Ze$, mass $M$ and density $n_{\rm ion}$ inside an electron gas with static dielectric function $\epsilon_{\rm e}(q)$. Their polarization is that of free charges, $vP_{\rm n}=\Omega_p^2/\omega^2$, with $\Omega_p^2=n_{\rm ion}Z^2e^2/(\varepsilon_0M)$, so $\epsilon=\epsilon_{\rm e}(q)-\Omega_p^2/\omega^2$ and

$$W(q,\omega)=\frac{v(q)}{\epsilon_{\rm e}(q)}\,\frac{\omega^2}{\omega^2-\omega_q^2},\qquad W_{\rm ph}(q,\omega)=\frac{v(q)}{\epsilon_{\rm e}(q)}\,\frac{\omega_q^2}{\omega^2-\omega_q^2},\qquad \omega_q^2=\frac{\Omega_p^2}{\epsilon_{\rm e}(q)}.$$

Electronic screening turns the ion plasma oscillation into an acoustic phonon, $\omega_q\to\Omega_pq/k_{\rm TF}$ at small $q$, with $k_{\rm TF}$ the Thomas–Fermi wavevector (Bohm–Staver sound; the dispersion and its Kohn anomaly are in §A.6). Below $\omega_q$ the total interaction is negative: electrons that exchange less energy than a phonon attract each other, because the slow ionic cloud overscreens them. At $\omega\to0$ the ions screen perfectly and $W\to0$. This frequency-dependent attraction, retarded in Giustino's sense because the ions respond late, is the pairing interaction of Eliashberg theory (§A.9).

Phonons are nuclei interacting through $W_{\rm e}$

The phonon propagator needs its own equation of motion. Newton's equation for $\Delta\hat{\boldsymbol\tau}_{\kappa p}$ (G Eq. 112) has the Coulomb force of the electrons and of all other nuclei on its right-hand side, with no Lorentz force and no radiation. A third probe, an external force $\mathbf F_{\kappa p}(t)$ coupled to the displacement, generates $\mathcal D_{\kappa\alpha p,\kappa'\alpha'p'}=\delta\langle\Delta\hat\tau_{\kappa\alpha p}\rangle/\delta F_{\kappa'\alpha'p'}$ (G Eq. 113), and differentiating Newton's equation gives a Dyson-like equation (G Eq. 116). In frequency space, with $f(\omega)=\int dt\,f(t)e^{i\omega t}$,

$$\sum_{\kappa''\alpha''p''}\big[M_\kappa\omega^2\delta_{\kappa\alpha p,\kappa''\alpha''p''}-\Pi^{\rm ph}_{\kappa\alpha p,\kappa''\alpha''p''}(\omega)\big]\mathcal D_{\kappa''\alpha''p'',\kappa'\alpha'p'}(\omega)=\delta_{\kappa\alpha p,\kappa'\alpha'p'}, \tag{G.118}$$
$$\begin{aligned}\Pi^{\rm ph}_{\kappa\alpha p,\kappa'\alpha'p'}(\omega)=\int d\br\,d\br'\,\big[&Z_\kappa\nabla_\alpha\delta(\br-\boldsymbol\tau^0_{\kappa p})W_{\rm e}(\br,\br',\omega)\\&+\delta_{\kappa p,\kappa'p'}\nabla_\alpha\langle\hat n(\br)\rangle v(\br,\br')\big]Z_{\kappa'}\nabla'_{\alpha'}\delta(\br'-\boldsymbol\tau^0_{\kappa'p'}).\end{aligned} \tag{G.119}$$

The first term couples two point nuclei through the electron-screened $W_{\rm e}(\omega)$. The second is Baym's "static force", from the equilibrium charge density. Holding the crystal fixed in the laboratory frame imposes the many-body acoustic sum rule

$$\sum_{\kappa'p'}\Pi^{\rm ph}_{\kappa\alpha p,\kappa'\alpha'p'}(\omega=0)=0\quad\text{for any }\alpha,\alpha', \tag{G.120}$$

and with it the self-energy takes its compact form:

$$\begin{aligned}\Pi^{\rm ph}_{\kappa\alpha p,\kappa'\alpha'p'}(\omega)=\sum_{\kappa''p''}Z_\kappa Z_{\kappa''}&\frac{\partial^2}{\partial r_\alpha\partial r'_{\alpha'}}\bigg|_{\br=\boldsymbol\tau^0_{\kappa p},\,\br'=\boldsymbol\tau^0_{\kappa''p''}}\\&\times\big[\delta_{\kappa'p',\kappa''p''}W_{\rm e}(\br,\br',\omega)-\delta_{\kappa p,\kappa'p'}W_{\rm e}(\br,\br',0)\big].\end{aligned} \tag{G.121}$$
Derivation: from (G.119) and (G.120) to (G.121)

Integrate the first term of (G.119) by parts twice. Each $\nabla\delta$ moves onto $W_{\rm e}$ with a minus sign, so the term is $A_{\kappa p,\kappa'p'}(\omega)\equiv Z_\kappa Z_{\kappa'}\,\partial^2W_{\rm e}(\br,\br',\omega)/\partial r_\alpha\partial r'_{\alpha'}$ at $\br=\boldsymbol\tau^0_{\kappa p}$, $\br'=\boldsymbol\tau^0_{\kappa'p'}$ (Cartesian indices implied). The static term is local in the nucleus, $\delta_{\kappa p,\kappa'p'}S_{\kappa p}$, and does not depend on $\omega$. The sum rule (G.120) at $\omega=0$ fixes it: $S_{\kappa p}=-\sum_{\kappa''p''}A_{\kappa p,\kappa''p''}(0)$. Hence

$$\Pi^{\rm ph}_{\kappa p,\kappa'p'}(\omega)=A_{\kappa p,\kappa'p'}(\omega)-\delta_{\kappa p,\kappa'p'}\sum_{\kappa''p''}A_{\kappa p,\kappa''p''}(0),$$

which is (G.121). On the diagonal, $\kappa'p'=\kappa p$, the first term and the $\kappa''p''=\kappa p$ part of the sum combine into $Z_\kappa^2\partial\partial'[W_{\rm e}(\omega)-W_{\rm e}(0)]$ at coincident points, and the rest of the sum, $-\sum_{\kappa''p''\neq\kappa p}A_{\kappa p,\kappa''p''}(0)$, is the static restoring force from all the other nuclei. The singular bare $v$, a nucleus interacting with itself, cancels in that difference because it does not depend on frequency.

So the phonon self-energy is the mixed second derivative of the electron-screened interaction between two point nuclei, and its frequency dependence is that of $\epsilon_{\rm e}(\omega)$. The second term of (G.121) is the "self" force constant that enforces the sum rule. At $\omega=0$, (G.121) gives the Born–Oppenheimer force constants of DFPT, dressed by the exact $\epsilon_{\rm e}(0)$; §A.6 starts from this split, $\Pi^{\rm ph}=\Pi^{\rm A}+\Pi^{\rm NA}(\omega)$, and solves (G.118). The quadratic term of (G.107) survives in the mean nuclear density,

$$\langle\hat n_{\rm n}(\br t)\rangle=n^0_{\rm n}(\br)-\frac{i\hbar}{2}\sum_{\kappa p,\alpha\alpha'}Z_\kappa\frac{\partial^2\delta(\br-\boldsymbol\tau^0_{\kappa p})}{\partial r_\alpha\partial r_{\alpha'}}\mathcal D_{\kappa\alpha p,\kappa\alpha'p}(t^+t), \tag{G.122}$$

a nucleus smeared by its zero-point motion, since $i\hbar\mathcal D(t^+t)=\langle\Delta\hat\tau_\alpha\Delta\hat\tau_{\alpha'}\rangle$. It enters $V_{\rm tot}$ and produces the Debye–Waller self-energy of §A.7.

Bridge to EPP · one Dyson equation instead of two (§X.1, §B.7)

Giustino needs two coupled Dyson equations, (G.90) for $W$ and (G.118) for $\mathcal D$. EPP needs one, $D=D^0+D^0\Pi_{jj}D$ (E.379), for the propagator of the total electromagnetic field, with current–current self-energies in place of density responses. §X.1 maps the two structures term by term, and §B.7 derives the phonon self-energy that replaces (G.121).

The Hedin–Baym equations

Equations (G.79), (G.84), (G.85), (G.87), (G.92)–(G.95), (G.110), (G.118), (G.121) and (G.122) close on themselves. Giustino collects them in his Table I and calls them the Hedin–Baym equations: the electronic ones are Hedin's (1965), the nuclear ones Baym's (1961). They hold at zero temperature in the harmonic approximation.

Eq.QuantityExpression (Giustino Table I, $\mathcal D$ and $\Pi^{\rm ph}$ renamed)
(93)electronic charge density$\langle\hat n_{\rm e}(1)\rangle=-i\hbar\sum_{\sigma_1}G(11^+)$
(122)nuclear charge density$\langle\hat n_{\rm n}(\br t)\rangle=n^0_{\rm n}(\br)-\frac{i\hbar}{2}\sum_{\kappa p,\alpha\alpha'}Z_\kappa\frac{\partial^2\delta(\br-\boldsymbol\tau^0_{\kappa p})}{\partial r_\alpha\partial r_{\alpha'}}\mathcal D_{\kappa\alpha p,\kappa\alpha'p}(t^+t)$
(79)total electrostatic potential$V_{\rm tot}(1)=\int d2\,v(12)\big[\langle\hat n_{\rm e}(2)\rangle+\langle\hat n_{\rm n}(2)\rangle\big]$
(84)equation of motion, electrons$\big[i\hbar\partial/\partial t_1+(\hbar^2/2m_{\rm e})\nabla^2(1)-V_{\rm tot}(1)\big]G(12)-\int d3\,\Sigma(13)G(32)=\delta(12)$
(118)equation of motion, nuclei$\sum_{\kappa''\alpha''p''}\big[M_\kappa\omega^2\delta_{\kappa\alpha p,\kappa''\alpha''p''}-\Pi^{\rm ph}_{\kappa\alpha p,\kappa''\alpha''p''}(\omega)\big]\mathcal D_{\kappa''\alpha''p'',\kappa'\alpha'p'}(\omega)=\delta_{\kappa\alpha p,\kappa'\alpha'p'}$
(85)electron self-energy$\Sigma(12)=i\hbar\int d(34)\,G(13)\Gamma(324)\big[W_{\rm e}(41^+)+W_{\rm ph}(41^+)\big]$
(94)screened Coulomb, electrons$W_{\rm e}(12)=v(12)+\int d(34)\,v(13)P_{\rm e}(34)W_{\rm e}(42)$
(92)electronic polarization$P_{\rm e}(12)=-i\hbar\sum_{\sigma_1}\int d(34)\,G(13)G(41^+)\Gamma(342)$
(95)electronic dielectric matrix$\epsilon_{\rm e}(12)=\delta(12)-\int d(3)\,v(13)P_{\rm e}(32)$
(87)vertex$\Gamma(123)=\delta(12)\delta(13)+\int d(4567)\,[\delta\Sigma(12)/\delta G(45)]\,G(46)G(75)\Gamma(673)$
(110)screened Coulomb, nuclei$\begin{aligned}W_{\rm ph}(12)=&\textstyle\sum_{\kappa\alpha p,\kappa'\alpha'p'}\int d(34)\,\epsilon_{\rm e}^{-1}(13)\nabla_{3,\alpha}V_\kappa(\br_3-\boldsymbol\tau^0_{\kappa p})\\&\times\mathcal D_{\kappa\alpha p,\kappa'\alpha'p'}(t_3t_4)\,\epsilon_{\rm e}^{-1}(24)\nabla_{4,\alpha'}V_{\kappa'}(\br_4-\boldsymbol\tau^0_{\kappa'p'})\end{aligned}$
(121)phonon self-energy$\begin{aligned}\Pi^{\rm ph}_{\kappa\alpha p,\kappa'\alpha'p'}(\omega)=&\textstyle\sum_{\kappa''p''}Z_\kappa Z_{\kappa''}(\partial^2/\partial r_\alpha\partial r'_{\alpha'})\\&\times\big[\delta_{\kappa'p',\kappa''p''}W_{\rm e}(\br,\br',\omega)-\delta_{\kappa p,\kappa'p'}W_{\rm e}(\br,\br',0)\big]_{\br=\boldsymbol\tau^0_{\kappa p},\,\br'=\boldsymbol\tau^0_{\kappa''p''}}\end{aligned}$

Three properties matter. The set is nonperturbative: it fixes the exact propagators self-consistently, not order by order in a coupling constant. It does not assume Born–Oppenheimer: $\Pi^{\rm ph}(\omega)$ and the vertex keep their frequency dependence, so the same equations cover insulators, doped semiconductors and metals. And setting $\mathcal D_{\kappa\alpha p,\kappa'\alpha'p'}=0$ removes $W_{\rm ph}$, $\Pi^{\rm ph}$ and the zero-point smearing, which returns Hedin's equations for clamped nuclei. The price is the harmonic approximation; going beyond it (Gillis 1970) is formidable. Table I contains no symbol $g$. The coupling lives in $\epsilon_{\rm e}^{-1}\nabla V_\kappa$ inside (G.110) and in $Z_\kappa\nabla\delta$ contracted with $W_{\rm e}$ in (G.121), which is why Giustino calls the electronic dielectric matrix $\epsilon_{\rm e}(\br,\br',\omega)$ "absolutely central". The map below shows how the equations feed each other.

Bridge to EPP · what gets replaced (§X.1)

Every bare Coulomb line in Table I is the instantaneous $v(12)$, coupled to charge densities. EPP keeps it as the longitudinal photon, adds the transverse photon and couples both to currents (§X.1, §B.4). For $c\to\infty$ it recovers $W=W_{\rm e}+W_{\rm e}\mathcal DW_{\rm e}$, but only for the dipolar, Born-charge part of the vertex, since its Lagrangian has no short-range coupling (§B.9).

Note on the source · G Eqs. 100, 108 and 127

(G.100). The total-density response should read $\int d3\,\epsilon_{\rm e}^{-1}(31)\,\delta\langle\hat n_{\rm n}(3)\rangle/\delta J(2)$, not $\epsilon_{\rm e}^{-1}(13)$. Only this order turns (G.96) into (G.105) (see the derivation above). The orders coincide for a symmetric $\epsilon_{\rm e}^{-1}$, and (G.104), (G.105), (G.110) are correct as printed. The same caveat applies to the first term of (G.115).

(G.108). The text says the harmonic truncation of (G.107) is the sole approximation, but (G.108) also keeps only the linear term of (G.107) in each density fluctuation. The dropped cross terms are three- and four-displacement correlators, i.e. two-phonon processes, so (G.108) and (G.110) are one-phonon expressions.

(G.127). The identity used in §A.6 to reach the DFPT force constants (G.128) is printed as

$$\frac{\partial\langle\hat n_{\rm e}(\br)\rangle}{\partial\tau^0_{\kappa\alpha p}}=-Z_\kappa\int d\br'\,\big[\epsilon_{\rm e}^{-1}(\br,\br';0)-\delta(\br,\br')\big]\nabla'_\alpha\delta(\br'-\boldsymbol\tau^0_{\kappa p}).$$

It should carry $+Z_\kappa$ and $\epsilon_{\rm e}^{-1}(\br',\br;0)$. Check: for perfect screening, $\epsilon_{\rm e}^{-1}\to0$, the electrons must follow the nucleus, $\partial n_{\rm e}/\partial\tau_\alpha=-Z_\kappa\nabla_\alpha\delta(\br-\boldsymbol\tau^0_{\kappa p})$, which the corrected sign gives. With the printed sign, (G.126) would yield $Z_\kappa Z_{\kappa'}\partial\partial'(2v-W_{\rm e})$ instead of (G.121).

Giustino also uses the letter $D$ for the nuclear density correlator (G.103), the displacement correlator (G.109), its matrix $\mathbf D(\omega)$ and the dynamical matrix $D^{\rm dm}$; the arguments tell them apart. Strictly, he notes, "phonon Green function" should be reserved for $-(i/\hbar)\langle\hat T\hat a_{\bq\nu}\hat a^\dagger_{\bq'\nu'}\rangle$.

A.6Giustino §V.A, §VII · Eqs. 123–146

Phonon self-energy: adiabatic vs nonadiabatic

DFPT phonons are built from the zero-frequency value of the many-body phonon self-energy. The frequency-dependent remainder, $\Pi^{\rm NA}(\omega)$, shifts and broadens them. It contains one bare and one screened electron–phonon vertex, with the static screening subtracted.

§A.5 showed that the nuclei interact through the electronically screened Coulomb interaction $W_{\rm e}$, with a phonon self-energy given by G Eq. (121). Here that result becomes the formulas that ab initio codes evaluate. Physically, a vibrating nucleus drags a cloud of screening electrons with it. If the electrons respond instantly, the screening is static and the phonon is the one DFPT computes. If they lag behind, the screening acquires a dynamical part, which shifts the phonon frequency and lets the phonon decay into electron–hole pairs. On this page Giustino's phonon Green's function $D$ is written $\mathcal D$ and his phonon self-energy $\Pi^{\rm ph}$; $\Pi^{\rm A}$ and $\Pi^{\rm NA}$ keep their names. Units are SI; in the mode basis $\Pi$ is a frequency and $\hbar\Pi$ an energy.

Phonons are poles of a propagator

A phonon is a resonance of the displacement–displacement correlation function $\mathcal D_{\kappa\alpha p,\kappa'\alpha'p'}(\omega)$. Inverting the nuclear equation of motion gives

$$\boldsymbol{\mathcal D}(\omega)=\left[\mathbf M\omega^2-\Pi^{\rm ph}(\omega)\right]^{-1}, \tag{G.123}$$

where $\mathbf M$ is the diagonal matrix of nuclear masses $M_\kappa$. The resonances satisfy $\Omega_\nu(\omega)=\omega$, where $\Omega_\nu^2(\omega)$ are the eigenvalues of $\mathbf M^{-1/2}\Pi^{\rm ph}(\omega)\mathbf M^{-1/2}$ (G Eq. 124). This is the dynamical-matrix problem of §A.1 with the force constants replaced by $\Pi^{\rm ph}(\omega)$. Because $\Pi^{\rm ph}$ is complex and frequency dependent, the roots can leave the real axis (finite lifetimes) and one "eigenmode" can have several roots.

The adiabatic split: $\Pi^{\rm A}$ is what DFPT computes

Giustino partitions the self-energy at zero frequency:

$$\Pi^{\rm ph}(\omega)=\Pi^{\rm A}+\Pi^{\rm NA}(\omega),\qquad \Pi^{\rm A}=\Pi^{\rm ph}(\omega=0). \tag{G.125}$$

Setting $\omega=0$ is the Born–Oppenheimer adiabatic approximation (Keating 1968): the electronic dielectric matrix $\epsilon_{\rm e}(\br,\br',\omega)$ is replaced by $\epsilon_{\rm e}(\br,\br',0)$ over the whole phonon range, so the electrons follow the nuclei instantaneously. With the acoustic sum rule, $\Pi^{\rm A}$ takes the Hellmann–Feynman form

$$\begin{aligned}\Pi^{\rm A}_{\kappa\alpha p,\kappa'\alpha'p'}=&\int\!d\br\,\frac{\partial\langle\hat n_{\rm e}(\br)\rangle}{\partial\tau_{\kappa'\alpha'p'}}\frac{\partial V^{\rm en}(\br)}{\partial\tau_{\kappa\alpha p}}+\int\!d\br\,\langle\hat n_{\rm e}(\br)\rangle\frac{\partial^2V^{\rm en}(\br)}{\partial\tau_{\kappa\alpha p}\partial\tau_{\kappa'\alpha'p'}}\\&+\frac{\partial^2U_{\rm nn}}{\partial\tau_{\kappa\alpha p}\partial\tau_{\kappa'\alpha'p'}}.\end{aligned} \tag{G.128}$$

These have the form of the DFPT interatomic force constants (§A.3): an induced-density term, an unperturbed-density term and the ion–ion term. The difference is that here the density response is governed by the exact many-body $\epsilon_{\rm e}(0)$ and the exact density, whereas DFPT uses $\epsilon^{{\rm H}xc}=1-(v^{\rm C}+f^{xc})\chi^0$ at clamped nuclei. In practice $\Pi^{\rm A}$ is replaced by the DFT force constants. Since $W_{\rm e}(\br,\br',\omega)=W_{\rm e}(\br',\br,-\omega)$, $\Pi^{\rm A}$ is real and symmetric: adiabatic phonons have real frequencies and live forever. In the eigenmode basis the adiabatic propagator is diagonal,

$$\mathcal D^{\rm A}_{\bq\nu\nu'}(\omega)=\frac{2\omega_{\bq\nu}}{\omega^2-\omega^2_{\bq\nu}}\,\delta_{\nu\nu'}, \tag{G.132}$$

which is the textbook free-boson form $\mathcal D^{\rm A}_{\bq\nu\nu}=1/(\omega-\omega_{\bq\nu}+i\eta)-1/(\omega+\omega_{\bq\nu}-i\eta)$ of G Eq. (134). Giustino stresses that this form "rests on the adiabatic approximation".

Physical picture: who is faster?

The adiabatic condition is $|\varepsilon_{m\bk+\bq}-\varepsilon_{n\bk}|\gg\hbar\omega_{\bq\nu}$ for the electronic transitions that the phonon couples (Giustino §VII). Insulators with eV gaps satisfy it easily. In a metal, intraband transitions cost about $\hbar v_Fq$; they are slower than the phonon when $q\lesssim\omega/v_F$, the window identified by Maksimov and Shulga. In a doped semiconductor with $\varepsilon_F\sim\hbar\omega$ the condition fails for all wave vectors up to a few $k_F$, not only near $\Gamma$ (still a small part of the zone, since $k_F$ is small). For metals the static response of the electron gas is even singular as $q,\omega\to0$, which DFPT codes tame by smearing the occupations (de Gironcoli 1995).

The Dyson equation: shifts, widths, new poles

Everything beyond the adiabatic reference goes into a Dyson equation:

$$\boldsymbol{\mathcal D}(\omega)=\boldsymbol{\mathcal D}^{\rm A}(\omega)+\boldsymbol{\mathcal D}^{\rm A}(\omega)\,\Pi^{\rm NA}(\omega)\,\boldsymbol{\mathcal D}(\omega). \tag{G.135}$$

In the mode basis the inverse propagator is

$$\mathcal D^{-1}_{\bq\nu\nu'}(\omega)=\frac{1}{2\omega_{\bq\nu}}\left[\delta_{\nu\nu'}\left(\omega^2-\omega^2_{\bq\nu}\right)-2\omega_{\bq\nu}\Pi^{\rm NA}_{\bq\nu\nu'}(\omega)\right]. \tag{G.136}$$

$\Pi^{\rm NA}$ acts in four ways: (i) the real part of its diagonal shifts the frequencies; (ii) the imaginary part broadens the lines; (iii) off-diagonal elements couple adiabatic modes; (iv) its frequency dependence can create new poles, for example coupled plasmon–phonon modes in degenerate polar semiconductors, "the electronic analog of photon polaritons". Keeping only the diagonal element of a nondegenerate mode, the complex zeros $\tilde\Omega_{\bq\nu}=\Omega_{\bq\nu}-i\gamma_{\bq\nu}$ of (G.136) satisfy

$$\tilde\Omega^2_{\bq\nu}=\omega^2_{\bq\nu}+2\omega_{\bq\nu}\Pi^{\rm NA}_{\bq\nu\nu}(\tilde\Omega_{\bq\nu}), \tag{G.137}$$

whose imaginary and real parts give the linewidth and the renormalized frequency:

$$\gamma_{\bq\nu}=-\frac{\omega_{\bq\nu}}{\Omega_{\bq\nu}}\,{\rm Im}\,\Pi^{\rm NA}_{\bq\nu\nu}(\Omega_{\bq\nu}-i\gamma_{\bq\nu}), \tag{G.138}$$
$$\Omega^2_{\bq\nu}=\omega^2_{\bq\nu}+\gamma^2_{\bq\nu}+2\omega_{\bq\nu}\,{\rm Re}\,\Pi^{\rm NA}_{\bq\nu\nu}(\Omega_{\bq\nu}-i\gamma_{\bq\nu}). \tag{G.139}$$

For small corrections these reduce to the Allen–Grimvall forms $\gamma_{\bq\nu}\simeq-{\rm Im}\,\Pi^{\rm NA}_{\bq\nu\nu}(\omega_{\bq\nu})$ and $\Omega_{\bq\nu}\simeq\omega_{\bq\nu}+{\rm Re}\,\Pi^{\rm NA}_{\bq\nu\nu}(\omega_{\bq\nu})$. The phonon lifetime is $\tau^{\rm ph}_{\bq\nu}=(2\gamma_{\bq\nu})^{-1}$.

Derivation: from (G.137) to (G.138)–(G.139), and why $\tau=1/2\gamma$

Write $\tilde\Omega^2=(\Omega-i\gamma)^2=\Omega^2-\gamma^2-2i\Omega\gamma$. The real part of (G.137) gives $\Omega^2-\gamma^2=\omega^2+2\omega\,{\rm Re}\,\Pi^{\rm NA}$, which is (G.139). The imaginary part gives $-2\Omega\gamma=2\omega\,{\rm Im}\,\Pi^{\rm NA}$, which is (G.138). Near $\omega\approx\Omega>0$,

$$\frac{2\omega_{\bq\nu}}{\omega^2-\tilde\Omega^2}\simeq\frac{\omega_{\bq\nu}/\Omega}{\omega-\Omega+i\gamma},$$

so the spectral function $-\frac1\pi{\rm Im}\,\mathcal D$ is a Lorentzian of half width at half maximum $\gamma$. In the time domain the amplitude decays as $e^{-i\Omega t-\gamma t}$ and the vibrational energy as $e^{-2\gamma t}$, hence $\tau^{\rm ph}=1/2\gamma$. Strictly, $\Pi^{\rm NA}$ must be evaluated at the complex frequency $\Omega-i\gamma$, which requires continuing the retarded self-energy below the real axis; in practice, and in the figure below, it is evaluated on the real axis.

Inside $\Pi^{\rm NA}$: one bare vertex, one screened vertex

Combining G Eqs. (119) and (125), only the frequency-dependent part of the screened interaction survives in the nonadiabatic self-energy:

$$\begin{aligned}\Pi^{\rm NA}_{\kappa\alpha p,\kappa'\alpha'p'}(\omega)=\int\!d\br\,d\br'\,&Z_\kappa\nabla_\alpha\delta(\br-\boldsymbol\tau^0_{\kappa p})\left[W_{\rm e}(\br,\br',\omega)-W_{\rm e}(\br,\br',0)\right]\\&\times Z_{\kappa'}\nabla'_{\alpha'}\delta(\br'-\boldsymbol\tau^0_{\kappa'p'}).\end{aligned} \tag{G.140}$$

The nuclear point charges interact through $W_{\rm e}$, and only the dynamical part of the screening makes phonons shift and decay. Inserting $W_{\rm e}=v+vP_{\rm e}W_{\rm e}$ (G Eq. 94), the gradients of $v$ and of $W_{\rm e}$ turn into electron–phonon couplings, and in the mode basis

$$\begin{aligned}\hbar\Pi^{\rm NA}_{\bq\nu,\bq'\nu'}(\omega)=&\int\!d\br\,d\br'\,g^{\rm b}_{\bq\nu}(\br)\,P_{\rm e}(\br,\br',\omega)\,g^{\rm cc}_{\bq'\nu'}(\br',\omega)\\&-\int\!d\br\,d\br'\,g^{\rm b}_{\bq\nu}(\br)\,P_{\rm e}(\br,\br',0)\,g^{*}_{\bq'\nu'}(\br',0),\end{aligned} \tag{G.141}$$

with the bare and dressed coupling functions

$$g^{\rm b}_{\bq\nu}(\br)=\Delta_{\bq\nu}V^{\rm en}(\br), \tag{G.142}$$
$$g_{\bq\nu}(\br,\omega)=\int\!d\br'\,\epsilon_{\rm e}^{-1}(\br,\br',\omega)\,g^{\rm b}_{\bq\nu}(\br'). \tag{G.143}$$

$g^{\rm cc}$ is defined like (G.143) with $g^{{\rm b},*}$ in place of $g^{\rm b}$ (G Eq. 144); since $\epsilon_{\rm e}$ is real at $\omega=0$, $g^{\rm cc}(\br,0)=g^*(\br,0)$. The bare vertex is the variation of the ionic (pseudo)potential, long ranged in metals; the dressed one is screened by the full electronic $\epsilon_{\rm e}^{-1}$ and is short ranged. Equation (G.141) is nonperturbative: it relies only on the harmonic approximation, and it agrees with Keating (1968) and with Scalapino's electron-gas result. Its structure is the main message of this section: the irreducible polarization $P_{\rm e}=GG\Gamma$ sits between a bare vertex on one side and a screened vertex on the other, and its static value is subtracted.

Why exactly one screened vertex? The lowest-order diagram that starts and ends on a phonon line has two bare vertices, $\Pi\simeq g^{\rm b}G_0G_0g^{\rm b}$. Dressing it means summing all chains of proper polarization insertions joined by $v$: $g^{\rm b}P g^{\rm b}+g^{\rm b}PvPg^{\rm b}+\dots=g^{\rm b}P\,\epsilon_{\rm e}^{-1}g^{\rm b}=g^{\rm b}Pg$. The whole chain can be absorbed into one end, which is the Dyson equation of the dressed vertex, $g=g^{\rm b}+vGG\Gamma g$ (G Fig. 1d; see §A.3). So one bare and one screened vertex around the irreducible bubble is exact, and exact RPA once $P\to\chi^0$. Screening the other end as well counts chains more than once: the two geometric series multiply, $\sum_{a,b}P(vP)^{a+b}=\sum_n(n+1)P(vP)^n$, so a chain with $n$ Coulomb links appears $n+1$ times. Leaving both ends bare keeps only the first term, screening to first order in $P$. The electron self-energy is different: in Fan–Migdal both ends of the internal phonon line sit on the electron line and each end is screened, so it has two screened vertices (§A.7).

From (G.141) to the working formula

Five approximations turn (G.141) into a Brillouin-zone sum: (i) $\Gamma=1$, the GW-type vertex; (ii) Kohn–Sham $G$ at clamped nuclei; (iii) RPA$+xc$ screening from DFT; (iv) the frequency dependence of the screened coupling is dropped, $g^{\rm cc}(\br,\omega)\simeq g^*(\br,0)$, an approximation that is "ubiquitous in the literature but it is never mentioned explicitly"; (v) spin degeneracy and time-reversal symmetry. The result is

$$\begin{aligned}\hbar\Pi^{\rm NA}_{\bq\nu\nu'}(\omega)=2\sum_{mn}\int\!\frac{d\bk}{\Omega_{\rm BZ}}\,&g^{\rm b}_{mn\nu}(\bk,\bq)\,g^*_{mn\nu'}(\bk,\bq)\\&\times\left[\frac{f_{m\bk+\bq}-f_{n\bk}}{\varepsilon_{m\bk+\bq}-\varepsilon_{n\bk}-\hbar(\omega+i\eta)}-\frac{f_{m\bk+\bq}-f_{n\bk}}{\varepsilon_{m\bk+\bq}-\varepsilon_{n\bk}}\right].\end{aligned} \tag{G.145}$$

The factor 2 is spin, $\eta\to0^+$, $g_{mn\nu}$ is the screened DFPT matrix element of G Eq. (38) and $g^{\rm b}_{mn\nu}$ the same with the bare ionic potential; at finite temperature $f$ becomes Fermi–Dirac. The first term in brackets is the bare polarizability $\chi^0(\bq,\omega)$ in the Kohn–Sham basis, the second its static value. The subtraction $\chi^0(\omega)-\chi^0(0)$ removes double counting: the static bubble is already inside $\Pi^{\rm A}$, because the DFT phonons were computed with static screening. Most calculations also replace $g^{\rm b}$ by $g$ and keep only the imaginary part. With ${\rm Im}\,1/(x-i0^+)=\pi\delta(x)$ and $\tau=1/2\gamma$ this gives the golden-rule linewidth

$$\frac{1}{\tau^{\rm ph}_{\bq\nu}}=\frac{2\pi}{\hbar}\,2\sum_{mn}\int\!\frac{d\bk}{\Omega_{\rm BZ}}\,|g_{mn\nu}(\bk,\bq)|^2\left(f_{n\bk}-f_{m\bk+\bq}\right)\delta\!\left(\varepsilon_{m\bk+\bq}-\varepsilon_{n\bk}-\hbar\omega_{\bq\nu}\right). \tag{G.146}$$

A phonon decays by creating an electron–hole pair of energy $\hbar\omega_{\bq\nu}$. All the calculations reviewed in Giustino §VII use $g^{\rm b}\to g$ (his footnote 8).

Subtlety: Eqs. (G.145) and (G.146) differ by $\epsilon(\bq,0)$

Equation (G.145) has the numerator $g^{\rm b}g^*$, Eq. (G.146) has $|g|^2$. With $g=\epsilon^{-1}g^{\rm b}$ they differ by the factor $\epsilon(\bq,0)$, which in a metal at small $q$ is about $(k_{\rm TF}/q)^2\gg1$. In a consistent RPA treatment the exact result of (G.141) is ${\rm Im}[g^{\rm b}P(\omega)g^{\rm cc}(\omega)]=|g(\omega)|^2\,{\rm Im}P(\omega)$ (derivation below). So the "common practice" $|g|^2$ is right when $\epsilon(\omega_{\bq\nu})\approx\epsilon(0)$, while pairing the bare vertex with a statically screened one, approximation (iv), overestimates the width by about $\epsilon(\bq,0)$. The bare/screened bookkeeping and the frequency dependence of the screened vertex have to be treated together. Giustino flags the replacement as something "it will be important to assess".

Derivation: ${\rm Im}[g^{\rm b}Pg^{\rm cc}]=|g|^2\,{\rm Im}P$ in the RPA

Take a homogeneous, $\bq$-diagonal RPA: $\epsilon(\omega)=1-vP(\omega)$, $g(\omega)=g^{\rm b}/\epsilon(\omega)$ and $g^{\rm cc}(\omega)=g^{{\rm b}*}/\epsilon(\omega)$. Then $g^{\rm b}P(\omega)g^{\rm cc}(\omega)=|g^{\rm b}|^2P/\epsilon$ and

$${\rm Im}\frac{P}{1-vP}=\frac{{\rm Im}\left[P\,(1-vP^*)\right]}{|\epsilon|^2}=\frac{{\rm Im}P}{|\epsilon(\omega)|^2},$$

because $vPP^*$ is real. Hence

$${\rm Im}[g^{\rm b}Pg^{\rm cc}]=\frac{|g^{\rm b}|^2\,{\rm Im}P(\omega)}{|\epsilon(\omega)|^2}=|g(\omega)|^2\,{\rm Im}P(\omega).$$

With approximation (iv), $g^{\rm cc}(\omega)\to g^*(0)$, the same product becomes $|g^{\rm b}|^2{\rm Im}P(\omega)/\epsilon(0)=\epsilon(0)\,|g(0)|^2\,{\rm Im}P(\omega)$: the cancellation between ${\rm Re}P\,{\rm Im}\,\epsilon^{-1}$ and ${\rm Im}P\,{\rm Re}\,\epsilon^{-1}$ is lost.

A doped 2D semiconductor: the nonadiabatic window

The figure below evaluates (G.145) for the simplest system where adiabaticity fails: one dispersionless optical phonon $\omega_0$ (adiabatic, so it already contains $\Pi^{\rm A}$) coupled by a constant intraband matrix element to a single parabolic 2D band holding $n$ electrons per unit area. With $g^{\rm b}g^*\to|g|^2$ as in (G.146), $\int d\bk/\Omega_{\rm BZ}=A_{\rm cell}\int d^2k/(2\pi)^2$ turns the bracket of (G.145) into the 2D Lindhard function, $\chi^0=N_0\tilde\chi$ with $N_0=m^*/\pi\hbar^2$ (both spins), so that

$$\hbar\Pi^{\rm NA}(Q,\omega)=G\left[\tilde\chi(Q,W)-\tilde\chi(Q,0)\right],$$

where $G=N_0A_{\rm cell}|g|^2$ is the coupling strength, $Q=q/k_F$, $W=(\hbar\omega+i\eta)/\varepsilon_F$, and the closed form (retarded, $T=0$, checked against direct $\bk$ integration) is

$$\tilde\chi(Q,W)=-\left[1+\frac{s(W-Q^2)+s(-W-Q^2)}{2Q^2}\right],\qquad s(z)=z\sqrt{1-4Q^2/z^2},$$

using the principal square root; statically $\tilde\chi(Q,0)=-1$ for $Q\le2$. The phonon spectral function follows from the diagonal of (G.136),

$$B(Q,\omega)=-\frac1\pi\,{\rm Im}\,\frac{2\omega_0}{\omega^2-\omega_0^2+2i\eta\omega-2\omega_0\Pi^{\rm NA}(Q,\omega)},$$

written with the retarded denominator; $\eta$ adds a small intrinsic width so that undamped modes stay visible.

Near the upper continuum edge the first-order and self-consistent solutions differ strongly: the hardened pole can sit just above the edge and stay sharp, as the spectral map shows, while the first-order formula already samples the continuum at $\omega_0$. For $\varepsilon_F\gg\hbar\omega_0$ the width approaches the Landau-damping limit $\hbar\gamma\approx G\,\hbar\omega_0/[\varepsilon_FQ\sqrt{4-Q^2}]$, valid for $\hbar\omega_0\ll\varepsilon_FQ$ and $Q$ not close to 2. Mode coupling (iii) and plasmon–phonon poles (iv) are absent: the model has one mode and uses the bare bubble $\chi^0$ without the Coulomb chain, hence no plasmon.

Physical picture: two limits that do not commute

At $\bq\to0$ the intraband part of the bracket in (G.145) depends on the order of limits. Static first: the static bubble tends to $\partial f/\partial\varepsilon=-\delta(\varepsilon_{\bk}-\varepsilon_F)$, a Fermi-surface softening contained in the adiabatic phonon, which the second term of the bracket removes. Dynamic first: at $\bq=0$ the dynamical term vanishes, because a vibration faster than $v_Fq$ cannot rearrange the Fermi sea. The net result is a stiffening, $\hbar\,{\rm Re}\,\Pi^{\rm NA}_{\bq=0}\simeq N_F\langle|g|^2\rangle_{\rm FS}>0$ with $N_F$ counting both spins, the approximation of Saitta et al. (2008) quoted by Giustino. In the figure it is the hardening by $\approx G$ at small $Q$.

Where nonadiabatic effects have been seen

In the Raman G band of graphene ($E_{2g}$, 1585 cm⁻¹, $\bq=0$; Giustino §VII) electrons near the Dirac points make "virtual" transitions with energies comparable to the phonon; the measured frequency versus gate doping follows the nonadiabatic calculation while the adiabatic one stays flat (Pisana et al. 2007; Giustino Fig. 8). This is a nonadiabatic Kohn anomaly: it sits at small $\bq$, where the static and dynamic limits of (G.145) differ (callout above). The $2k_F$ anomaly of the jellium model below is an adiabatic one. The renormalization is typically about 1%, but reaches about 300 cm⁻¹ in graphite intercalation compounds (Saitta et al. 2008) and 7% at small $\bq$ in CaC$_6$ (Calandra, Profeta and Mauri 2010). In MgB$_2$ the calculation overshoots (761 vs 600 cm⁻¹). Saitta et al. suggested that finite electron lifetimes, absent from the Kohn–Sham $G$ of approximation (ii), partly wash out the effect. Linewidths from (G.146), or Allen's double-delta simplification (G Eq. 185), range from about 1 meV (Nb) to 30 meV (MgB$_2$).

Jellium: adiabatic phonons and the Kohn anomaly

The simplest $\Pi^{\rm A}$ belongs to point ions of valence $Z$ and mass $M$ in an electron gas. In G Eq. (121) at $\omega=0$ the ions interact through $W_{\rm e}(q,0)=v(q)/\epsilon_{\rm e}(q,0)$. Treating the ions as a uniform fluid (no lattice) with one ion per volume $\Omega$, the longitudinal mode obeys (cf. G Eqs. 121, 128; Bardeen–Pines)

$$M\omega_q^2=\frac{Z^2e^2}{\varepsilon_0\Omega}\,\frac{1}{\epsilon_{\rm e}(q,0)}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\omega_q^2=\frac{\Omega_p^2}{\epsilon_{\rm e}(q,0)},\qquad\Omega_p^2=\frac{Z^2e^2}{\varepsilon_0\Omega M}:$$

the bare ionic plasma oscillation, screened statically. With Thomas–Fermi screening, $\epsilon=1+k_{\rm TF}^2/q^2$, the mode is acoustic with the Bohm–Staver velocity $v_s=\Omega_p/k_{\rm TF}=(Zm_e/3M)^{1/2}v_F$. With the Lindhard function of §A.2, $\epsilon_{\rm e}(q,0)$ is continuous at $q=2k_F$ but its slope diverges logarithmically, because $2k_F$ is the largest momentum that a zero-energy electron–hole pair can carry across the Fermi sphere. The phonon inherits the singularity: $d\omega/dq$ diverges at $2k_F$. This is the Kohn anomaly (Kohn 1959), the reciprocal-space face of the Friedel oscillations that Giustino §VI.A.2 mentions for metals. It is an adiabatic, static-screening feature that DFPT reproduces and smearing blunts. Nonadiabatic corrections are small here: $\omega/qv_F\approx v_s/v_F=(Zm_e/3M)^{1/2}\sim10^{-3}$–$10^{-2}$, Migdal's small parameter.

Bridge to EPP: same Dyson equation, same bare–screened pair, photon lines instead of Coulomb lines

EPP §7 dresses its bare phonon propagator $F^0=\mathcal D^{\rm A}/\hbar$ by emission and reabsorption of photons and obtains a Dyson equation of exactly this form, $F=F^0+F^0\Omega^{\rm e}F$ (E.398), whose pole condition is (G.137) with $\Omega^{\rm e}=\hbar\Pi$ (§B.7). Its electron-induced part has one photon line dressed by electrons and one bare, and factorizes into bare vertex, bubble and screened vertex, the structure of (G.141) (§B.8). The match is structural, not term by term (§B.8 discusses EPP's modified bubble and its singular intraband current vertex), and double counting is avoided in a different way (last row of the table):

ObjectGiustino (this section)EPP §7
Reference propagator$\mathcal D^{\rm A}=2\omega_{\bq\nu}/(\omega^2-\omega_{\bq\nu}^2)$ (G.132)$\hbar F^0_\sigma$, bare short-range phonons
Self-energy$\hbar\Pi^{\rm NA}$ (G.141), (G.145)$\Omega^{\rm e}=\Omega^0+\Delta\Omega^{\rm e}$ (E.399–402)
Bare vertex$g^{\rm b}=\Delta_{\bq\nu}V^{\rm en}$, Coulomb line $v$$g^{{\rm dyn},0}$, bare photon line $D^0$
Screened vertex$g=\epsilon_{\rm e}^{-1}g^{\rm b}$, approximation (iv): static$g^{\rm dyn}$, dressed photon line $D^{\rm e}$, $\omega$-dependent
Avoiding double countingsubtract $\chi^0(0)$, already in DFPT $\Pi^{\rm A}$start from short-range force constants, regenerate the long-range part from $D$ (EPP p. 21)

Coulomb lines become photon propagators (longitudinal plus transverse), Born charges $Z^*$ replace the bare $Z_\kappa$, and only the long-range polar channel is treated.

Note on the source

Giustino writes the Saitta approximation as an average "over the wave vectors $\bk$ in the Brillouin zone". Derived from (G.145), the intraband static term gives $\delta(\varepsilon_{n\bk}-\varepsilon_F)$, so it is a Fermi-surface average, and $N_F$ must count both spins given the explicit factor 2 in (G.145). Elsewhere (e.g. G Eq. 192) Giustino's $N_F$ is per spin; in that convention the formula reads $2N_F\langle|g|^2\rangle_{\rm FS}$. G Eq. (127), used to obtain (G.128), has a sign and argument-order slip that leaves (G.128) unaffected; see the note at the end of §A.5.

A.7Giustino §V.B.1–2, §V.B.5–6, §VIII · Eqs. 147–174, 186–192

Electron self-energy: Fan–Migdal, Debye–Waller, kinks and satellites

An electron in a crystal drags a cloud of displaced ions and sees a crystal potential blurred by zero-point motion. Here these two pictures become the Fan–Migdal and Debye–Waller self-energies. You will see why Fan–Migdal carries two screened vertices, and how it produces ARPES kinks, mass enhancement and polaron satellites.

Clamped nuclei as the reference

DFT and GW band structures are computed for nuclei frozen at their equilibrium positions. Giustino takes this as the zeroth order. Setting the displacement correlation function to zero in the Hedin–Baym equations of §A.5 leaves Hedin's equations at clamped nuclei (G Eqs. 147–150). Their Green's function is $G^{\rm cn}$, and their self-energy $\Sigma^{\rm cn}_{\rm e}=i\hbar G^{\rm cn}\Gamma^{\rm cn}W^{\rm cn}_{\rm e}$ (G Eq. 150) is the familiar GW world. Everything that the moving nuclei add is then collected in one self-energy:

$$ G(12)=G^{\rm cn}(12)+\int d(34)\,G^{\rm cn}(13)\,\Sigma^{\rm ep}(34)\,G(42), \tag{G.151}$$
$$ \Sigma^{\rm ep}=\Sigma^{\rm FM}+\Sigma^{\rm DW}+\Sigma^{\rm dGW}, \tag{G.152}$$
$$ \begin{align} \Sigma^{\rm FM}(12)&=i\hbar\int d(34)\,G(13)\,\Gamma(324)\,W_{\rm ph}(41^+), \tag{G.153}\\ \Sigma^{\rm DW}(12)&=\int d3\,v(13)\big[\langle\hat n(3)\rangle-\langle\hat n^{\rm cn}(3)\rangle\big]\,\delta(12), \tag{G.154}\\ \Sigma^{\rm dGW}(12)&=\Sigma_{\rm e}(12)-\Sigma^{\rm cn}_{\rm e}(12). \tag{G.155}\end{align}$$

Here $1\equiv(\br_1,t_1)$, $v$ is the bare Coulomb interaction, $\hat n$ the total electron-plus-nuclear density (in units of the electron charge), $\Gamma$ Hedin's vertex, and $W=W_{\rm e}+W_{\rm ph}$ the screened interaction split into electronic and phonon parts. This is not an approximation: (G.151)–(G.155) regroup the Hedin–Baym equations exactly, within the harmonic approximation. Fan–Migdal is $W_{\rm ph}$ inserted into Hedin's $\Sigma=i\hbar G\Gamma W$, a dynamic term. Debye–Waller is the change of the self-consistent electrostatic potential $V_{\rm tot}$ because the nuclear charge is smeared around its equilibrium position, a static term. dGW is the change of the electronic GW self-energy because $G$, the density and $W_{\rm e}$ are modified by the coupling; it has never been investigated and is dropped here. We write Giustino's $D$ (his nuclear density correlator and his phonon propagator) as $\mathcal D$, to keep $D$ free for EPP's photon propagator. All equations are SI, as in the review; $\Sigma$ is an energy written as a function of the angular frequency $\omega$.

Why (G.152) is exact

Invert the equation of motion of the full electron Green's function (G Eq. 84), with $\Sigma=i\hbar G\Gamma(W_{\rm e}+W_{\rm ph})$ (G Eq. 85), and do the same for the clamped problem (G Eq. 147). Subtracting the two gives, in operator notation,

$$ G^{-1}=G^{{\rm cn},-1}-\big(V_{\rm tot}-V^{\rm cn}_{\rm tot}\big)\delta-\big(\Sigma_{\rm e}-\Sigma^{\rm cn}_{\rm e}\big)-i\hbar G\Gamma W_{\rm ph},\qquad \Sigma_{\rm e}\equiv i\hbar G\Gamma W_{\rm e}. $$

The potentials are $V_{\rm tot}(1)=\int d2\,v(12)\langle\hat n(2)\rangle$ (G Eq. 79, external field switched off) and $V^{\rm cn}_{\rm tot}(1)=\int d2\,v(12)\langle\hat n^{\rm cn}(2)\rangle$ (G Eq. 148). Their difference is exactly (G.154). The last two terms are (G.155) and (G.153). Multiplying by $G^{\rm cn}$ on the left and $G$ on the right turns $G^{-1}=G^{{\rm cn},-1}-\Sigma^{\rm ep}$ into the Dyson equation (G.151).

+ +

After Giustino Fig. 2(b)–(e), with the vertex $\Gamma$ omitted ($\Gamma=1$ in practice).

Physical picture

In GW, the correlation part of $\Sigma$ describes how an added carrier polarizes the other electrons, which then act back on it. Fan–Migdal is the same story with the lattice as the polarizable medium: the added carrier pushes the ions, and their displacement field pulls back on the carrier. In a polar crystal this is literally the Fröhlich polaron of §A.4. Debye–Waller needs no dynamics at all. Each nucleus is a fuzzy charge cloud of mean-square radius $\langle u^2\rangle$, and the electron simply sees the averaged, slightly washed-out potential.

Fan–Migdal is GW with two screened vertices

The phonon-mediated interaction of §A.5 is $W_{\rm ph}=W_{\rm e}\mathcal DW_{\rm e}$ (G Eq. 105), with $\mathcal D(34)$ the density–density correlation function of the nuclei (G Eq. 103; Giustino prints $D$). To first order in the displacements (G Eq. 110) it becomes, schematically, $W_{\rm ph}=\epsilon_{\rm e}^{-1}\nabla V_\kappa\;\mathcal D\;\epsilon_{\rm e}^{-1}\nabla V_{\kappa'}$, with the displacement correlator $\mathcal D_{\kappa\alpha p,\kappa'\alpha'p'}$ (G Eq. 109), the phonon propagator. Each end of the phonon line carries the bare nuclear-potential gradient screened by the full electronic $\epsilon_{\rm e}^{-1}$: the screened coupling $g=\epsilon_{\rm e}^{-1}g^{\rm b}$ (G Eqs. 143–144). Inserting this into (G.153) and expanding $\mathcal D$ in normal modes gives

$$ \begin{aligned} \Sigma^{\rm FM}(12)=i\sum_{\nu\nu'}\int\frac{d\omega}{2\pi}\frac{d\bq}{\Omega_{\rm BZ}}\,d(34)\,e^{-i\omega(t_4-t_1^+)}\,G(13)\,\Gamma(324)\\ \times\, g^{\rm cc}_{\bq\nu}(\br_4,\omega)\,\mathcal D_{\bq\nu\nu'}(\omega)\,g_{\bq\nu'}(\br_1,\omega). \end{aligned} \tag{G.156}$$

Symbolically $\Sigma^{\rm FM}=g^2\mathcal DG\Gamma$, and both $g$ and $g^{\rm cc}$ are screened. The phonon self-energy of §A.6 has one bare and one screened vertex (G Eq. 141): there the electron bubble between the two vertices supplies the screening chain, and it may be absorbed into one end only. In $\Sigma^{\rm FM}$ no bubble sits between the ends. Each end of the internal phonon line attaches directly to the propagating electron and needs its own screening chain, hence the $\epsilon_{\rm e}^{-1}$ on both sides of $W_{\rm ph}$. Conveniently, the screened DFPT matrix element of §A.3 is then the right object at both vertices.

vs

The working formula, at finite temperature and retarded

To make (G.156) computable Giustino makes five approximations: (i) $\Gamma(123)=\delta(13)\delta(23)$, the GW-type vertex; (ii) Kohn–Sham $G$ at clamped nuclei; (iii) the adiabatic phonon propagator $\mathcal D^{\rm A}$ (G Eq. 134); (iv) RPA+$xc$ screening of the vertex, as in DFPT; and (v) a frequency-independent coupling, $g_{\bq\nu}(\br,\omega)\simeq g_{\bq\nu}(\br,0)$. Closing the frequency contour in the upper half-plane then gives the Kohn–Sham matrix elements

$$ \begin{aligned} \Sigma^{\rm FM}_{nn'\bk}(\omega)=\frac{1}{\hbar}\sum_{m\nu}\int\frac{d\bq}{\Omega_{\rm BZ}}\,&g^*_{mn\nu}(\bk,\bq)\,g_{mn'\nu}(\bk,\bq)\\ \times\bigg[&\frac{1-f_{m\bk+\bq}}{\omega-\varepsilon_{m\bk+\bq}/\hbar-\omega_{\bq\nu}+i\eta}+\frac{f_{m\bk+\bq}}{\omega-\varepsilon_{m\bk+\bq}/\hbar+\omega_{\bq\nu}-i\eta}\bigg]. \end{aligned} \tag{G.157}$$

Here $g$ is the matrix element of G Eq. (38): an energy, independent of $N_p$, with the BZ integral normalized as an average; $\eta\to0^+$. The first term is an intermediate state with an empty band state plus an emitted phonon. The second is an occupied state, a hole, plus a phonon. Equation (G.157) holds at $T=0$ and is time-ordered. At finite temperature (Matsubara sums, then continuation to the real axis) the bracket becomes

$$ \left[\frac{1-f_{m\bk+\bq}}{\cdots+i\eta}+\frac{f_{m\bk+\bq}}{\cdots-i\eta}\right]\;\to\;\left[\frac{1-f_{m\bk+\bq}+n_{\bq\nu}}{\cdots+i\eta}+\frac{f_{m\bk+\bq}+n_{\bq\nu}}{\cdots+i\eta}\right], \tag{G.158}$$

with Fermi–Dirac $f$ and Bose–Einstein $n$. For an electron above $E_F$, $1-f+n$ weights phonon emission (spontaneous plus stimulated) and $f+n$ absorption. For a hole at $T=0$ only the $f$ term is resonant: the hole emits a phonon by moving to an occupied state closer to $E_F$. The second $i\eta$ has changed sign: (G.158) is the retarded self-energy, with all poles below the real axis and ${\rm Im}\,\Sigma\le0$ for every state. Only this form gives a positive spectral function. Evaluated at the band energy, its imaginary part gives the golden-rule rate $1/\tau=2|{\rm Im}\,\Sigma|/\hbar$ used for lifetimes in §A.8.

Approximations hiding in (G.157)

"Retarded" has a third meaning here: the causal analytic structure of $G$ and $\Sigma$. It is neither EPP's finite speed of light nor Giustino's frequency-dependent electronic screening (his §IV); approximation (v) discards the latter at the vertex. Migdal level. The self-energy is built from bare propagators, so diagrams beyond the Migdal approximation are omitted (Giustino §V.B.6). Adiabatic phonons. By (iii), the nonadiabatic phonon shifts and widths of §A.6 do not feed back.

Debye–Waller: the crystal potential, blurred

Each nucleus jitters with a mean-square amplitude proportional to $(2n_{\bq\nu}+1)\hbar/2M\omega_{\bq\nu}$. Expanding $\langle\hat n\rangle$ in (G.154) to second order in these displacements gives a tadpole, a phonon line that starts and ends at the same time:

$$ \Sigma^{\rm DW}(12)=\delta(12)\,\frac{i\hbar}{2}\sum_{\substack{\kappa\alpha p\\ \kappa'\alpha'p'}}\frac{\partial^2V_{\rm tot}(1)}{\partial\tau^0_{\kappa\alpha p}\,\partial\tau^0_{\kappa'\alpha'p'}}\,\mathcal D_{\kappa\alpha p,\kappa'\alpha'p'}(t_1^+,t_1). \tag{G.159}$$

Here $\tau^0_{\kappa\alpha p}$ is the equilibrium coordinate $\alpha$ of atom $\kappa$ in cell $p$, and the equal-time propagator is just the mean-square displacement divided by $i\hbar$, $\langle\Delta\hat\tau\Delta\hat\tau'\rangle/i\hbar$. Deriving (G.159) needs one extra assumption, that electron operators and displacements are uncorrelated (Gillis 1970). With (vi) $\mathcal D\to\mathcal D^{\rm A}$ and (vii) $V_{\rm tot}\to V^{\rm KS}$,

$$ \begin{align} \Sigma^{\rm DW}_{nn'\bk}&=\sum_\nu\int\frac{d\bq}{\Omega_{\rm BZ}}\,g^{\rm DW}_{nn'\nu\nu}(\bk,\bq,-\bq), \tag{G.160}\\ g^{\rm DW}_{nn'\nu\nu}(\bk,\bq,-\bq)&\;\to\;g^{\rm DW}_{nn'\nu\nu}(\bk,\bq,-\bq)\,(2n_{\bq\nu}+1). \tag{G.161}\end{align}$$

The replacement (G.161) is the finite-temperature form; $2n+1=\coth(\hbar\omega/2k_BT)$ counts zero-point plus thermal motion. The second-order matrix element is that of the Debye–Waller Hamiltonian, with $\Delta_{\bq\nu}v^{\rm KS}$ the phonon-induced change of the Kohn–Sham potential of §A.2:

$$ g^{\rm DW}_{mn\nu\nu'}(\bk,\bq,\bq')=\tfrac12\big\langle u_{m\bk+\bq+\bq'}\big|\Delta_{\bq\nu}\Delta_{\bq'\nu'}v^{\rm KS}\big|u_{n\bk}\big\rangle_{\rm uc}. \tag{G.40}$$

Combining the two (Giustino §VIII) shows what kind of object this is:

$$ \Sigma^{\rm DW}_{nn\bk}=\langle u_{n\bk}|V_{\rm DW}|u_{n\bk}\rangle_{\rm uc},\qquad V_{\rm DW}(\br)=\Omega_{\rm BZ}^{-1}\sum_\nu\int d\bq\,\big(n_{\bq\nu}+\tfrac12\big)\,\Delta_{\bq\nu}\Delta_{-\bq\nu}v^{\rm KS}(\br). \tag{G.190}$$

$V_{\rm DW}$ is a static, local, real potential. It has no frequency dependence, so it produces no kink, and no imaginary part, so it gives no lifetime. In the homogeneous electron gas it is a $\bk$-independent constant. In real crystals it varies smoothly within a band but very differently between bands. This is why kink analyses in metals drop it, while band-gap renormalization cannot (§A.8). Fan–Migdal at second order in $g$ and Debye–Waller at first order in $g^{\rm DW}$ are of the same order in $\langle u^2\rangle$, and they partly cancel.

Spectral function, quasiparticle weight and the kink

If $\Sigma^{\rm ep}$ only shifts the poles of $G$ slightly, the renormalized energies follow from the Brillouin–Wigner (BW) condition

$$ E_{n\bk}=\varepsilon_{n\bk}+{\rm Re}\,\Sigma^{\rm ep}_{n\bk}(\tilde E_{n\bk}/\hbar), \tag{G.164}$$

with broadening $\Gamma_{n\bk}={\rm Im}\,\Sigma^{\rm ep}_{n\bk}(\tilde E_{n\bk}/\hbar)$ (G Eq. 165) and $\tilde E=E+i\Gamma$. Rayleigh–Schrödinger (RS) perturbation theory evaluates $\Sigma$ at the bare energy instead. When electronic energy scales are comparable to phonon energies, as in metals and doped or narrow-gap semiconductors, no single pole is adequate and one needs the full spectral function:

$$ A(\bk,\omega)=\sum_n\frac{-(1/\pi)\,{\rm Im}\,\Sigma^{\rm ep}_{nn\bk}(\omega)}{\big[\hbar\omega-\varepsilon_{n\bk}-{\rm Re}\,\Sigma^{\rm ep}_{nn\bk}(\omega)\big]^2+\big[{\rm Im}\,\Sigma^{\rm ep}_{nn\bk}(\omega)\big]^2}, \tag{G.172}$$
$$ Z_{n\bk}=\Big[1-\hbar^{-1}\,\partial{\rm Re}\,\Sigma^{\rm ep}_{nn\bk}(\omega)/\partial\omega\big|_{\omega=E_{n\bk}/\hbar}\Big]^{-1}. \tag{G.174}$$

Linearizing (G.172) near each pole gives Lorentzians of weight $Z$ and half-width $Z|{\rm Im}\,\Sigma|$ (G Eq. 173), with the same $Z$ you know from GW. Differentiating (G.164) along $\bk$, and neglecting the explicit $\bk$ dependence of $\Sigma$, gives the velocity renormalization $\mathbf V_{n\bk}=Z_{n\bk}\mathbf v_{n\bk}=\mathbf v_{n\bk}/(1+\lambda_{n\bk})$, with

$$ \lambda_{n\bk}=Z^{-1}_{n\bk}-1=-\hbar^{-1}\,\partial{\rm Re}\,\Sigma_{nn\bk}(\omega)/\partial\omega\big|_{\omega=E_{n\bk}/\hbar}. \tag{G.189}$$

For a parabolic band whose Fermi wave vector is fixed by Luttinger's theorem, this is a mass enhancement $m_{\rm ep}=m^*(1+\lambda)$.

Why the kink sits at $-\hbar\omega_0$

At $T=0$ a hole at energy $E<0$ can decay by emitting a real phonon only if an occupied state exists at $E+\hbar\omega_0$, that is, only if $|E|>\hbar\omega_0$. Inside the window $|E|<\hbar\omega_0$ the hole is dressed by virtual phonons: heavy, with weight $Z$, but long-lived. Outside it, emission opens, ${\rm Im}\,\Sigma$ jumps to $-\pi\lambda\hbar\omega_0/2$ (constant density of states), and ${\rm Re}\,\Sigma$ decays, so the band returns to its bare dispersion with a large width. The kink is the boundary between the two regimes. Graphene shows it between 150 and 200 meV, weakly because $\lambda\sim0.1$ (Giustino §VIII).

The Eliashberg function and the mass-enhancement parameter

For ARPES, Giustino rewrites (G.157)+(G.158) in spectral form, with all electron energies measured from $E_F$:

$$ \begin{aligned} \Sigma^{\rm FM}_{nn\bk}(\omega,T)=\int_{-\infty}^{+\infty}\!d\varepsilon\int_0^\infty\! d\varepsilon'\,\alpha^2F_{n\bk}(\varepsilon,\varepsilon')\bigg[&\frac{1-f(\varepsilon/k_BT)+n(\varepsilon'/k_BT)}{\hbar\omega-\varepsilon-\varepsilon'+i\hbar\eta}\\ +&\frac{f(\varepsilon/k_BT)+n(\varepsilon'/k_BT)}{\hbar\omega-\varepsilon+\varepsilon'+i\hbar\eta}\bigg], \end{aligned} \tag{G.186}$$
$$ \alpha^2F_{n\bk}(\varepsilon,\varepsilon')=\sum_{m\nu}\int\frac{d\bq}{\Omega_{\rm BZ}}\,|g_{mn\nu}(\bk,\bq)|^2\,\delta(\varepsilon-\varepsilon_{m\bk+\bq})\,\delta(\varepsilon'-\hbar\omega_{\bq\nu}). \tag{G.187}$$

The Eliashberg function $\alpha^2F$ is positive, temperature independent and contains all the material-specific information. It is proportional to the rate at which state $|n\bk\rangle$ scatters into states at energy $\varepsilon$ by emitting or absorbing a phonon of energy $\varepsilon'$. With an isotropic average, particle–hole symmetry and phonon energies neglected next to electron energies, $|{\rm Im}\,\Sigma|$ at $T=0$ becomes the cumulative integral $\pi\int_0^{|E|}d\varepsilon'\,\alpha^2F(\varepsilon')$ (from G Eq. 188). That is a step at $\hbar\omega_{\rm ph}$ for an Einstein mode, as in the Be(0001) surface state with an onset at 40–80 meV (Giustino Fig. 11). The Eliashberg coupling $\lambda=2\int d\varepsilon'\,\alpha^2F(\varepsilon')/\varepsilon'$, which Giustino prints as Eq. (206) with the isotropic Fermi-surface $\alpha^2F$ of his superconductivity section (§A.9), is the slope $-\partial_E{\rm Re}\,\Sigma|_{E_F}$ of (G.189) under the same assumptions. In the model above, $\alpha^2F$ at $E_F$ is the Einstein spectrum $(\lambda\hbar\omega_0/2)\,\delta(\varepsilon'-\hbar\omega_0)$, so the slider sets this $\lambda$; the readout $\lambda_{\rm eff}$ deviates slightly because the band is finite and lacks particle–hole symmetry.

The same $\lambda$ enhances the low-temperature electronic heat capacity, which follows from Grimvall's entropy formula (G Eq. 191) with $\Sigma^{\rm FM}\simeq-\lambda\hbar\omega$:

$$ C_{\rm e}=T\frac{\partial S_{\rm e}}{\partial T}=\frac{2}{3}\pi^2k_B^2N_F(1+\lambda_{n\bk})\,T, \tag{G.192}$$

where the prefactor implies $N_F$ per spin. The enhancement holds only for $k_BT\ll\hbar\omega_{\rm ph}$; at high temperature it disappears. The same $\lambda$ controls superconducting $T_c$ (§A.9).

Reading $\lambda$ off ARPES

Estimating $\lambda$ from the ratio of band velocities above and below the kink requires the unknown bare velocity, fitted with ad hoc models; near van Hove singularities this overestimates $\lambda$ significantly (Giustino §VIII). Without particle–hole symmetry, as in doped graphene, ${\rm Re}\,\Sigma$ tends to a linear asymptote instead of decaying.

Beyond Dyson: the cumulant and polaron satellites

The Dyson equation with the one-phonon self-energy (G.157) never has two phonons present at the same time. It can therefore produce at most one satellite per phonon mode, and in the single-level model below that satellite sits too far from the quasiparticle. This is the same failure you know from plasmon satellites in GW. The cure is also the same, the cumulant expansion (Giustino §V.B.6, unnumbered):

$$ G_{n\bk}(t)=\frac{i}{\hbar}\exp\!\Big[-i\frac{\varepsilon_{n\bk}}{\hbar}t+C_{n\bk}(t)\Big]. $$

The cumulant $C$ is obtained from a low-order self-energy such as Fan–Migdal, and the exponential generates the higher-order diagrams automatically. Verdi, Caruso and Giustino (2017) used it to reproduce the polaron satellites measured by ARPES in $n$-doped TiO$_2$.

Cumulant for one level and one phonon

Take an occupied level $\varepsilon_0$ and let the hole created in it at $t=0$ couple with constant $g$ to a dispersionless phonon $\hbar\omega_0$ (Langreth's core-hole problem, an independent-boson model). Define the Huang–Rhys factor $S=|g|^2/(\hbar\omega_0)^2$. The Fan–Migdal self-energy (G.157), occupied term only and retarded, is $\Sigma(E)=|g|^2/(E-\varepsilon_0+\hbar\omega_0+i\eta)$. Dyson's $G=[E-\varepsilon_0-\Sigma]^{-1}$ then has exactly two poles, at $x_\pm=E-\varepsilon_0=\tfrac{\hbar\omega_0}{2}\big(-1\pm\sqrt{1+4S}\big)$, with weights $Z_\pm=\big[1+S(\hbar\omega_0)^2/(x_\pm+\hbar\omega_0)^2\big]^{-1}$ that sum to 1.

Matching the cumulant to the same second-order term gives, for the hole branch ($t<0$), $C(t)=S\big(e^{i\omega_0t}-1-i\omega_0t\big)$. Exponentiating,

$$ e^{C(t)}=e^{-S}\,e^{-iS\omega_0t}\sum_{n\ge0}\frac{S^n}{n!}\,e^{in\omega_0t}\quad\Rightarrow\quad A(E)=\sum_{n\ge0}e^{-S}\frac{S^n}{n!}\,\delta\big(E-\varepsilon_0-S\hbar\omega_0+n\hbar\omega_0\big). $$

The quasiparticle sits at $\varepsilon_0+S\hbar\omega_0$, closer to $E_F$, with weight $e^{-S}$. Replicas follow at exact multiples of $\hbar\omega_0$ with Poisson (Franck–Condon) weights. For this model the second-order cumulant is exact (Langreth 1970). Both methods agree to first order in $S$: $x_+\simeq S\hbar\omega_0$ and $Z_+\simeq e^{-S}\simeq1-S$.

The cumulant is also where first-principles work meets the older model-Hamiltonian literature (Giustino §V.B.6). Choosing $\varepsilon_{n\bk}$, $\omega_{\bq\nu}$ and $g$ by hand in G Eq. (1), usually with tight-binding bands, Einstein phonons and coupling linear in the displacements, gives the Fröhlich, Holstein and Su–Schrieffer–Heeger models and their Hubbard-type extensions; the single-level model above is the simplest of them. Such models can be solved beyond the approximations of (G.157), nonperturbatively, by Lang–Firsov transformations, path integrals, exact diagonalization or variational and quantum Monte Carlo. They map out the polaron questions a Dyson-level calculation cannot answer: weak versus strong coupling, large versus small polarons, bandlike versus hopping transport. Giustino notes that the cumulant is closely related to Berciu's momentum-average approximation for the Holstein polaron, and in 2017 he judged that the study of polarons with ab initio many-body techniques was "yet to begin". EPP does not reach this far, since it derives no electron self-energy (§Z.1).

Note on the source

The prefactor $i/\hbar$ of the cumulant formula belongs to the hole branch ($t<0$), appropriate for ARPES; for electrons it is $-i/\hbar$. The Fig. 4 caption calls the cutoff both $\varepsilon_{\rm max}$ and $\varepsilon_c$ and does not say whether $N_F$ counts both spins, so $|g|^2=\hbar\omega_0/N_F$ means $\lambda=2$ or $\lambda=1$; our default $\lambda=1.2$ sits between.

Bridge to EPP: the missing piece

EPP derives no electron self-energy. It dresses photons with $\Pi_{jj}$ (§B.5, §B.6) and phonons with $\Omega^{\rm e}$ (§B.7), and finds its electrodynamic Fröhlich vertices inside the phonon self-energy (§B.8). The natural analogue of (G.153) is an electron exchanging the total photon propagator $D$, dressed by electrons and ions, through current vertices. For $c\to\infty$ its longitudinal part reduces to $W_{\rm e}$ plus the polar part of $W_{\rm ph}$: GW plus the Fröhlich part of Fan–Migdal. The transverse part adds current–current terms of order $(v/c)^2$ and polariton effects inside the light cone, $q\lesssim q_c=\sqrt{\epsilon^\infty}\,\omega/c$ (§X.1). Such a theory would keep frequency-dependent vertices, relaxing approximation (v), but it would lack short-range deformation-potential coupling (absent from EPP's Lagrangian) and Debye–Waller (no second-order vertex; the $A^2$ term is only an analogy). EPP's "$n_B=0$" rule (EPP §4.5, §B.5) does not carry over, since (G.158) needs both $n$ and $f$. See §X.2 and §Z.1.

A.8Giustino §V.B.3–4, §IX.A, §X.A · Eqs. 162–170, 193–199

Band gaps vs temperature, lifetimes and the Fröhlich catastrophe

Atoms never stand still, not even at zero temperature, so every band energy is shifted and broadened by the lattice. Here the self-energies of §A.7 become measurable numbers: the temperature-dependent gap with its zero-point renormalization, and carrier lifetimes. You will also see why the adiabatic Allen–Heine formula diverges in polar crystals, and why the cure is the phonon energy $\hbar\omega$, not the speed of light.

Quasiparticle energies from Fan–Migdal plus Debye–Waller

An electron in a vibrating crystal feels the lattice in two ways. It sees a crystal potential blurred by the zero-point and thermal motion of the ions (Debye–Waller), and it polarizes the lattice around itself by emitting and reabsorbing virtual phonons (Fan–Migdal). Both effects are second order in the displacement, so both scale with $\langle u^2\rangle\propto(2n_{\bq\nu}+1)\hbar/2M\omega_{\bq\nu}$. At $T=0$ they leave a zero-point renormalization (ZPR); as the phonon populations $n_{\bq\nu}(T)$ grow, the shift grows with them.

Formally, take the clamped-nuclei Kohn–Sham or GW energies $\varepsilon_{n\bk}$ as the reference (§A.7). In the Kohn–Sham basis the Dyson equation (G Eq. 151) becomes

$$ \begin{align} G^{-1}_{nn'\bk}(\omega)&=G^{{\rm cn},-1}_{nn'\bk}(\omega)-\Sigma^{\rm ep}_{nn'\bk}(\omega), \tag{G.162}\\ G^{-1}_{nn'\bk}(\omega)&=(\hbar\omega-\tilde\varepsilon_{n\bk})\,\delta_{nn'}-\Sigma^{\rm ep}_{nn'\bk}(\omega),\qquad \tilde\varepsilon_{n\bk}=\varepsilon_{n\bk}\pm i\hbar\eta, \tag{G.163}\end{align}$$

with the upper sign for occupied states. For a nondegenerate state, neglecting the off-diagonal $\Sigma^{\rm ep}_{nn'\bk}$, and if $\Sigma^{\rm ep}$ only moves the pole slightly, $\varepsilon_{n\bk}\to\tilde E_{n\bk}=E_{n\bk}+i\Gamma_{n\bk}$, the real part of the new pole follows from the Brillouin–Wigner condition (G.164) of §A.7, and the imaginary part is

$$ \Gamma_{n\bk}={\rm Im}\,\Sigma^{\rm ep}_{n\bk}(\tilde E_{n\bk}/\hbar). \tag{G.165}$$

Here $\Gamma_{n\bk}$ is a linewidth, not the vertex function. Inserting the finite-temperature Fan–Migdal (G.157)+(G.158) and Debye–Waller (G.160)+(G.161) self-energies into (G.164) gives Giustino's temperature-dependent "band structure renormalization":

$$ \begin{aligned} E_{n\bk}=\varepsilon_{n\bk}&+\sum_\nu\int\frac{d\bq}{\Omega_{\rm BZ}}\sum_m|g_{mn\nu}(\bk,\bq)|^2\\ &\times{\rm Re}\bigg[\frac{1-f_{m\bk+\bq}+n_{\bq\nu}}{E_{n\bk}-\varepsilon_{m\bk+\bq}-\hbar\omega_{\bq\nu}+i\Gamma_{n\bk}}+\frac{f_{m\bk+\bq}+n_{\bq\nu}}{E_{n\bk}-\varepsilon_{m\bk+\bq}+\hbar\omega_{\bq\nu}+i\Gamma_{n\bk}}\bigg]\\ &+\sum_\nu\int\frac{d\bq}{\Omega_{\rm BZ}}\,g^{\rm DW}_{nn\nu\nu}(\bk,\bq,-\bq)\,(2n_{\bq\nu}+1). \end{aligned} \tag{G.166}$$

The coupling $g_{mn\nu}(\bk,\bq)$ is the screened DFPT matrix element of G Eq. (38), an energy without $N_p$; $f_{m\bk+\bq}$ and $n_{\bq\nu}$ are Fermi–Dirac and Bose–Einstein occupations, and the $\bq$ integrals are Brillouin-zone averages (SI units throughout). Equation (G.166) rests on the harmonic approximation and on approximations (i)–(vii) of §A.7. Allen and Heine (1976) made two more: Rayleigh–Schrödinger instead of Brillouin–Wigner ($E_{n\bk}\to\varepsilon_{n\bk}$, $\Gamma_{n\bk}\to0$ inside the bracket), and phonon energies dropped from the denominators. The occupations then cancel, $(1-f+n)+(f+n)=1+2n$, and one obtains the adiabatic Allen–Heine formula

$$ \begin{aligned} E_{n\bk}=\varepsilon_{n\bk}+\sum_\nu\int\frac{d\bq}{\Omega_{\rm BZ}}\bigg[&\sum_m\frac{|g_{mn\nu}(\bk,\bq)|^2}{\varepsilon_{n\bk}-\varepsilon_{m\bk+\bq}}\\ &+g^{\rm DW}_{nn\nu\nu}(\bk,\bq,-\bq)\bigg](2n_{\bq\nu}+1). \end{aligned} \tag{G.167}$$

Setting $n_{\bq\nu}=0$ defines the zero-point renormalization $\Delta E^{\rm ZP}_{n\bk}=E_{n\bk}(T=0)-\varepsilon_{n\bk}$. Allen and Heine originally reached (G.167) by expanding adiabatic energies in the displacements and averaging with Bose–Einstein statistics; the field theory lands on the same formula.

Two different "adiabatic" approximations

Both rest on the same Born–Oppenheimer assumption, that $\hbar\omega_{\bq\nu}$ is small next to the electronic energy differences involved, but they apply it to different processes. The adiabatic phonons of §A.6 use static electronic screening, $\epsilon_{\rm e}(\omega=0)$: the electrons follow the ions instantly. In an insulator the electronic excitations that screen a phonon cross the gap, so this is excellent. The adiabatic Allen–Heine formula drops $\hbar\omega_{\bq\nu}$ next to $\varepsilon_{n\bk}-\varepsilon_{m\bk+\bq}$: the electron sees a frozen lattice distortion. Near a band extremum the intraband differences $\varepsilon_{n\bk}-\varepsilon_{n\bk+\bq}$ go to zero as $\bq\to0$, so the assumption always fails for small $\bq$, even in a wide-gap insulator. With nonpolar coupling that region carries little weight; with the polar $1/q^2$ coupling it dominates, which is the root of the Fröhlich catastrophe below.

Allen–Heine in practice: Debye–Waller from first-order matrix elements

The Debye–Waller term needs second derivatives of $V^{\rm KS}$, which are expensive. Allen and Heine avoided them with translational invariance: rigidly translating the crystal cannot change an eigenvalue, even when the crystal has already been displaced. Second-order perturbation theory turns this into two sum rules (derivation below). In the rigid-ion approximation, where $V^{\rm KS}$ is a sum of atom-centred potentials, only on-site second derivatives survive, and they become products of first-order matrix elements at $\bq=0$:

$$ \Sigma^{\rm DW}_{nn\bk}=-{\sum_{\nu m}}'\int\frac{d\bq}{\Omega_{\rm BZ}}\,\frac{g^{2,{\rm DW}}_{mn\nu}(\bk,\bq)}{\varepsilon_{n\bk}-\varepsilon_{m\bk}}\,(2n_{\bq\nu}+1). \tag{G.195}$$

The denominator connects states at the same $\bk$, and the overall sign is opposite to Fan–Migdal: the Debye–Waller term looks like a Fan term with the opposite sign, which is what guarantees zero shift for a uniform translation. The effective matrix element $g^{2,{\rm DW}}$ costs only first-order DFPT plus matrix multiplications. The rigid-ion error is about 10 meV in diamond and below 4 meV in all cases tested by Poncé et al. (2014). In diamond, Fan–Migdal and Debye–Waller are of comparable magnitude, so neither can be dropped.

The two sum rules and the effective Debye–Waller element

Translational invariance to first and second order in the displacements gives

$$ \sum_{\kappa p}\langle\psi_{n\bk}|\partial_{\kappa\alpha p}V^{\rm KS}|\psi_{n\bk}\rangle_{\rm sc}=0, \tag{G.193}$$ $$ \begin{aligned} \sum_{\kappa'p'}\langle\psi_{n\bk}|\partial^2_{\kappa\alpha p,\kappa'\alpha'p'}V^{\rm KS}|\psi_{n\bk}\rangle_{\rm sc}=&-2\,{\rm Re}\sum_{\kappa'p'}{\sum_{m\bq}}'\\ &\times\frac{\langle\psi_{n\bk}|\partial_{\kappa\alpha p}V^{\rm KS}|\psi_{m\bk+\bq}\rangle_{\rm sc}\langle\psi_{m\bk+\bq}|\partial_{\kappa'\alpha'p'}V^{\rm KS}|\psi_{n\bk}\rangle_{\rm sc}}{\varepsilon_{n\bk}-\varepsilon_{m\bk+\bq}}, \end{aligned} \tag{G.194}$$

where $\partial_{\kappa\alpha p}\equiv\partial/\partial\tau_{\kappa\alpha p}$, "sc" is an integral over the Born–von Kármán supercell, and the prime excludes degenerate states. The first rule says that the matrix elements of the three translational modes at $\bq=0$ vanish, another form of the acoustic sum rule. In the rigid-ion approximation only $\kappa'p'=\kappa p$ survives on the left of (G.194), which expresses the on-site second derivative through first derivatives. With Eqs. (20), (33)–(35), (38) and a canonical average over adiabatic nuclear states this gives (G.195) with

$$ g^{2,{\rm DW}}_{mn\nu}(\bk,\bq)=\sum_{\kappa\alpha,\kappa'\alpha'}\frac{t^\nu_{\kappa\alpha,\kappa'\alpha'}(\bq)}{2\omega_{\bq\nu}}\,h^*_{mn,\kappa\alpha}(\bk)\,h_{mn,\kappa'\alpha'}(\bk), \tag{G.196}$$ $$ t^\nu_{\kappa\alpha,\kappa'\alpha'}(\bq)=\frac{e_{\kappa\alpha\nu}(\bq)\,e^*_{\kappa\alpha'\nu}(\bq)}{M_\kappa}+\frac{e_{\kappa'\alpha\nu}(\bq)\,e^*_{\kappa'\alpha'\nu}(\bq)}{M_{\kappa'}}, \tag{G.197}$$ $$ h_{mn,\kappa\alpha}(\bk)=\sum_\nu(M_\kappa\omega_{0\nu})^{1/2}\,e_{\kappa\alpha\nu}(0)\,g_{mn\nu}(\bk,0). \tag{G.198}$$

$h$ is, up to normalization, the Cartesian matrix element $\langle\psi_{m\bk}|\partial_{\kappa\alpha,\bq=0}V^{\rm KS}|\psi_{n\bk}\rangle$, recovered from the mode-resolved $g$ at $\Gamma$ (real eigenvectors assumed). For the three translational modes at $\bq=0$ one sets the effective element to zero. Like (G.167), (G.195) needs sums over many empty states; Gonze, Boulanger and Côté (2011) replace most of them by a Sternheimer-type DFPT solution.
