The Varshni curve and the zero-point renormalization

To see the generic shape, Giustino takes a semiconductor with parabolic, nondegenerate bands whose extrema couple to all states through one dispersionless phonon $\omega_0$, with Debye–Waller elements much smaller than Fan–Migdal. The dominant denominators in (G.167) are then intraband, $\varepsilon_{n\bk}-\varepsilon_{n\bk+\bq}\simeq\pm\hbar^2|\bq|^2/2m^*_n$ (upper sign for the valence band). The states just above the conduction-band minimum push it down, and the states just below the valence-band maximum push it up: level repulsion closes the gap,

$$ E_g(T)=E_g^{\rm cn}-|\Delta E_g^{\rm ZP}|\,\big[1+2n(\hbar\omega_0/k_BT)\big]. \tag{G.168}$$

Here $n(x)=1/(e^x-1)$ is the Bose–Einstein occupation and $1+2n(x)=\coth(x/2)$. There are two regimes. For $k_BT\ll\hbar\omega_0$ the Bose factor is exponentially small and the gap sits on a plateau at $E_g^{\rm cn}-|\Delta E_g^{\rm ZP}|$; it stays within 10% of the zero-point shift up to $k_BT\approx\hbar\omega_0/3$. For $k_BT\gg\hbar\omega_0$, $1+2n\simeq2k_BT/\hbar\omega_0+\hbar\omega_0/6k_BT$, so the gap falls linearly with slope $-2k_B|\Delta E_g^{\rm ZP}|/\hbar\omega_0$. The linear asymptote extrapolated to $T=0$ lands on $E_g^{\rm cn}$, not on the measured $E_g(0)$, and this is how the ZPR is extracted from experiment.

The red shift is the Varshni effect, first measured by Becker and Fan (1949), which prompted Fan's 1951 theory. It is not universal: copper halides and lead-halide perovskites show an "inverse Varshni" blue shift, and some chalcopyrites are nonmonotonic. Magnitudes can be large. For the direct gap of diamond, Giustino, Louie and Cohen (2010) confirmed a zero-point renormalization above 0.5 eV with DFT-LDA. Antonius et al. (2014) found that GW-corrected matrix elements increase the renormalization by up to about 200 meV; with them it is 628 meV (Giustino Fig. 13), because DFT over-screens the coupling (§A.9). In Fig. 13 their DFPT-LDA curve lies 0.23 eV above the GW one at $T=0$, which implies an LDA value near 0.4 eV if both share one clamped-nuclei gap; the review does not comment on the difference from the earlier value above 0.5 eV.

Note on the source: Fig. 3

Fig. 3. The caption gives $\hbar\omega_0=100$ meV, but the printed curves follow (G.168) with $\hbar\omega_0\approx50$ meV (the figure above offers both presets), and the lifetime axis is off by a factor of about 2.5. Signs. $\Gamma_{n\bk}<0$ for electrons and $>0$ for holes holds for the time-ordered (G.157); with the retarded (G.158), ${\rm Im}\,\Sigma\le0$ for every state, hence $|\Gamma|$ in $\tau$. The numerical checks and two smaller slips near (G.198) are listed in §Z.2.

Lifetimes from the imaginary part

The imaginary part of the pole says how long a carrier stays in $|n\bk\rangle$. The persistence amplitude decays as $\exp(-|\Gamma_{n\bk}|\,|t'-t|/\hbar)$, so the probability decays twice as fast and the lifetime is $\tau_{n\bk}=\hbar/(2|\Gamma_{n\bk}|)$. Replacing $\tilde E_{n\bk}\to\varepsilon_{n\bk}$ in the Fan–Migdal self-energy and taking the imaginary part gives the zero-temperature golden rule (G Eq. 169). The retarded finite-temperature form (G.158) gives

$$ \begin{aligned} \frac{1}{\tau_{n\bk}}=\frac{2\pi}{\hbar}\sum_{m\nu}\int\frac{d\bq}{\Omega_{\rm BZ}}\,|g_{mn\nu}(\bk,\bq)|^2\Big[&(1-f_{m\bk+\bq}+n_{\bq\nu})\,\delta(\varepsilon_{n\bk}-\hbar\omega_{\bq\nu}-\varepsilon_{m\bk+\bq})\\ +&(f_{m\bk+\bq}+n_{\bq\nu})\,\delta(\varepsilon_{n\bk}+\hbar\omega_{\bq\nu}-\varepsilon_{m\bk+\bq})\Big]. \end{aligned} \tag{G.170}$$

This is Fermi's golden rule. The first line is phonon emission, stimulated ($n$) plus spontaneous ($1$), reduced by Pauli blocking of the final state ($-f$); the second is absorption. Debye–Waller does not contribute, because its diagonal elements are real. Neglecting $\hbar\omega$ in the delta functions, Giustino's toy model gives $\Gamma_{n\bk}(T)=\Gamma^{\rm ZP}_{n\bk}[1+2n(\hbar\omega_0/k_BT)]$: width and shift share one Bose factor, as in the figure above. A rigorous treatment multiplies the broadening by the quasiparticle weight $Z_{n\bk}$ of §A.7 and evaluates it at $E_{n\bk}$. For photoluminescence linewidths of lead-iodide perovskites the bare golden rule overestimates the data, and this $Z$ factor restores agreement (Giustino §X.A).

vs

In a polar semiconductor, carriers near the band edge scatter mainly with the LO phonon, through the long-range Fröhlich coupling of §A.4 (G Eqs. 2 and 7, $N_p$ dropped): $|g(\bq)|^2=\frac{e^2}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\frac{4\pi}{\Omega}\frac{\hbar\omega_{\rm LO}}{2}\big(\frac{1}{\epsilon^\infty}-\frac{1}{\epsilon^0}\big)\frac{1}{q^2}$, with $\Omega$ the cell volume and $\epsilon^\infty$, $\epsilon^0$ the high-frequency and static dielectric constants. For one parabolic band of mass $m^*$, otherwise empty ($f=0$), (G.170) integrates in closed form (derivation below):

$$ \begin{aligned} \frac{1}{\tau(\varepsilon)}&=2\alpha\omega_{\rm LO}\sqrt{\frac{\hbar\omega_{\rm LO}}{\varepsilon}}\Big[n\,{\rm arsinh}\sqrt{\frac{\varepsilon}{\hbar\omega_{\rm LO}}}+(n+1)\,{\rm arsinh}\sqrt{\frac{\varepsilon}{\hbar\omega_{\rm LO}}-1}\;\Theta(\varepsilon-\hbar\omega_{\rm LO})\Big],\\ \alpha&=\frac{e^2}{4\pi\varepsilon_0\hbar}\sqrt{\frac{m^*}{2\hbar\omega_{\rm LO}}}\,\Big(\frac{1}{\epsilon^\infty}-\frac{1}{\epsilon^0}\Big). \end{aligned} $$

Here $\varepsilon$ is the carrier energy above the band edge, $n=n(\hbar\omega_{\rm LO}/k_BT)$, and $\alpha$ is the dimensionless Fröhlich constant (SI; the standard definition, not printed in Giustino). Below the threshold $\varepsilon=\hbar\omega_{\rm LO}$ a carrier can only absorb phonons, so its rate is proportional to $n$ and freezes out at low temperature. Above it, spontaneous emission switches on with a steep $\sqrt{\varepsilon-\hbar\omega_{\rm LO}}$ onset. This is the low-energy end of Giustino's Fig. 15 for GaAs (Bernardi et al. 2015, Eq. (170) with Wannier interpolation): relaxation times of order a picosecond at the band bottom, a few hundred femtoseconds in the Γ valley, a sharp drop when the L valley opens at $E_L\approx0.25$ eV, and a few femtoseconds at 1.5 eV.

Adiabatic versus nonadiabatic: the Fröhlich catastrophe

Poncé et al. (2015) noticed that in polar crystals the adiabatic correction (G.167) to band extrema diverges as the broadening $\eta\to0$ on dense Brillouin-zone grids. The reason is power counting (Giustino §IX.A.1). Near an extremum the bands are parabolic, $|\varepsilon_{n\bk}-\varepsilon_{n\bk+\bq}|\approx\hbar^2q^2/2m^*$, and the long-range polar element (G Eq. 180) gives $|g|^2\propto1/q^2$. The intraband integrand of (G.167) therefore behaves as $q^{-4}$, while $d\bq=4\pi q^2dq$, and $\int dq/q^2$ diverges at small $q$.

Keeping the phonon energy cures it. In (G.166) the emission denominator at the band bottom is $-(\hbar^2q^2/2m^*+\hbar\omega_{\rm LO})$. It no longer vanishes as $q\to0$: below the polaron wave vector $q_p=(2m^*\omega_{\rm LO}/\hbar)^{1/2}$, where the kinetic energy transferred equals one phonon, it levels off at $-\hbar\omega_{\rm LO}$, so the small-$q$ integrand, $q^2\cdot q^{-2}/\hbar\omega_{\rm LO}$, stays finite. For the conduction-band minimum at $T=0$, with Rayleigh–Schrödinger denominators, a spherical zone of radius $q_D$ and a grid that resolves only $q\ge q_{\rm min}=q_D/N_q$ ($N_q$ points per direction), the two prescriptions give

$$ \Delta E^{\rm NA}=-\alpha\hbar\omega_{\rm LO}\,\frac{2}{\pi}\Big[\arctan\frac{q_D}{q_p}-\arctan\frac{q_{\rm min}}{q_p}\Big],\qquad \Delta E^{\rm A}=-\alpha\hbar\omega_{\rm LO}\,\frac{2}{\pi}\,q_p\Big(\frac{1}{q_{\rm min}}-\frac{1}{q_D}\Big). $$

The nonadiabatic shift converges to the weak-coupling polaron shift $-\alpha\hbar\omega_{\rm LO}$ once $q_{\rm min}\ll q_p$ and $q_D\gg q_p$, although slowly: the missing part falls only as $1/N_q$. The adiabatic shift grows linearly with $N_q$, without limit.

Derivation: closed forms for the polar model

Write the Fröhlich element as $|g(q)|^2=A/q^2$ with $A=\frac{e^2}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\frac{4\pi}{\Omega}\frac{\hbar\omega_{\rm LO}}{2}\big(\frac1{\epsilon^\infty}-\frac1{\epsilon^0}\big)$, and use $\int d\bq/\Omega_{\rm BZ}\to(4\pi/\Omega_{\rm BZ})\int q^2dq\int d\mu/2$. The $q^2$ cancels the $1/q^2$. With $q_p^2=2m^*\omega_{\rm LO}/\hbar$ and the definition of $\alpha$ one finds $(4\pi/\Omega_{\rm BZ})A=(2/\pi)\,\alpha(\hbar\omega_{\rm LO})^2/q_p$.

Band-edge shift. At the CBM ($\bk=0$, $f=0$) the bracket of (G.166) at $T=0$ with $E\to\varepsilon$, $\Gamma\to0$ keeps only the emission term $-1/(\hbar^2q^2/2m^*+\hbar\omega_{\rm LO})=-(q_p^2/\hbar\omega_{\rm LO})/(q^2+q_p^2)$. Hence $\Delta E^{\rm NA}=-\alpha\hbar\omega_{\rm LO}(2/\pi)\int_{q_{\rm min}}^{q_D}dq\,q_p/(q^2+q_p^2)$, which is the arctangent form; with $q_{\rm min}\to0$, $q_D\to\infty$ it is $-\alpha\hbar\omega_{\rm LO}$. The adiabatic (G.167) drops $\hbar\omega_{\rm LO}$: the integrand becomes $q_p/q^2$, giving $\Delta E^{\rm A}$. The rule $q_{\rm min}=q_D/N_q$ mimics a uniform grid; a finite broadening $\eta$ plays the same regularizing role.

Scattering rate. Take $f=0$ in (G.170), so the weights are $n+1$ (emission) and $n$ (absorption). For $\bk\neq0$ the delta functions fix the angle: $\delta(\varepsilon_k\mp\hbar\omega_{\rm LO}-\varepsilon_{\bk+\bq})$ integrated over $\mu=\cos\theta$ gives $m^*/(\hbar^2kq)$ when a solution exists. Emission requires $k-\sqrt{k^2-q_p^2}<q<k+\sqrt{k^2-q_p^2}$, and $\int dq/q=2\,{\rm arcosh}(k/q_p)=2\,{\rm arsinh}\sqrt{\varepsilon/\hbar\omega_{\rm LO}-1}$. Absorption allows $\sqrt{k^2+q_p^2}-k<q<\sqrt{k^2+q_p^2}+k$, giving $2\,{\rm arsinh}(k/q_p)$. The prefactor in front of $\int dq/q$ is $(2\pi/\hbar)(\Omega/8\pi^3)\,2\pi A\,m^*/(\hbar^2k)=\Omega Am^*/(2\pi\hbar^3k)$; with the factor 2 from the logarithms it becomes $\Omega Am^*/(\pi\hbar^3k)=2\alpha\omega_{\rm LO}\,q_p/k$, and $q_p/k=\sqrt{\hbar\omega_{\rm LO}/\varepsilon}$. This is the rate formula above, the textbook result for polar-optical scattering; we checked it against direct numerical integration of (G.170).

Physical picture: a slow electron in a fast lattice

Dropping $\hbar\omega$ treats the zero-point displacements as a frozen random distortion that the electron adjusts to instantly. That is fine at short wavelengths, where a scattering event changes the electron's energy by much more than $\hbar\omega_{\rm LO}$. For $q\ll q_p$ the change, $\hbar^2q^2/2m^*$, is smaller than $\hbar\omega_{\rm LO}$: during one ionic oscillation the electron barely moves, so it cannot exploit these long-wavelength fluctuations as if they were static. Instead the ions follow the electron and build a polarization cloud of radius about $1/q_p$ (40 Å in GaAs) that travels with it, the large polaron of §A.4. The frozen-lattice formula keeps collecting energy from ever longer wavelengths of the dipole field, where its denominators vanish, and the sum diverges.

Giustino lists the remedies: principal-value integration with finite $\omega_{\bq\nu}$, taking $\omega\to0$ afterwards (Fan 1951); analytic integration near $\bq=0$ (Nery and Allen 2016); the Brillouin–Wigner form (G.166) with $\eta$ replaced by the physical linewidth $\Gamma_{n\bk}$; or full spectral functions (Kawai et al. 2014; Antonius et al. 2015). The Fröhlich part of the ZPR is not small. Botti and Marques (2013) computed $W$ including lattice screening, with a Lyddane–Sachs–Teller model dielectric function, and found ZPRs above 1 eV in LiF, LiCl, NaCl and MgO. Nery and Allen found a Fröhlich contribution of 45 meV out of 150 meV for GaN; the model below gives about 40 meV with literature parameters.

Bridge to EPP: what finite $c$ does and does not do

Everything here is electrostatic: "nonadiabatic" means keeping $\hbar\omega_{\bq\nu}$ in electron denominators, not photons. In EPP the Coulomb interaction is the longitudinal photon, and the longitudinal kernel is $c$-independent (§X.1), so the LO Fröhlich vertex that drives this divergence is not changed by retardation in EPP's sense (finite $c$) at all. Finite $c$ adds transverse-photon coupling of TO phonons for $q\lesssim q_c=\sqrt{\epsilon^\infty}\,\omega/c\sim10^{-4}$ Å$^{-1}$, inside the rose band above (EPP §7.2, §B.8). Even if that region were removed entirely, the adiabatic integral cut at $q_c$ would still give a shift of order $-0.7$ eV for GaAs. What EPP's dynamical vertex does add is the frequency dependence of the electronic screening, $\epsilon^\infty\to\hat\epsilon^{\rm e}(\bq,\omega)$, which is retardation in Giustino's sense and which his approximation (v) drops; in doped polar semiconductors, where plasmons and LO phonons mix, this could change Fröhlich shifts and lifetimes, but EPP does not derive an electron self-energy. See §Z.1.

Nonperturbative adiabatic calculations

An alternative skips perturbation theory and matrix elements. Expand $\varepsilon_{n\bk}$ to second order in the atomic displacements and average over the harmonic nuclear wavefunction with phonon numbers $\{n_{\bq\nu}\}$:

$$ \langle\varepsilon_{n\bk}\rangle_{\{n_{\bq\nu}\}}=\varepsilon_{n\bk}+\sum_\nu\int\frac{d\bq}{\Omega_{\rm BZ}}\big(n_{\bq\nu}+\tfrac12\big)\frac{\partial\varepsilon_{n\bk}}{\partial n_{\bq\nu}}, \tag{G.199}$$

with the formal definition $\partial/\partial n_{\bq\nu}\equiv\Delta_{\bq\nu}\Delta_{-\bq\nu}$; a canonical average turns $n_{\bq\nu}$ into its Bose–Einstein value. This is the starting point of Allen and Cardona (1981). Evaluating the second derivatives perturbatively gives back Allen–Heine. Evaluating them by finite differences of eigenvalues in supercells displaced along the phonon eigenvectors (frozen phonons) needs no rigid-ion approximation and can go beyond the harmonic approximation, at a high cost that Monte Carlo sampling, a single "optimum" configuration (Zacharias and Giustino 2016) or nondiagonal supercells (Lloyd-Williams and Monserrat 2015) reduce. The Williams–Lax average of the dielectric function over nuclear configurations applies the same idea to optical spectra (G Eq. 201, §A.9). Being adiabatic, (G.199) treats long-wavelength polar modes like (G.167), so one expects its Fröhlich part to grow with supercell size (our inference from the model above; the review does not discuss it).

What these formulas leave out

(G.166)–(G.170) are harmonic, at the Migdal level, with adiabatic phonons and a fixed lattice parameter, so the thermal-expansion contribution to $E_g(T)$, which measured gaps include, is not part of them. The linewidth trend of Fig. 3(b) needs states at least one phonon energy away from a band extremum, and the toy model misses the low-temperature subtleties of Allen and Nery (2017). DFT matrix elements are usually too small: the ZPR scales roughly as $(\epsilon^\infty)^{-2}$, so a 20% error in the screening becomes about 40% in the ZPR (Giustino §XII, §A.9).

A.9Giustino §VI.B, §IX.B, §X.B, §XI, §XII · Eqs. 181–184, 186–212

Light as an external field, transport and superconductivity

The last applied chapters of the review turn $g_{mn\nu}(\bk,\bq)$ into quantities people measure: the absorption edge of an indirect-gap semiconductor, carrier mobilities and superconducting critical temperatures. In all of them the only interaction is electrostatic, and light, where it appears at all, is a classical field that acts on electrons only. Seeing exactly where that assumption sits sets up the step to EPP.

Indirect absorption: light from outside, momentum from a phonon

In silicon the valence-band maximum is at Γ, while the conduction-band minimum lies near X, at $|\bk|\approx1$ Å$^{-1}$ (literature value, illustrative). A photon at the gap carries $q=n_{\rm r}E_g/\hbar c\approx2\times10^{-3}$ Å$^{-1}$ inside the crystal (refractive index $n_{\rm r}\approx3.5$, literature value), hundreds of times too little. Below the direct gap the electron can therefore be promoted only if a phonon is emitted or absorbed at the same time and supplies the missing crystal momentum. The process is second order: one electron–photon vertex and one electron–phonon vertex, in either order.

Giustino notes that the systematic route would be the screening function $\epsilon_{\rm e}$ of G Eq. (95), evaluated with the Green's function dressed by $\Sigma^{\rm ep}$ (G Eq. 151). He quotes instead the standard result of second-order time-dependent perturbation theory, due to Hall, Bardeen and Blatt (Giustino §IX.B; SI units, $\epsilon_0$ is the vacuum permittivity):

$$ \begin{aligned} \alpha(\omega)=\frac{\pi e^2}{\epsilon_0 c\,\Omega}\,\frac{1}{\omega\,n_{\rm r}(\omega)}&\int\frac{d\bk\,d\bq}{\Omega_{\rm BZ}^2}\sum_{mn\nu}\sum_{s=\pm1}\big(f_{n\bk}-f_{m\bk+\bq}\big)\\ &\times\bigg|\,\be\cdot\sum_p\bigg[\frac{\mathbf v_{np}(\bk)\,g_{pm\nu}(\bk,\bq)}{\varepsilon_{p\bk}-\varepsilon_{n\bk}-\hbar\omega}+\frac{g_{np\nu}(\bk,\bq)\,\mathbf v_{pm}(\bk+\bq)}{\varepsilon_{p\bk+\bq}-\varepsilon_{n\bk}+s\hbar\omega_{\bq\nu}}\bigg]\bigg|^2\\ &\times\big(n_{\bq\nu}+\tfrac12+\tfrac s2\big)\,\delta\big(\varepsilon_{m\bk+\bq}-\varepsilon_{n\bk}-\hbar\omega+s\hbar\omega_{\bq\nu}\big). \end{aligned} \tag{G.200}$$

The first term in the bracket is "photon first": a vertical transition into a virtual state $p\bk$, followed by phonon scattering into the final state $m\,\bk+\bq$. The second is "phonon first": scattering into a virtual state $p\,\bk+\bq$, followed by a vertical optical transition. The two amplitudes add before the modulus is squared. $s=+1$ is phonon emission, with weight $n_{\bq\nu}+1$ and onset at $\hbar\omega=E_g+\hbar\omega_{\bq\nu}$; $s=-1$ is phonon absorption, with weight $n_{\bq\nu}$ and onset at $E_g-\hbar\omega_{\bq\nu}$. Here $\mathbf v_{mn}$ are matrix elements of the velocity operator, $\be$ is the polarization, $n_{\rm r}(\omega)$ the real part of the refractive index, $\Omega$ the unit-cell volume and $f_{n\bk}$ the electron occupations.

+

Both diagrams are drawn for emission ($s=+1$); for absorption the zigzag line comes in instead of going out. The photon line ends in a cross. That is the standard mark of an external field: the line is not a propagator but a prescribed classical vector potential, inserted at a vertex in the electric-dipole approximation (photon momentum set to zero). It couples through $\be\cdot\mathbf v$ to electrons only. Nothing in (G.200) lets light act on the ions, and the medium's own response to light enters only through the number $n_{\rm r}(\omega)$, put in by hand. In the infrared, where a polar crystal absorbs strongly by driving TO phonons through their Born charges (the reststrahlen band), the formula is silent; it is built for photons above the gap. EPP replaces the cross by a photon propagator, so that light becomes part of the system (callout below).

What (G.200) assumes

Besides the classical field and the electric-dipole approximation (valid up to photon energies of a few eV): independent particles, so no excitons and no local fields (Allen–Heine has been combined with the BSE, but not in this formula); clamped-nuclei band energies in the δ function and in both denominators. The occupation factor $(f_n-f_m)(n+\frac12+\frac s2)$ differs from the exact net rate by terms of order $f_m(1-f_n)$, negligible in a semiconductor.

Note on the source

Read literally with the convention of G Eq. (38), $g_{pm\nu}(\bk,\bq)=\langle u_{p\bk+\bq}|\Delta_{\bq\nu}v^{\rm KS}|u_{m\bk}\rangle$, which does not connect an intermediate state $p\bk$ to a final state $m\,\bk+\bq$. The intended amplitude, up to an overall complex conjugate that drops out under $|\cdot|^2$, is

$$ \be\cdot\sum_p\bigg[\frac{g_{mp\nu}(\bk,\bq)\,\mathbf v_{pn}(\bk)}{\varepsilon_{p\bk}-\varepsilon_{n\bk}-\hbar\omega}+\frac{\mathbf v_{mp}(\bk+\bq)\,g_{pn\nu}(\bk,\bq)}{\varepsilon_{p\bk+\bq}-\varepsilon_{n\bk}+s\hbar\omega_{\bq\nu}}\bigg].$$

Strictly, emission involves the $-\bq$ phonon, which time reversal makes immaterial for $|g|$.

Temperature: two slopes and a moving edge

For two parabolic bands, a dispersionless phonon of each branch and constant matrix elements, the $\bk$ and $\bq$ integrals in (G.200) collapse to a convolution of two square-root densities of states, and every branch contributes a parabola above its threshold (cf. G.200; derivation below):

$$ \begin{aligned} \alpha(\omega)=\frac{C}{\hbar\omega}\sum_\nu w_\nu\Big[&(n_\nu+1)\,(\hbar\omega-E_g-\hbar\omega_\nu)^2\,\Theta(\hbar\omega-E_g-\hbar\omega_\nu)\\ +\,&n_\nu\,(\hbar\omega-E_g+\hbar\omega_\nu)^2\,\Theta(\hbar\omega-E_g+\hbar\omega_\nu)\Big]. \end{aligned}$$

In a plot of $\sqrt\alpha$ these are nearly straight segments with kinks at the thresholds $E_g\pm\hbar\omega_\nu$ (the Macfarlane–Roberts analysis). Below $E_g$ only phonon absorption contributes, and it freezes out as $n_\nu\to0$.

The clamped-nuclei energies in the δ function make the onset independent of temperature. That is why the theoretical curves of Giustino's Fig. 14 had to be shifted rigidly to the measured onsets at 296 K and 78 K. Patrick and Giustino (2014) and Zacharias and Giustino (2016) showed that the Allen–Heine renormalization of §A.8 moves the energies of real transitions but not those of virtual ones, so it belongs only in the δ function and the first denominator. Alternatively, Zacharias, Patrick and Giustino (2015) average the clamped-nuclei $\epsilon_2$ over nuclear configurations (Williams–Lax):

$$ \epsilon_2(\omega;T)=\frac1Z\sum_{\{n_{\bq\nu}\}}e^{-E_{\{n_{\bq\nu}\}}/k_BT}\,\big\langle\epsilon_2(\omega)\big\rangle_{\{n_{\bq\nu}\}}. \tag{G.201}$$

Here $\langle\epsilon_2(\omega)\rangle_{\{n_{\bq\nu}\}}$ is the clamped-nuclei $\epsilon_2$ averaged over the nuclear wavefunction with phonon numbers $\{n_{\bq\nu}\}$, $E_{\{n_{\bq\nu}\}}$ is the energy of that nuclear state and $Z$ the partition function. The idea is simple: in a supercell with displaced atoms crystal momentum is no longer conserved, so indirect transitions become vertical ones. Initial states are treated quantum mechanically and final states as a quasiclassical continuum. The result is an adiabatic approximation to (G.200) that contains the temperature-dependent band structure automatically.

Derivation: from (G.200) to the parabolic edge

Take a filled valence band with its maximum at Γ and an empty conduction band with its minimum at $\bk_c$, both parabolic, so $f_{n\bk}-f_{m\bk+\bq}=1$. The phonon must carry $\bq\approx\bk_c$; neglect its dispersion there, $\omega_{\bq\nu}\to\omega_\nu$, and treat $|g|$, the velocity matrix elements, the denominators and $n_{\rm r}$ as constants. For fixed $\nu$ and $s$, change variables from $\bq$ to $\bk'=\bk+\bq$: the $\bk$ integral then runs over the valence states and the $\bk'$ integral over the conduction states independently:

$$ \int\! d\bk\,d\bq\;\delta(\cdots)\;\propto\int_0^\infty\!\!dx\int_0^\infty\!\!dy\,\sqrt x\,\sqrt y\;\delta(x+y-\Delta_s)=\frac{\pi}{8}\,\Delta_s^2\,\Theta(\Delta_s),\qquad \Delta_s=\hbar\omega-E_g-s\hbar\omega_\nu ,$$

with $x$ the hole energy below the valence maximum and $y$ the electron energy above the conduction minimum. Multiplying by the weight $n_\nu+\frac12+\frac s2$ and the prefactor $1/\omega$ of (G.200), and absorbing all constants into $C$ and the relative branch strengths $w_\nu$, gives the edge formula. The integral is $\Delta^2\,B(\tfrac32,\tfrac32)=\pi\Delta^2/8$.

Bridge to EPP: light becomes part of the system

In EPP the photon is a quantized field with its own propagator $D$ (§B.4), not a prescribed external potential. In EPP's Gaussian units, electrons couple to it through the current vertex $-\frac1c\bj\cdot\bA$ plus the diamagnetic $A^2$ term, and ions through their Born dipoles, $\frac1c\dot\bp\cdot\bA$ (E Eq. 134). Absorption then follows from the imaginary part of one current–current photon self-energy, $\Pi_{jj}=\Pi^{\rm e}+\Pi^{\rm ion}$, and the dielectric function, hence $n_{\rm r}$, comes from the same object instead of being put in by hand (§B.3, §B.5). $\Pi^{\rm ion}$ contains exactly what (G.200) lacks: one-phonon infrared absorption at $\omega_{\rm TO}$ through the Born charges. In this language (G.200) would be the lowest phonon-dressed correction to the electronic bubble $\Pi^{\rm e}$, with a phonon line inside it (self-energy and vertex insertions). The manuscript does not work out that diagram, so phonon-assisted absorption remains open in EPP (§Z.1).

Transport: from lifetimes to mobility

The golden-rule rates $1/\tau_{n\bk}$ of G Eq. (170) (§A.8) also feed the semiclassical Boltzmann equation. An electric field $\bE$ moves the occupations slightly away from their equilibrium values $f^0_{n\bk}$, and linearizing in the deviation gives (Giustino §X.B)

$$ \frac{\partial f^0_{n\bk}}{\partial\varepsilon_{n\bk}}\,\mathbf v_{n\bk}\cdot(-e)\bE=-\sum_\nu\int\frac{d\bq}{\Omega_{\rm BZ}}\,\Gamma_{mn\nu}(\bk,\bq)\,\Big[\big(f_{n\bk}-f^0_{n\bk}\big)-\big(f_{m\bk+\bq}-f^0_{m\bk+\bq}\big)\Big], \tag{G.202}$$
$$ \begin{aligned} \Gamma_{mn\nu}(\bk,\bq)=\sum_{s=\pm1}\frac{2\pi}{\hbar}\,&|g_{mn\nu}(\bk,\bq)|^2\,f^0_{n\bk}\big(1-f^0_{m\bk+\bq}\big)\\ &\times\big(n_{\bq\nu}+\tfrac12-\tfrac s2\big)\,\delta\big(\varepsilon_{n\bk}+s\hbar\omega_{\bq\nu}-\varepsilon_{m\bk+\bq}\big). \end{aligned} \tag{G.203}$$

The left side is the drift term; the right side is scattering out of $|n\bk\rangle$ minus scattering in, with $\Gamma$ the equilibrium transition rate including Pauli factors (here $s=+1$ is absorption and $s=-1$ emission; the band sum over $m$ is implicit). Solving (G.202) self-consistently for all $f_{n\bk}$ gives the current $\bJ$, the conductivity and the mobility (conductivity per unit carrier charge density). Dropping the in-scattering term is the energy relaxation-time approximation (RTA). For $n$-type Si (Li 2015, Giustino Fig. 16) the exact solution, the energy-RTA and the momentum-RTA (which weights each process by the velocity it removes along the field) nearly coincide, and all three overestimate the measured mobility, most at low temperature; Giustino suggests the DFT matrix elements as a possible cause (Sec. XII, below). In polar materials the dominant scattering is by LO phonons through the long-range Fröhlich vertex (§A.4), the same term that makes the adiabatic band renormalization diverge (§A.8).

Superconductivity: from $\alpha^2F$ to $T_c$

Pairing uses the same $|g|^2$. An electron moving through the crystal leaves behind a lattice distortion that relaxes only on the phonon time scale $1/\omega_{\rm ph}$, and a second electron arriving later is attracted to it. Exchange of a virtual phonon thus gives an attraction between electrons near the Fermi surface, which competes with their Coulomb repulsion. The isotropic Eliashberg function is the double Fermi-surface average of $|g|^2$, resolved in phonon energy; its state-resolved form (G Eq. 187, which enters the Fan–Migdal self-energy G Eq. 186) and the mass enhancement it produces are in §A.7. Twice its $1/\omega$ moment is the coupling strength $\lambda$, and its logarithmic moment gives the characteristic phonon frequency:

$$ \alpha^2F(\omega)=\frac{1}{N_{\rm F}}\int\frac{d\bk\,d\bq}{\Omega^2_{\rm BZ}}\sum_{mn\nu}|g_{mn\nu}(\bk,\bq)|^2\,\delta(\varepsilon_{n\bk}-\varepsilon_{\rm F})\,\delta(\varepsilon_{m\bk+\bq}-\varepsilon_{\rm F})\,\delta(\hbar\omega-\hbar\omega_{\bq\nu}), \tag{G.205}$$
$$ \lambda=2\int_0^\infty\frac{\alpha^2F(\omega)}{\omega}\,d\omega, \tag{G.206}$$
$$ \omega_{\log}=\exp\bigg[\frac2\lambda\int_0^\infty d\omega\,\frac{\alpha^2F(\omega)}{\omega}\log\omega\bigg]. \tag{G.207}$$

$N_{\rm F}$ is the density of states at the Fermi level per spin and per cell, as the prefactor of G Eq. (192) implies. The weight $1/\omega$ makes soft phonons count more in $\lambda$; $\omega_{\log}$ is a geometric mean, and the unit inside $\log\omega$ cancels. Both enter the McMillan formula in the form refined by Allen and Dynes:

$$ k_BT_c=\frac{\hbar\omega_{\log}}{1.2}\exp\bigg[-\frac{1.04\,(1+\lambda)}{\lambda-\mu^*(1+0.62\lambda)}\bigg]. \tag{G.204}$$

The Coulomb pseudopotential follows Morel and Anderson, $1/\mu^*=1/\mu+\log(\omega_{\rm p}/\omega_{\rm ph})$, with $\hbar\omega_{\rm p}$ a plasma energy, $\hbar\omega_{\rm ph}$ the largest phonon energy, and $\mu=N_{\rm F}\langle\langle V_{n\bk,n'\bk'}\rangle\rangle_{\rm FS}$ the double Fermi-surface average of the screened Coulomb interaction between time-reversed pairs, $V_{n\bk,n'\bk'}=\langle\bk'n',-\bk'n'|W|\bk n,-\bk n\rangle$. Giustino writes $W$; physically this is the electronic part $W_{\rm e}$ of §A.5, since the phonon part is already in $\lambda$. Equation (G.204) assumes an isotropic, single-gap superconductor. In practice $\mu^*$ is adjusted within 0.1–0.2, which makes $T_c$ uncertain at moderate coupling, and $T_c$ vanishes once $\lambda\le\mu^*/(1-0.62\mu^*)$.

Why $\mu^*$ is small

The bare repulsion $\mu$ acts on the electronic time scale $1/\omega_{\rm p}$; the phonon-mediated attraction is delayed by about $1/\omega_{\rm ph}$, so paired electrons avoid each other in time. The logarithm records that separation of scales: with $\mu=0.4$, $\hbar\omega_{\rm p}=10$ eV and $\hbar\omega_{\rm ph}=50$ meV (illustrative), $\mu^*=0.13$. This is "retardation" in Giustino's sense, the frequency dependence of an interaction that is still electrostatic; the finite speed of light plays no role.

Beyond (G.204), the anisotropic Migdal–Eliashberg theory solves coupled equations for the renormalization $Z_{n\bk}(i\omega_j)$ and the gap $\Delta_{n\bk}(i\omega_j)$ on the fermion Matsubara axis (G Eqs. 208–209, below), with the coupling

$$ \lambda_{n\bk,n'\bk'}(i\omega)=\frac{N_{\rm F}}{\hbar}\sum_\nu\frac{2\omega_{\bq\nu}}{\omega^2_{\bq\nu}+\omega^2}\,|g_{nn'\nu}(\bk,\bq)|^2,\qquad \bq=\bk'-\bk. \tag{G.210}$$

The fraction is minus the bare phonon propagator on the bosonic Matsubara axis (Giustino's phonon Green's function, written $\mathcal D$ on this page). So $\lambda(i\omega)$ is the phonon-mediated interaction $W_{\rm ph}=W_{\rm e}\mathcal DW_{\rm e}$ of §A.5, projected on Cooper pairs, and its static Fermi-surface average returns (G.206). For MgB$_2$ (Margine and Giustino 2013, Giustino Fig. 17) it yields two gaps, about 7.5–9 meV and 1–2.5 meV at low temperature (on the σ and π Fermi-surface sheets, in the standard literature assignment), and $T_c=50$ K against 39 K measured; the empirical $\mu^*$ accounts for part of the difference. Superconducting DFT removes $\mu^*$ altogether, building the Coulomb kernel $\mathcal K^{\rm ee}$ from the screened interaction:

$$ \Delta_{n\bk}=-\mathcal Z_{n\bk}\Delta_{n\bk}-\sum_{n'\bk'}\frac{\mathcal K_{n\bk,n'\bk'}\,\Delta_{n'\bk'}}{2E_{n'\bk'}}\tanh\Big(\frac{E_{n'\bk'}}{2k_BT}\Big),\qquad E^2_{n\bk}=\varepsilon^2_{n\bk}+|\Delta_{n\bk}|^2, \tag{G.211}$$

with $\Delta_{n\bk}$ the pairing field in the Kohn–Sham basis, $\mathcal K=\mathcal K^{\rm ep}+\mathcal K^{\rm ee}$, $\mathcal Z_{n\bk}$ a renormalization term built from $g$ and the phonons (the analog of $Z$ in G.208), and $\varepsilon_{n\bk}$ measured from $\varepsilon_{\rm F}$. The gap has no explicit frequency dependence; retardation, again in Giustino's sense, enters through the kernels.

The anisotropic Migdal–Eliashberg equations (G.208)–(G.209)
$$ Z_{n\bk}(i\omega_j)=1+\frac{\pi k_BT}{N_{\rm F}}\sum_{n'\bk'j'}\frac{\omega_{j'}/\omega_j}{\sqrt{\hbar^2\omega^2_{j'}+\Delta^2_{n'\bk'}(i\omega_{j'})}}\,\lambda_{n\bk,n'\bk'}(i\omega_j-i\omega_{j'})\,\delta(\varepsilon_{n'\bk'}-\varepsilon_{\rm F}), \tag{G.208}$$
$$ \begin{aligned} Z_{n\bk}(i\omega_j)\Delta_{n\bk}(i\omega_j)=\frac{\pi k_BT}{N_{\rm F}}\sum_{n'\bk'j'}&\frac{\Delta_{n'\bk'}(i\omega_{j'})}{\sqrt{\hbar^2\omega^2_{j'}+\Delta^2_{n'\bk'}(i\omega_{j'})}}\\ &\times\big[\lambda_{n\bk,n'\bk'}(i\omega_j-i\omega_{j'})-N_{\rm F}V_{n\bk,n'\bk'}\big]\,\delta(\varepsilon_{n'\bk'}-\varepsilon_{\rm F}). \end{aligned} \tag{G.209}$$

Here $i\omega_j=i(2j+1)\pi k_BT/\hbar$ and $\sum_{\bk'}$ stands for $\Omega_{\rm BZ}^{-1}\int d\bk'$. They are solved self-consistently at each $T$; $T_c$ is the highest temperature with a nontrivial $\Delta_{n\bk}(i\omega_j)$, and real-axis gaps follow by analytic continuation. $Z_{n\bk}(i\omega_j)$ is the mass renormalization function; Giustino calls it analogous to $Z_{n\bk}$ of G Eq. (189), but in the normal state at low frequency it tends to $1+\lambda$, the inverse of that quasiparticle weight. Likewise $\lambda_{n\bk}$ of G Eq. (189) is a band velocity renormalization, not the Fermi-surface average $\lambda$ of (G.206).

In metals, both the Boltzmann equation (G.202) and the Eliashberg equations (G.208)–(G.209) couple states on, or near, the Fermi surface, and converging their zone integrals can take up to $10^6$ wave vectors. Besides Wannier interpolation (§A.4), Giustino §VI.B reviews Allen's Fermi-surface harmonics. They trade three-dimensional zone integrals for one-dimensional energy integrals by expanding any state-resolved function as

$$ A_{n\bk}=\sum_L A_L(\varepsilon_{n\bk})\,\Phi_L(\bk), \tag{G.181}$$

with harmonics $\Phi_L(\bk)$ orthogonal on each constant-energy surface and normalized to the density of states $N(\varepsilon)$ (G Eq. 182). A linear system such as the linearized Boltzmann equation then becomes a small matrix problem in $L$ and $\varepsilon$, provided a few harmonics suffice. Allen built $\Phi_L$ from polynomials in the band velocity, without establishing that the set is complete. Eiguren and Gurtubay (2014) made the basis complete by defining the harmonics as eigenstates of a modified Helmholtz equation on the Fermi surface (G Eq. 184). Applications include the photoemission kink of YBa$_2$Cu$_3$O$_7$ and the Seebeck coefficient of Li. This is numerical machinery with no counterpart in EPP, and EPP needs none for it: its electrodynamic corrections live inside the light cone, $q\lesssim q_c\sim10^{-4}$ Å$^{-1}$, while Fermi-surface integrals sample $q$ up to $2k_{\rm F}$.

Is the DFT vertex too weak?

Combining G Eqs. (38), (142) and (143), the vertex is the bare electron–nucleus perturbation screened by the many-body, frequency-dependent electronic dielectric matrix (Giustino §XII):

$$ g_{mn\nu}(\bk,\bq)=\Big\langle u_{m\bk+\bq}\Big|\int d\br'\,\epsilon_{\rm e}^{-1}(\br,\br',\omega)\,\Delta_{\bq\nu}v^{\rm en}(\br')\Big|u_{n\bk}\Big\rangle_{\rm uc}. \tag{G.212}$$

DFPT replaces $\epsilon_{\rm e}$ by the static RPA+$xc$ screening $\epsilon^{{\rm H}xc}$ of G Eq. (54). With the DFT band-gap problem this overscreens, so $g$ comes out too small. The evidence is scattered but consistent: GW raises the matrix elements of the graphene and graphite $A_1'$ and $E_{2g}$ modes by almost 40%; PBE0 and GW raise $\lambda$ of C$_{60}$ by 42% and 48%; HSE triples $\lambda$ in Ba$_{1-x}$K$_x$BiO$_3$, bringing $T_c$ from (G.204) to 31 K against 32 K measured; PBE0 lifts the H$_3$S estimate from 201–217 K to 253–270 K; GW raises the zero-point gap renormalization of diamond by 40%, but by only about 5% in LiF, MgO and TiO$_2$. Not all properties suffer equally. The Allen–Heine renormalization carries two screened vertices and scales as $\epsilon_\infty^{-2}$, while adiabatic phonon frequencies carry screening only through a term scaling as $\epsilon_\infty^{-1/2}$; a 20% error in $\epsilon_\infty$ thus means about 40% in the band renormalization and 10% in the frequencies. For a GW practitioner, (G.212) contains the same $\epsilon^{-1}$ as $W$, and the "constant screening" scheme of Faber et al. (vary $G$ in a frozen-phonon calculation, keep $W$ fixed) reproduces full GW couplings within 10%.

Note on the source: Secs. X.B–XII

Giustino's semiclassical current lacks a factor $1/\Omega$; the relaxation-time statement after (G.203) needs the Pauli factors that $\Gamma$ already contains; (G.210) holds as printed only after time reversal and relabelling; and Sec. XII writes "underestimates" where its argument needs "overestimates". Details and corrected forms are in §Z.2. One point matters for reading (G.209): it is written with the unrenormalized $N_{\rm F}V$, which with a finite Matsubara cutoff must be replaced by a cutoff-dependent $\mu^*$. That is what the Migdal–Eliashberg calculations Giustino reviews use: empirical in most, computed from the RPA screened interaction in Margine, Lambert and Giustino (2016).

Bridge to EPP: transport and pairing are electrostatic

Every kernel in this chapter is built from Coulomb lines. The pairing interaction $\lambda-\mu^*$ is $-N_{\rm F}\langle W_{\rm e}+W_{\rm ph}\rangle$ on the Fermi surface, with the electronic part reduced by (Giustino's) retardation. EPP does not treat transport or pairing, but in its language both pieces are the longitudinal sector of one photon propagator dressed by electrons and ions, and EPP's screened vertex generalizes (G.212) from $\epsilon_{\rm e}^{-1}v$ to the electron-dressed propagator $D^{\rm e}$ (§B.8). Transverse photon exchange would add current–current terms of relative order $(v_{\rm F}/c)^2$ (our estimate). For scattering, electrodynamic corrections live at $q\lesssim q_c=\sqrt{\epsilon_\infty}\,\omega_{\rm LO}/c\approx6\times10^{-5}$ Å$^{-1}$ in GaAs, far below the thermal wave vectors of carriers ($\approx0.02$ Å$^{-1}$ at 300 K), so mobilities and band renormalizations should stay electrostatic to excellent accuracy (§X.1).

What Part A assumed

Four assumptions run through all nine chapters of Part A, and Part B relaxes each of them, at least in part:

  1. One interaction. Every interaction line is built from the instantaneous, longitudinal Coulomb interaction $v(12)=v(\br_1,\br_2)\,\delta(t_1-t_2)$; even the lattice enters only as a second channel of the same screened interaction, $W=W_{\rm e}+W_{\rm ph}$ (§A.5).
  2. One kind of retardation. The only delay is the frequency dependence of the screened interaction: electronic screening $\epsilon_{\rm e}(\omega)$, and the phonon propagator inside $W_{\rm ph}$, whose slow time scale makes $\mu^*$ small. The finite speed of light never appears.
  3. Classical light. Photons enter as an external field coupled to electrons through $\be\cdot\mathbf v$, as in (G.200); the refractive index is an input, and ions do not couple to light at all.
  4. Polar coupling by hand. The Fröhlich vertex and the LO–TO splitting are added analytically from $Z^*$ and $\epsilon^\infty$ computed separately (G Eq. 180, and the Gonze–Lee term that Giustino cites in §VI.A.3 but does not print, §A.4).

The Bridge (§X.1) shows that the first two are the $c\to\infty$ limit of one electrodynamic theory, and that in it light becomes a propagator while matter, electronic and ionic alike, becomes a single self-energy.

Bridge

From electron–phonon to electron–phonon–photon

Part A rests on the four assumptions collected at the end of §A.9: a single instantaneous, longitudinal Coulomb interaction; "retardation" only in the sense of frequency-dependent electronic screening; light as a classical external field; and polar coupling added by hand through $Z^*$ and $\epsilon^\infty$.

Part B replaces all of this with one Lagrangian for electrons, ions and the electromagnetic field, one photon propagator $D=D^{l}+D^{t}$ and one current–current self-energy $\Pi_{jj}=\Pi^{\rm e}+\Pi^{\rm ion}$. Coulomb's law comes back as the longitudinal photon. The LO–TO splitting, the Fröhlich vertex and $\epsilon^\infty$ stop being inputs and come out of Dyson equations. The two Bridge sections map one language onto the other before Part B builds the new one.

X.1Giustino §IV ↔ EPP §§4–7

From instantaneous Coulomb to the full electromagnetic field

Giustino's screened interaction $W$ is the longitudinal, $c\to\infty$ corner of EPP's photon propagator $D$. By the end you will know how little of momentum space lies outside that corner, where that little matters anyway (optics, the zone centre), and why the order of the limits $q\to0$ and $c\to\infty$ is not a technicality.

Every line in Part A is a Coulomb line

Giustino's many-body Hamiltonian (G Eqs. 62–69) is nonrelativistic and contains a single interaction, $v(\br,\br')=e^2/(4\pi\varepsilon_0|\br-\br'|)$ in SI units, acting between all charges, electrons and nuclei alike. In space-time it is instantaneous: $v(12)=v(\br_1,\br_2)\,\delta(t_1-t_2)$, stated under G Eq. (74). The probe that generates the Hedin–Baym equations is a scalar potential $\varphi$ coupled to the total charge density. Sec. IV contains no vector potential, no current vertex and no transverse photon. Every dashed line of Part A, bare or screened, is this one longitudinal field.

Screening organizes those lines into Dyson series. With clamped nuclei $W_{\rm e}=v+vP_{\rm e}W_{\rm e}$ (G Eq. 94) is the $W$ of GW and BSE. Letting the nuclei move adds a second channel, $W=W_{\rm e}+W_{\rm e}\mathcal DW_{\rm e}$ (G Eqs. 104–105, §A.5). Here $\mathcal D$ is Giustino's nuclear density–density correlator (G Eq. 103, printed $D$; the letter $D$ is kept for EPP's photon propagator). In the harmonic approximation the vertices at the two ends of $W_{\rm e}\mathcal DW_{\rm e}$ are the dynamically screened gradients $\epsilon_{\rm e}^{-1}\nabla V_\kappa$ (G Eq. 110). All of Part A rests on these two equations for one scalar function.

Two meanings of "retardation"

Giustino keeps what he calls retardation effects. Following Bardeen–Pines and Baym, he does not replace $\epsilon_{\rm e}^{-1}$ in G Eq. (110) by its static value, which would be the Born–Oppenheimer choice made by Hedin and Lundqvist (Giustino p. 18). That retardation is the finite response time of the electron gas. EPP adds a second, independent one: the finite time the field needs to cross a distance. Both make an interaction depend on frequency, which is why they are easy to conflate. They live on different axes.

Giustino: dynamical screeningEPP adds: finite speed of light
What is delayedthe response of the electrons, $\epsilon_{\rm e}(\br,\br',\omega)$the field itself, which travels at $c$
Where it liveson the frequency axis, at fixed $q$on the momentum axis, through $x=cq/\omega$
Small parameter$\hbar\omega_{\rm ph}/E_{\rm el}$ ($E_{\rm el}$: gap, plasmon or Fermi energy)$\omega/cq=1/x$
Dropping it givesadiabatic screening: static $\epsilon_{\rm e}$, DFPT force constants and verticesthe electrostatic limit: only the longitudinal (Coulomb) sector, i.e. all of Part A
Where it mattersmetals, doped semiconductors, graphene (§A.6)optics, polaritons, LO–TO at Γ (§B.6, §B.7)
Carried in EPP by$\hat\epsilon^{\rm e}(\bq,\omega)$, E Eq. (432)$D^{0t}$, E Eq. (372)

Below, "retarded" means finite $c$ and "dynamical" means frequency-dependent screening. EPP itself once calls $c\to\infty$ the "retarded limit" (just before E Eq. 418); it means the instantaneous, non-retarded limit (§Z.2).

What EPP puts in its place

EPP starts one level lower (§B.2, §B.4). Electrons and harmonic ions couple only to the vector potential $\bA$, in the temporal gauge $\Phi=0$. The ions couple through their Born-charge dipoles, $\frac1c\dot\bp\cdot\bA$ with $\bp=\hat Z^*\bQ$ (E Eqs. 134–135). There is no explicit electron–phonon term, and no short-range (deformation-potential) coupling at all: only the polar channel is carried by the field. Quantizing the field gives two transverse photons per wave vector, with $\hbar\omega=\hbar cq$ (E Eq. 214). The longitudinal component has no restoring force and no dynamics of its own. Gauss's law ties it to the charges, and its field energy $\frac1{8\pi}\int\bE_l^2$ is exactly the instantaneous Coulomb energy of electrons and ionic bound charges (E Eq. 235). Coulomb's law is not postulated; it is what the longitudinal part of the field does.

In Sec. 6 the manuscript writes both parts as $3\times3$ propagators of $\bA$. The units are Gaussian, and the charges sit in the vertices, so $v(q)=4\pi/q^2$ carries no $e^2$:

$$D^{0l}_{\mu\nu}(\bq,\omega)=-\frac{4\pi c}{q^2}\,\frac{q_\mu q_\nu}{\omega^2},\tag{E.374}$$
$$D^{0t}_{\mu\nu}(\bq,\omega)=-\frac{4\pi c}{q^2}\,\frac{q^2\delta_{\mu\nu}-q_\mu q_\nu}{\omega^2-\omega_\bq^2+i\eta},\tag{E.372}$$
$$D^{0}_{\mu\nu}(\bq,\omega)=D^{0l}_{\mu\nu}(\bq,\omega)+D^{0t}_{\mu\nu}(\bq,\omega)=\frac{4\pi c}{\omega^2}\,\frac{-q_\mu q_\nu+\frac{\omega^2}{c^2}\delta_{\mu\nu}}{q^2-\frac{\omega^2}{c^2}-i\eta},\tag{E.375}$$

with $\omega_\bq=cq$. With the projectors $P^L_{\mu\nu}=\hat q_\mu\hat q_\nu$ and $P^T=1-P^L$ the two pieces separate cleanly:

$$D^0=-\frac{4\pi c}{\omega^2}\,P^L\;+\;\frac{4\pi}{c}\,\frac{P^T}{q^2-\omega^2/c^2}.$$

The first term is Coulomb in vector form. In the Coulomb picture a charge produces $\bE=-\nabla\phi$. In the temporal gauge the same field is $\bE=\frac{i\omega}{c}\bA$, so the scalar potential becomes a longitudinal vector potential, $\bA_l=-\frac{c}{\omega}\bq\,\phi$. Continuity, $\bq\cdot\bj=\omega\rho$ (E Eq. 335 in $\bq$-space), turns the charge source into a current source. Applying both conversions to $v(q)=4\pi/q^2$ gives $D^{0l}_{\mu\nu}=-\frac{c}{\omega^2}q_\mu q_\nu\,v(q)$, which is E Eq. (374). Its longitudinal projection, $-4\pi c/\omega^2$, does not depend on $q$: there is no light cone in it. The second term is the retarded photon, with its pole on the light cone $\omega=cq$. Their sum is the free Maxwell propagator in the temporal gauge, as E Eq. (375) states.

Physical picture: a photon that cannot travel

The longitudinal mode has kinetic energy but no $q^2A^2$ restoring term, so it neither oscillates nor propagates. It is slaved to the charges at every instant, which is why its energy is the instantaneous Coulomb energy. In the temporal gauge a static charge produces an $\bA_l$ that grows linearly in time (constant $\bE=-\frac1c\partial_t\bA$), and that is the meaning of the $1/\omega^2$ double pole of E Eq. (374). Transverse photons do propagate, at $c$. "Instantaneous Coulomb" and "retarded radiation" are two polarizations of the same field.

Subtlety: is the longitudinal propagator zero or not?

EPP finds $D^{0l}=0$ in its §4.7 (E Eq. 263) and uses the nonzero E Eq. (374) from §6 on. Both are right, for different objects, and drawing both would count Coulomb twice; §B.6 sorts this out, including why "identical to the free Maxwell propagator" holds only in the temporal gauge.

Two Dyson equations, one structure

To write every line as a $3\times3$ propagator, every density bubble must first be rewritten as a current–current correlator. Charge conservation does this. EPP derives a set of connection formulas (E Eqs. 341–350), the central one being

$$\Pi^{i}_{\rho\rho}(\br,\br',\omega)=-\frac{c}{\omega^2}\sum_{\mu\nu}\partial_\mu\partial'_\nu\,\Pi^{i}_{jj\mu\nu}(\br,\br',\omega),\qquad i={\rm e,\,ion}.\tag{E.350}$$

In a homogeneous medium this reads $\Pi_{\rho\rho}=-\frac{c}{\omega^2}\,\bq\cdot\Pi_{jj}\cdot\bq$: Giustino's density response is the longitudinal projection of EPP's current response. With the rule $\rho\to j$, $v\to D^{0l}$ (E Eq. 377), the mixed scalar–vector perturbation series collapses into a single $3\times3$ Dyson equation:

$$D=D^0+D^0\,\Pi_{jj}\,D,\qquad D^0=D^{0l}+D^{0t},\qquad \Pi_{jj}=\Pi^{\rm e}_{jj}+\Pi^{\rm ion}_{jj}.\tag{E.379}$$

Both bubbles in E Eq. (379) are bare (irreducible). From Sec. 7 on, the manuscript marks bare bubbles with a superscript 0, $\Pi^{\rm e,0}_{jj}$ and $\Pi^{\rm ion,0}_{jj}$, and keeps $\Pi^{\rm e}_{jj}$, $\Pi^{\rm ion}_{jj}$ for the dressed ones. We use that notation from here on. The match with Giustino becomes line by line if the electrons are resummed first. The electron-dressed photon is $D^{\rm e}=D^0+D^0\Pi^{\rm e,0}_{jj}D^{\rm e}$ (E Eq. 388). The bare ionic bubbles strung together by $D^{\rm e}$ form the dressed ionic correlator $\Pi^{\rm ion}_{jj}=\Pi^{\rm ion,0}_{jj}+\Pi^{\rm ion,0}_{jj}D^{\rm e}\Pi^{\rm ion,0}_{jj}+\dots$ (E Eq. 387). It equals $-JFJ^*$, with $J$ the Born-charge current vertex and $F$ the dressed phonon propagator (E Eqs. 392–398). E Eq. (379) is then equivalent to the right-hand column (this rearrangement follows from E Eqs. 379, 387 and 388; the text does not write it in this form):

$$\begin{aligned} W_{\rm e}&=v+v\,P_{\rm e}\,W_{\rm e} & &\quad\longleftrightarrow\quad & D^{\rm e}&=D^0+D^0\,\Pi^{\rm e,0}_{jj}\,D^{\rm e},\\ W&=W_{\rm e}+W_{\rm e}\,\mathcal D\,W_{\rm e} & &\quad\longleftrightarrow\quad & D&=D^{\rm e}+D^{\rm e}\,\Pi^{\rm ion}_{jj}\,D^{\rm e}. \end{aligned}$$

The dictionary reads off directly: $v\leftrightarrow D^0$, $P_{\rm e}\leftrightarrow\Pi^{\rm e,0}_{jj}$, $W_{\rm e}\leftrightarrow D^{\rm e}$, $\mathcal D\leftrightarrow\Pi^{\rm ion}_{jj}$ (point nuclei with charges $Z_\kappa$ become Born-charge dipoles) and $W\leftrightarrow D$. Each density correlator on the left is the longitudinal projection of the current correlator on the right, through E Eq. (350). In the electrostatic limit the correspondence is an identity rather than an analogy: the surviving sector of $D^{\rm e}$ is $-\frac{c}{\omega^2}q_\mu q_\nu W^{\rm e}$ (E Eq. 441), with $W^{\rm e}\equiv D^{\rm e}_{11}$ the RPA screened Coulomb interaction (E Eq. 437). The index 1 in $D_{11}$ is not the Cartesian $x$: it labels the scalar (Coulomb) slot of the $4\times4$ field propagator of EPP §6, whose other three slots are the components of $\bA$ (§B.6). Two differences remain even there. EPP's $\Pi^{\rm e,0}$ is RPA without exchange–correlation and without crystal local fields (E Eqs. 380–383 keep only $\bG=\bG'=0$), so its $W^{\rm e}$ uses the head of the RPA dielectric matrix rather than Giustino's exact $\epsilon_{\rm e}^{-1}$. And EPP's ions are point Born-charge dipoles, so only the long-range (dipolar) part of Giustino's vertex $\epsilon_{\rm e}^{-1}\nabla V_\kappa$ survives. The short-range coupling is absent from the EPP Lagrangian, and the short-range force constants enter only through the bare phonon frequencies. The full concept table is in §X.2.

Bridge for the GW/BSE reader

The $W$ in your GW or BSE code is $W_{\rm e}$ of G Eq. (94). In EPP's language it is $D^{\rm e}_{11}$ (E Eq. 437), the scalar entry of the electron-dressed photon propagator at $c\to\infty$. The frequency dependence you keep in a full-frequency or plasmon-pole $W$ is retardation of the first kind. EPP adds the second kind, through the transverse part of $D^{\rm e}$, and the dressed ionic correlator: $D=D^{\rm e}+D^{\rm e}\Pi^{\rm ion}_{jj}D^{\rm e}$, whose longitudinal part is Giustino's $W_{\rm ph}$ with Born-charge vertices.

How big is the light cone?

Contract $D^0$ with a longitudinal current and you get $-4\pi c/\omega^2$ for every $q$. Contract it with a transverse current and you get $-4\pi c/(\omega^2-c^2q^2)$. The ratio of the two,

$$\left|\frac{D^0_T}{D^0_L}\right|=\frac{1}{|1-x^2|},\qquad x=\frac{cq}{\omega},$$

is all the retardation the free field contains. Deep inside the light cone ($x\ll1$) the two polarizations are equal, at its edge ($x=1$) the transverse one is resonant, and far outside it the transverse part is suppressed by $(\omega/cq)^2$. The same ratio sets how strongly a TO phonon, whose ionic current is transverse, couples through the field; §B.8 develops this. In a medium whose electrons respond with a constant $\epsilon_\infty$ (an insulator below its gap), the isotropic solution of E Eq. (380) is $D_L=-4\pi c/(\omega^2\epsilon_\infty)$ and $D_T=-4\pi c/(\omega^2\epsilon_\infty-c^2q^2)$. The edge of the cone moves to $q_c=\sqrt{\epsilon_\infty}\,\omega/c$, and the ratio becomes $\epsilon_\infty/|\epsilon_\infty-x^2|$ (derivation below).

Derivation: projector form and the dressed propagators

From E Eq. (372), $q^2\delta_{\mu\nu}-q_\mu q_\nu=q^2P^T_{\mu\nu}$, so $D^{0t}=-4\pi c\,P^T/(\omega^2-c^2q^2)=\frac{4\pi}{c}P^T/(q^2-\omega^2/c^2)$. From E Eq. (374), $D^{0l}=-\frac{4\pi c}{\omega^2}P^L$. Over a common denominator the sum is $\frac{4\pi c}{\omega^2}\big[-q^2P^L+\frac{\omega^2}{c^2}(P^L+P^T)\big]/(q^2-\omega^2/c^2)$, which is E Eq. (375).

For an isotropic self-energy $\Pi=\Pi_LP^L+\Pi_TP^T$, the Dyson equation $D=D^0+D^0\Pi D$ decouples because $P^LP^T=0$:

$$D_L=\frac{D^0_L}{1-D^0_L\Pi_L}=-\frac{4\pi c}{\omega^2\,\epsilon_L},\qquad D_T=\frac{D^0_T}{1-D^0_T\Pi_T}=-\frac{4\pi c}{\omega^2\epsilon_T-c^2q^2},\qquad \epsilon_{L,T}=1+\frac{4\pi c\,\Pi_{L,T}}{\omega^2}.$$

An insulator below its gap has $\Pi^{\rm e}\propto\omega^2$ (E Eq. 383), so $\epsilon_L=\epsilon_T=\epsilon_\infty$. Then $|D_T/D_L|=\epsilon_\infty/|\epsilon_\infty-c^2q^2/\omega^2|$. Poles of $D_L$ ($\epsilon_L=0$) are plasmons and LO phonons; poles of $D_T$ ($c^2q^2=\omega^2\epsilon_T$) are polaritons (§B.6).

The numbers are what make Giustino's framework work. With $\hbar c=1973.27$ eV Å, a 50 meV phonon in vacuum has $q_c=2.5\times10^{-5}$ Å$^{-1}$, the GaAs TO phonon (33.3 meV, $\epsilon_\infty=10.9$) $5.6\times10^{-5}$ Å$^{-1}$, the in-plane TO phonon of hBN (169.9 meV, $\epsilon_\infty=4.87$) $1.9\times10^{-4}$ Å$^{-1}$, and a 2 eV exciton in vacuum $1.0\times10^{-3}$ Å$^{-1}$. The Brillouin zone extends about 1 Å$^{-1}$ from $\Gamma$. The figure lets you move the frequency and, as a thought experiment, the speed of light.

Two conclusions follow. First, wherever an electron–phonon calculation samples the zone, from the polaron scale to the zone edge, the transverse field at phonon frequencies is suppressed by four orders of magnitude or more. DFPT, GW and BSE are electrostatic for good reason. The Fröhlich catastrophe of adiabatic Allen–Heine theory is not cured by a finite speed of light either: the LO Fröhlich vertex is longitudinal and does not depend on $c$ at any $q$. It is cured by keeping the phonon frequency in the energy denominators (§A.8). Second, the region where the transverse field matters is exactly where optics happens. Absorbed light carries $q\approx q_c$, and the non-analytic LO–TO splitting lives at $q\to0$. A theory of infrared response and polaritons cannot drop $D^{0t}$, even though transport never notices it. The same holds for a 2D sheet, where the cone is equally thin and modes inside it radiate (§B.10).

The order of limits

At fixed $\omega$ and apart from the overall factor $4\pi c/\omega^2$, E Eq. (375) depends on $q$ and $c$ only through the direction $\hat q$ and the ratio $x=cq/\omega$ (multiply numerator and denominator by $c^2/\omega^2$):

$$D^0_{\mu\nu}=-\frac{4\pi c}{\omega^2}\;\frac{x^2\,\hat q_\mu\hat q_\nu-\delta_{\mu\nu}}{x^2-1}.$$

The point $q=0$, $1/c=0$ is therefore a non-analytic point, and the two orders of the limit give different tensors:

$$D^0_{\alpha\beta}(\bq=0,\omega)=-\frac{4\pi c}{\omega^2}\,\delta_{\alpha\beta},\tag{E.408}$$
$$\lim_{c\to\infty}D^0_{\mu\nu}(\bq,\omega)=-\frac{4\pi c}{\omega^2}\,\frac{q_\mu q_\nu}{q^2}.\tag{E.442}$$

Taking $q\to0$ at finite $c$ ($x\to0$) gives an isotropic tensor: deep inside the light cone longitudinal and transverse currents feel the same field. Taking $c\to\infty$ at finite $q$ ($x\to\infty$) leaves only the longitudinal projector: Coulomb alone, which is Giustino's world. Power counting of the dressed propagator gives the same verdict: only the $ll$ sector survives (E Eq. 434), as §B.9 shows term by term.

This is not a formality. Applied to the phonon self-energy, $\bq\to0$ at finite $c$ gives EPP's E Eq. (410), the $q=0$ end of the upper phonon polariton with an unscreened, isotropic shift, while $c\to\infty$ taken first gives E Eq. (454), the Gonze–Lee LO–TO splitting. §B.7 works out both orders with GaAs numbers; the crossover sits at $q_c\approx6\times10^{-5}$ Å$^{-1}$ for GaAs, the edge of the shaded cone in the GaAs preset above.

X.2Concept map · notation · diagram glyphs

A dictionary between the two formalisms

Every object in Giustino's electron–phonon theory has an EPP counterpart, a generalization, or no counterpart yet. This section is the lookup table: concepts, symbols and units, and diagram glyphs, side by side.

The two papers describe the same crystal with different bookkeeping. Giustino's field theory has electrons, phonons and one interaction, the instantaneous Coulomb potential, which couples to charge densities (§A.5). EPP has electrons, bare short-range phonons and one field, the vector potential $\bA$, which couples to currents (§X.1). Three substitutions translate almost everything, and most of the tables below apply them over and over. They are derived in §X.1, §B.6 and §B.7; here they are collected for lookup.

Three substitutions

Lines. A Coulomb line $v(\bq)=4\pi/q^2$ (Gaussian units, charges in the vertices) becomes the longitudinal photon propagator, which acts on currents instead of charges:

$$D^{0l}_{\mu\nu}(\bq,\omega)=-\frac{4\pi c}{q^2}\,\frac{q_\mu q_\nu}{\omega^2}. \tag{E.374}$$

Its electron-screened version is the $ll$ sector of the electron-dressed photon propagator $D^{\rm e}$. With $D^{\rm e}_{11}\equiv W^{\rm e}$ (Eq. E.437), the electrostatic limit reads

$$\lim_{c\to\infty}D^{\rm e}_{\mu\nu}(\bq,\omega)=-\frac{c}{\omega^2}\,q_\mu q_\nu\,W^{\rm e}(\bq,\omega). \tag{E.441}$$

Bubbles and vertices. Charge conservation, $\nabla\cdot\bj=i\omega\rho$, ties every density correlator to the current–current correlator. Giustino's polarization $P$ is therefore the longitudinal projection of EPP's photon self-energy, up to the factor $e^2$ (Giustino's densities count electrons, EPP's $\rho$ is a charge density):

$$\Pi^i_{\rho\rho}(\br,\br',\omega)=-\frac{c}{\omega^2}\sum_{\mu\nu}\partial_\mu\partial'_\nu\,\Pi^i_{jj\mu\nu}(\br,\br',\omega);\qquad i={\rm e,\,ion}. \tag{E.350}$$

In $\bq$ space this is $\Pi_{\rho\rho}=-\frac{c}{\omega^2}\,\bq\cdot\Pi_{jj}\cdot\bq$. The same identity turns each density vertex into the longitudinal part of a current vertex (Eq. E.428).

Phonons. The phonon propagators agree up to a factor $\hbar$. Both are built from the dimensionless $a+a^\dagger$, but Giustino defines the mode-basis propagator as $-i\langle T\cdots\rangle$ (Eq. G.133), while EPP defines $F=-\frac{i}{\hbar}\langle TQQ\rangle$ with $Q=a+a^\dagger$ (Eq. E.251):

$$\mathcal D^{\rm A}_{\bq\nu\nu'}(\omega)=\frac{2\omega_{\bq\nu}}{\omega^2-\omega^2_{\bq\nu}}\,\delta_{\nu\nu'}, \tag{G.132}$$
$$F^0_\sigma(\bq,\omega)=2\,\frac{\omega_\sigma(\bq)}{\hbar}\,\frac{1}{\omega^2-\omega^2_\sigma(\bq)+i\eta}, \tag{E.390}$$

so $\mathcal D^{\rm A}_{\bq\nu}=\hbar F_\sigma$ in the mode basis. What dresses them differs. Giustino's phonon self-energy $\Pi^{\rm ph}$ couples point nuclei through $W_{\rm e}$ (Eq. G.121). EPP's phonon emits and reabsorbs an electron-screened photon through Born-charge currents:

$$\Omega^{\rm e}_{\sigma\sigma'}(\bq,\omega)=-\sum_{\alpha\beta}J^*_{\alpha\sigma}(\bq,\omega)\,D^{\rm e}_{\alpha\beta}(\bq,\omega)\,J_{\beta\sigma'}(\bq,\omega). \tag{E.399}$$

The displayed EPP equations are in Gaussian units with charge-dimensioned Born charges; Giustino's are SI. The notation table below gives the conversions.

Reading a diagram across

Take a Giustino diagram built from Coulomb lines, such as $W$, $W_{\rm ph}$ or the phonon self-energy. Replace each dashed Coulomb line by a dashed longitudinal-photon line and draw a wavy transverse line beside it. Replace each dot where a Coulomb line meets an electron (a density vertex) by a square (a current vertex). Attach the phonon to the field through a Born-charge current vertex $J$ instead of a bare nuclear charge. Sending $c\to\infty$ deletes the wavy lines again and returns Giustino's diagram, except that the Born charge $Z^*$ stands where the nuclear charge $Z_\kappa$ stood and only the long-range (dipolar) part of the coupling is kept.

Concept map

Each row places one concept in both papers and says what changes. The filter sorts rows into four classes: same physics in different notation; generalized, where EPP contains Giustino's object as its electrostatic ($c\to\infty$) limit; new in EPP; and missing in EPP. One row carries two labels. The links point to the primer sections that treat the concept.
