Applying the conversions to one number

Two rules do most of the work. Gaussian charges become SI charges with $e^2\to e^2/4\pi\varepsilon_0$, and EPP's Born charges already contain the electron charge, $Z^*_{\rm EPP}=|e|Z^*_{\rm G}$. The factor $N^{-1/2}$ sits inside EPP's $g$ and outside Giustino's. Both papers compute the long-range (Fröhlich) vertex, so it makes a good test. For a cubic diatomic crystal with Born charges $\pm Z^*$ and reduced mass $\mu$, take the longitudinal mode along $\bq$, keep $\bG=0$ and set the Bloch overlap to one. Giustino's Eq. (G.180) with $N_p$ dropped, and EPP's screened electrostatic vertex (E p. 98, with $\hat\epsilon^{\rm e}\to\epsilon^\infty$ and the factor $e$ restored in $\rho$), reduce to

$$\begin{aligned}|g^{\rm G}(q)|&=\frac{4\pi}{\Omega}\,\frac{e^2}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\,\frac{Z^*_{\rm G}}{q\,\epsilon^\infty}\Big(\frac{\hbar}{2\mu\,\omega_{\rm LO}}\Big)^{1/2},\\ \sqrt N\,|g^{\rm dyn}(q)|&=\frac{4\pi}{\Omega_{\rm uc}}\,\frac{|e|\,Z^*_{\rm EPP}}{q\,\epsilon^\infty}\Big(\frac{\hbar}{2\mu\,\omega_\sigma}\Big)^{1/2}.\end{aligned}$$

With $|e|Z^*_{\rm EPP}=e^2Z^*_{\rm G}$ and the Gaussian $e^2\equiv e^2/4\pi\varepsilon_0$, the prefactors agree. One real difference remains: the frequency in the zero-point amplitude. Giustino's $\omega_{\bq\nu}$ is the DFPT phonon, which for the LO mode already contains the long-range shift. EPP's $\omega_\sigma$ is the bare short-range phonon, here equal to $\omega_{\rm TO}$. The figure computes both, together with Fröhlich's vertex (Eqs. G.2 and G.7) and EPP's unscreened vertex (E p. 95).

Derivation: why the dressed residue removes the factor $\sqrt{\omega_{\rm LO}/\omega_\sigma}$

This argument is derived on this page; neither paper discusses the normalization. In the electrostatic limit with static screening, $\Omega^{\rm e}_{\sigma\sigma}$ is frequency independent (Eqs. E.452, E.454), and the diagonal Dyson solution (Eq. E.405) becomes

$$F_\sigma(\omega)=\frac1\hbar\,\frac{2\omega_\sigma}{\omega^2-\tilde\omega^2},\qquad \tilde\omega^2=\omega_\sigma^2+\frac{2\omega_\sigma\Omega^{\rm e}_{\sigma\sigma}}{\hbar}=\omega_{\rm LO}^2 .$$

Rewrite it as the free propagator of a mode at $\tilde\omega$ times a weight:

$$F_\sigma(\omega)=\frac{\omega_\sigma}{\tilde\omega}\cdot\frac1\hbar\,\frac{2\tilde\omega}{\omega^2-\tilde\omega^2}.$$

Any quantity of the form "vertex × phonon × vertex", such as the phonon-mediated interaction $W_{\rm ph}$ (or a Fan–Migdal self-energy, once EPP derives one), then contains $|g^{\rm dyn}|^2\,\omega_\sigma/\tilde\omega$ times the free propagator at $\tilde\omega$. Since $|g^{\rm dyn}|^2\propto1/\omega_\sigma$, the product scales as $1/\tilde\omega=1/\omega_{\rm LO}$, exactly like $|g^{\rm G}|^2$ multiplied by $\mathcal D^{\rm A}/\hbar$ at $\omega_{\rm LO}$. The physical check is classical: $W_{\rm ph}=W-W_{\rm e}=\frac{v}{(\epsilon^\infty)^2}\,\frac{\omega_p^2}{\omega^2-\omega_{\rm LO}^2}$ for $\epsilon(\omega)=\epsilon^\infty+\omega_p^2/(\omega_{\rm TO}^2-\omega^2)$, and both bookkeepings reproduce it.

Diagram glyphs

Giustino draws electrons, phonons, Coulomb lines and two kinds of e–ph vertex (his Figs. 1–2). EPP adds three kinds of photon line and separates charge vertices from current vertices (its Figs. 7–14). Below, both sets are drawn in this page's visual language: blue electrons, amber zigzag phonons, rose for the whole electromagnetic field (dashed: longitudinal; wavy: transverse; a wavy line over a dashed one: both polarizations, as in $D^0$; heavy or double: dressed, as in $D^{\rm e}$), dots for charge vertices and squares for current vertices. EPP colours its own figures differently ($D^{0l}$ red, $D^0$ magenta, $D^{\rm e}$ blue).

What EPP does not (yet) contain

Five pieces of Part A have no EPP counterpart yet: short-range (deformation-potential) coupling, which must still come from DFPT under EPP's double-counting rule (§B.1); electron self-energies; exchange–correlation and local fields; phonon-assisted optics; and out-of-plane dipoles in 2D. The "− missing in EPP" filter of the concept map lists them row by row, and §Z.1 discusses them.

Same word, different meaning

  • Retardation. Frequency-dependent screening (Giustino) versus finite speed of light (EPP): §X.1. EPP's "retarded limit $c\to\infty$" means the instantaneous limit.
  • LO–TO splitting. E.410 is the $q=0$ upper polariton without electrons; the readout $\hbar\tilde\omega(q=0)$ above gives about 57.5 meV for the GaAs-like preset, whose $Z^*\approx2.18$ is fixed by the measured splitting (56 meV with the literature $Z^*=2.07$). The electrostatic splitting is E.454: §B.7.
  • Longitudinal photon. $D^{0l}=0$ (E.263) versus the Coulomb propagator (E.374): §B.6.
  • Screened vertices. One bare and one screened in phonon self-energies, two screened in Fan–Migdal: §A.6, §A.7, §B.8.

Using the dictionary in Part B

Each translation is derived where it first appears: Coulomb as the longitudinal photon in §B.4, the gauge-invariant $\Pi_{jj}$ in §B.5, the connection formulas and the total propagator $D$ in §B.6, $\Omega^{\rm e}$ and the LO–TO shift in §B.7, the vertices $g^{\rm dyn,0}$ and $g^{\rm dyn}$ in §B.8, and the return to Giustino's formulas in §B.9. The Hedin–Baym side of every row is in §A.5 and §A.6.

Part B

The electron–phonon–photon (EPP) formalism

Part B follows the manuscript “Theory of the Electron-Phonon-Photon coupling”, a 102-page derivation cited below as EPP, with its equations tagged (E.n). Its programme is to put the electromagnetic field back into the electron–phonon problem of Part A: one Lagrangian for valence electrons, harmonic ions and the field, from which Coulomb's law, the Fröhlich vertex, $\epsilon^\infty$ and the LO–TO splitting all follow. The manuscript is a draft, so typos and inconsistencies are flagged where they occur, in grey “Note on the source” boxes, and collected in Z.2. Corrected forms are shown only where the correction is unambiguous, and results marked [derived] are worked out on this page rather than printed in either paper.

Units change along the way. Sections 1–2 need none, §3 is in SI (stated by EPP), and from §4 on the manuscript uses Gaussian units without announcing the switch ($\bE=-\tfrac1c\partial_t\bA$, $1/8\pi$ in the field energy, $\tfrac ec\mathbf v\cdot\bA$ for the electron current). Convert with $e^2/4\pi\varepsilon_0\to e^2$ and $1/\varepsilon_0\to4\pi$. Part B follows the source and says which system each displayed equation uses. EPP's Born charges carry the dimension of charge, $Z^*_{\rm EPP}=|e|\,Z^*_{\rm G}$. The electron charge is $-e$ with $e>0$ in §3, but from §4 on $e$ is the signed charge ($e<0$ for electrons), again without notice. EPP's own symbols are kept: $D$ is the photon propagator, $\Pi_{jj}$ the photon self-energy, $F$ the phonon propagator and $\Omega^{\rm e}$ the phonon self-energy. Giustino's phonon Green function and self-energy appear as $\mathcal D$ and $\Pi^{\rm ph}$.

The ten sections form one derivation chain. The lattice and the bare vertex (§B.1) enter one Lagrangian for electrons, ions and field (§B.2), whose classical solution is the polar crystal as a dielectric (§B.3). Quantizing the field gives transverse photons and returns Coulomb's law as the longitudinal photon (§B.4). Electrons and ions dress the photon through one RPA self-energy (§B.5), and charge conservation assembles the total propagator and its polaritons (§B.6). Phonons dressed by electron-screened photons acquire the LO–TO splitting (§B.7) and an electrodynamic Fröhlich vertex (§B.8). Letting $c\to\infty$ recovers Giustino (§B.9), and a sheet geometry shows why 2D crystals have no LO–TO splitting at Γ (§B.10).

B.1EPP §§1–3 · Eqs. 1–131

Same lattice, bare vertex, electrostatic polar coupling

EPP's first 25 pages rebuild three objects in its own notation: the quantized displacement of an atom, the bare electron–phonon vertex of a rigid-ion crystal, and Verdi and Giustino's long-range polar vertex. By the end you will know which of them survive into the electrodynamic theory, and why its bare phonons may contain only short-range force constants.

No physics in this section is new relative to Part A. What is new is the bookkeeping. EPP keeps every quantity bare, says explicitly what a DFT starting point already contains, and sets up the polar vertex as the electrostatic seed that the photon theory of §§B.4–B.9 must reproduce.

The diagonalization machine (EPP §1)

Section 1 turns the harmonic lattice Hamiltonian (E.5), with $3sN$ coupled Cartesian displacements $Q_{i{\rm a}\mu}$ (cell $i$ of $N$, atom ${\rm a}$ of $s$, direction $\mu$), into $3sN$ independent oscillators. The physics, the diatomic chain and the zero-point length are in §A.1. What matters here is the machinery, because EPP reuses it step for step to quantize the transverse photon field (§B.4). EPP announces “the three steps” of diagonalizing (E.5): a Fourier transform, then mass scaling followed by a unitary rotation, then quantization. Each substitution is a linear canonical transformation that removes one kind of coupling:

EPP stepSubstitutionCoupling removedResult
1 · Fourier transform
E.7–E.17		$Q_{i{\rm a}\mu}=N^{-1/2}\sum_{\bk}e^{i\bk\bR^0_i}Q_{\bk{\rm a}\mu}$between cellsone $3s\times3s$ problem per $\bk$
2a · Mass scaling
E.18–E.24		$Q_{\bk{\rm a}\mu}=\tilde Q_{\bk{\rm a}\mu}/\sqrt{m_{\rm a}}$unequal masses in the kinetic termkinetic energy is the unit matrix
2b · Unitary rotation
E.25–E.45		$\tilde Q_{\bk{\rm a}\mu}=\sum_\alpha e_{{\rm a}\mu\alpha}(\bk)\,q_{\bk\alpha}$between the $3s$ componentsnormal coordinates $q_{\bk\alpha}$
3 · Quantization, ladder operators
E.46–E.78		$q_{\bk\alpha}=\sqrt{\hbar/2\omega_\alpha(\bk)}\,(a_{\bk\alpha}+a^+_{-\bk\alpha})$between $\bk$ and $-\bk$phonons

After step 1 the Hamiltonian is a sum of independent $\bk$ blocks,

$$H=\sum_{\bk\in{\rm BZ}}\sum_{{\rm a}\mu}\frac{P_{\bk{\rm a}\mu}P_{-\bk{\rm a}\mu}}{2m_{\rm a}}+\frac12\sum_{\bk\in{\rm BZ}}\sum_{{\rm a}\mu,{\rm b}\nu}\Omega^2_{{\rm a}\mu{\rm b}\nu}(\bk)\,Q_{\bk{\rm a}\mu}Q_{-\bk{\rm b}\nu}, \tag{E.17}$$

with the dynamical matrix $\Omega^2(\bk)=\sum_{\boldsymbol\delta}e^{i\bk\boldsymbol\delta}k(\boldsymbol\delta)$ of (E.15), the lattice Fourier transform of the force constants (EPP's “elastic matrix” $k$). It has the units of a force constant. EPP also uses the letter $\Omega$ for the crystal volume, $\Omega=N\Omega_{\rm uc}$, and later for the phonon self-energy $\Omega^{\rm e}$: three unrelated objects. Step 2 first rescales by $\sqrt{m_{\rm a}}$ and defines $\tilde\Omega^2_{{\rm a}\mu{\rm b}\nu}=\Omega^2_{{\rm a}\mu{\rm b}\nu}/\sqrt{m_{\rm a}m_{\rm b}}$ (E.24):

$$H=\frac12\sum_{{\rm a}\mu}\sum_{\bk\in{\rm BZ}}\tilde P_{\bk{\rm a}\mu}\tilde P_{-\bk{\rm a}\mu}+\frac12\sum_{{\rm a}\mu,{\rm b}\nu}\sum_{\bk\in{\rm BZ}}\tilde\Omega^2_{{\rm a}\mu{\rm b}\nu}(\bk)\,\tilde Q_{\bk{\rm a}\mu}\tilde Q_{-\bk{\rm b}\nu}. \tag{E.23}$$

The kinetic energy is now the unit matrix in the $3s$-dimensional ${\rm a}\mu$ space, and, in EPP's words, “the unit matrix will remain immune to the unitary transformation.” Without this step the eigenproblem would be the generalized one, $\Omega^2\mathbf x=\omega^2M\mathbf x$, and rotating onto the eigenvectors of $\Omega^2$ would mix the masses back into the kinetic term. The second half of step 2 diagonalizes the Hermitian $\tilde\Omega^2(\bk)$ with the unitary matrix $U(\bk)=[\mathbf e_1(\bk),\dots,\mathbf e_{3s}(\bk)]$ of its orthonormal eigenvectors (E.25–E.28):

$$U^+\tilde\Omega^2U=\mathrm{diag}\left(\omega_1^2,\omega_2^2,\dots,\omega_{3s}^2\right). \tag{E.29}$$

EPP's worked example (E.30), $\tilde\Omega^2=\left[\begin{smallmatrix}3&2\\2&3\end{smallmatrix}\right]$ with $\omega^2=1$ and 5 and $U$ a 45° rotation, is the starting point of the figure below. It is the dimerized chain of §A.1 at the zone edge. Inserting $\tilde Q_{\bk{\rm a}\mu}=\sum_\alpha e_{{\rm a}\mu\alpha}(\bk)q_{\bk\alpha}$ (E.39) leaves $H=\sum_{\bk\alpha}H_{\bk\alpha}$ with

$$H_{\bk\alpha}=\frac12p_{\bk\alpha}p_{-\bk\alpha}+\frac12\omega^2_\alpha(\bk)\,q_{\bk\alpha}q_{-\bk\alpha}. \tag{E.45}$$

That is one oscillator per $(\bk,\alpha)$, except that $q_{\bk\alpha}$ is complex with $q_{-\bk\alpha}=q^+_{\bk\alpha}$, so $\bk$ still talks to $-\bk$. Pairing $a_{\bk\alpha}$ with $a^+_{-\bk\alpha}$ in (E.72)–(E.73) removes this last coupling and gives (E.78). Retracing the substitutions gives the displacement operator, boxed in the source:

$$\boxed{Q_{i{\rm a}\mu}=\frac{1}{\sqrt N}\sum_{\alpha=1}^{3s}\sum_{\bk\in{\rm BZ}}\sqrt{\frac{\hbar}{2m_{\rm a}\omega_\alpha(\bk)}}\,e_{{\rm a}\mu\alpha}(\bk)\left(a_{\bk\alpha}+a^+_{-\bk\alpha}\right)e^{i\bk\bR^0_i}} \tag{E.83}$$

Here the superscript $+$ is EPP's Hermitian conjugate, and the phonon wavevector, called $\bk$ in §1, becomes $\bq$ from §2 on. (E.83) is Giustino's (G.20) with his reference mass $M_0$ cancelled. Together with its momentum partner (E.84), it is the only phonon object the rest of the manuscript needs. Inserted into the potential of a vibrating ion, (E.83) gives the bare vertex below; with $\mathbf e\to\mathbf e^{\mathcal L}$ it gives the polar vertex; and (E.84) gives the ionic current vertex of the photon self-energy (§B.5).

Physical picture: principal axes, possibly complex

In the plane of two mass-scaled coordinates $(\tilde Q_1,\tilde Q_2)$, contours of kinetic energy are circles and contours of potential energy are ellipses. The normal coordinates are the principal axes of the ellipse, and a rotation can diagonalize both quadratic forms only because the kinetic contours are round. When $\tilde\Omega^2$ has a complex off-diagonal element, as it does at a generic $\bk$, the “axes” are complex vectors. In each mode the atoms then oscillate with a fixed relative phase, the intracell part of a running wave.

Note on the source: symmetric or Hermitian? (E.15) and pp. 8–9

EPP diagonalizes the potential term of (E.43) by contracting $\sum e_{{\rm a}\mu\alpha}\tilde\Omega^2_{{\rm a}\mu{\rm b}\nu}e^*_{{\rm b}\nu\beta}$ (p. 8) and invoking a symmetry, $\tilde\Omega^2_{{\rm b}\nu{\rm a}\mu}=\tilde\Omega^2_{{\rm a}\mu{\rm b}\nu}$ (p. 9), that the Hermitian dynamical matrix has only where it is real (Γ, zone-boundary points, the (E.30) example). Elsewhere the step needs $e^{-i\bk\boldsymbol\delta}$ in (E.15), which is Giustino's convention (G.14) and the one this page uses; the printed (E.15) equals his $D^{\rm dm}(-\bk)$. Frequencies are unaffected. The last matrix of the figure shows the failure. The full note, with the on-site block and the “isotropy property”, is the source note of §A.1.

The bare vertex (EPP §2)

Section 2 lets valence electrons feel the vibrations. Each ion, nucleus plus frozen core, carries a local, transferable pseudopotential $v_{\rm a}(\br)$ and drags it rigidly along:

$$V_{\rm cr}(\br)=\sum_{i{\rm a}}v_{\rm a}(\br-\bR_{i{\rm a}}). \tag{E.92}$$

To first order in the displacements $\bR_{i{\rm a}}=\bR^0_{i{\rm a}}+\bQ_{i{\rm a}}$ (E.98),

$$\Delta V_{\rm cr}(\br)=-\sum_{i{\rm a}\mu}\partial_\mu v_{\rm a}(\br-\bR^0_{i{\rm a}})\,Q_{i{\rm a}\mu}, \tag{E.100}$$

and in Fourier space

$$v_{\rm a}(\br-\bR^0_{i{\rm a}})=\int\frac{d\bq'}{(2\pi)^3}\,V_{\rm a}(\bq')\,e^{i\bq'(\br-\bR^0_i)}, \tag{E.101}$$

where $V_{\rm a}(\bq')=e^{-i\bq'\br^0_{\rm a}}v_{\rm a}(\bq')$ keeps the basis phase of atom ${\rm a}$. The gradient becomes $iq'_\mu$. Writing $\Delta V_{\rm cr}$ in second quantization over the frozen-lattice Bloch states $\phi^0_{n\bk}=\Omega^{-1/2}e^{i\bk\br}u^0_{n\bk}$ ($\Omega$ is the crystal volume), inserting (E.83) and doing the lattice sum gives $\Delta V^0_{\rm cr}=\sum g^0_{nm\alpha}(\bk,\bq)\,c^+_{n\bk}c_{m\bk-\bq}(a_{\bq\alpha}+a^+_{-\bq\alpha})$ (E.108) with the boxed bare matrix element

$$\boxed{\begin{aligned}g^0_{nm\alpha}(\bk,\bq)=-\frac{i}{\Omega_{\rm uc}}\sum_{\bG}\sum_{{\rm a}\mu}&\sqrt{\frac{\hbar}{2Nm_{\rm a}\omega^0_\alpha(\bq)}}\;e^0_{{\rm a}\mu\alpha}(\bq)\,(q_\mu+G_\mu)\\&\times V_{\rm a}(\bq+\bG)\,\rho^0_{n\bk,m\bk-\bq}(-\bG)\end{aligned}} \tag{E.107}$$

and the charge vertex

$$\rho^0_{n\bk,m\bk+\bq}(\bG)=\mel{\phi^0_{n\bk}}{e^{-i(\bq+\bG)\br}}{\phi^0_{m\bk+\bq}}. \tag{E.106}$$
Derivation: from (E.100) to (E.107)

Insert (E.101) into (E.100). The derivative of $e^{i\bq'(\br-\bR^0_i)}$ brings down $iq'_\mu$, so $\Delta V_{\rm cr}(\br)=-i\sum_{i{\rm a}\mu}Q_{i{\rm a}\mu}\int\frac{d\bq'}{(2\pi)^3}q'_\mu V_{\rm a}(\bq')e^{i\bq'(\br-\bR^0_i)}$ (E.102). In second quantization over $\phi^0_{n\bk}$ (E.103–E.104) the $\br$ dependence sits in $\mel{\phi^0_{n\bk}}{e^{i\bq'\br}}{\phi^0_{m\bk'}}=\delta_{\bk',\bk-\bq'}\,\rho^0_{n\bk,m\bk-\bq'}(\bG=0)$ (E.105). The Kronecker delta holds modulo $\bG$, which is EPP's umklapp warning.

Now replace $Q_{i{\rm a}\mu}$ by (E.83), with phonon wavevector $\bq$, bare $\omega^0_\alpha$ and $e^0_{{\rm a}\mu\alpha}$. The cell sum $\sum_ie^{i(\bq-\bq')\bR^0_i}=N\sum_{\bG}\delta_{\bq',\bq+\bG}$, together with $\int d\bq'/(2\pi)^3\to\Omega^{-1}\sum_{\bq'}$, turns the integral into a sum over $\bq'=\bq+\bG$ with $\bq\in$ BZ. The prefactor $N/\Omega$ times the $N^{-1/2}$ of (E.83) equals $1/(\Omega_{\rm uc}\sqrt N)$ with $\Omega_{\rm uc}=\Omega/N$, which is how $N$ ends up inside the square root of (E.107). Finally, the periodic gauge $\phi_{m,\bk-\bq-\bG}=\phi_{m,\bk-\bq}$ and $c_{m\bk-\bq-\bG}=c_{m\bk-\bq}$ give $\rho^0_{n\bk,m\bk-\bq-\bG}(\bG=0)=\rho^0_{n\bk,m\bk-\bq}(-\bG)$ in the notation of (E.106). Collecting factors gives (E.107)–(E.108).

Read (E.107) factor by factor. The zero-point amplitude $\sqrt{\hbar/2Nm_{\rm a}\omega^0_\alpha}$ includes the $1/\sqrt N$ that Giustino keeps outside his $g$. The projection $(\bq+\bG)\cdot\mathbf e^0_{\rm a}$ means that at $\bG=0$ only displacements along $\bq$ couple; umklapp terms let transverse modes couple too. $V_{\rm a}(\bq+\bG)$ is the bare pseudopotential form factor, and $\rho^0$ is the pair density that RPA and BSE codes call the oscillator strength. With $s=1$, $\bG=0$ and plane waves ($\rho=\delta_{nm}$), (E.107) is Bloch's 1929 matrix element (G.2) with $V_0\to V_{\rm a}(\bq)/\Omega_{\rm uc}$ (§A.2).

“Bare” has teeth. A pseudo-ion of valence $Z_v$ has a Coulomb tail, $V_{\rm a}(\bq)\to-Z_ve^2/\epsilon_0q^2$ in SI, so the factor $(\bq\cdot\mathbf e^0_{\rm a})V_{\rm a}(\bq)$ diverges as $1/q$ at small $q$ for every mode. Acoustic modes are not spared; their zero-point factor $\omega^{-1/2}$ makes the divergence stronger still. Valence screening must remove this divergence in metals (Bardeen) and in nonpolar insulators, and reduce it to the dipolar Fröhlich form in polar insulators (below). Adding the bare bands, the bare phonons and the valence electron–electron Coulomb interaction gives EPP's bare model Hamiltonian:

$$\begin{aligned}H={}&\sum_{n\bk}E^0_{n\bk}c^+_{n\bk}c_{n\bk}+\sum_{\alpha=1}^{3s}\sum_{\bq\in{\rm BZ}}\hbar\omega^0_\alpha(\bq)\left(a^+_{\bq\alpha}a_{\bq\alpha}+1/2\right)\\&+\sum_{\alpha=1}^{3s}\sum_{\bk\bq\in{\rm BZ}}\sum_{nm}g^0_{nm\alpha}(\bk,\bq)\,c^+_{n\bk}c_{m\bk-\bq}\left(a_{\bq\alpha}+a^+_{-\bq\alpha}\right)\\&+\frac12\int d\br\int d\br'\,\Psi^+_0(x)\Psi^+_0(x')V(\br,\br')\Psi_0(x')\Psi_0(x).\end{aligned} \tag{E.109}$$

Here $V(\br,\br')$ is the bare Coulomb interaction and $\Psi_0(x)=\sum_{n\bk}\phi^0_{n\bk}(\br)c_{n\bk}(t)$. The stated approximations are harmonic ions and frozen cores. Three more are implicit: linear coupling only (no Debye–Waller term), local pseudopotentials, and rigid ions.

Bridge to Giustino: Eq. (G.1) with the Coulomb term left in

The first three terms of (E.109) have the structure of the first two lines of (G.1). Four differences matter. (i) Every parameter is bare, while Giustino's $\varepsilon_{n\bk}$, $\omega_{\bq\nu}$ and $g$ are DFT/DFPT quantities; (E.107) is the plane-wave form of his bare vertex $g^{\rm b}$ (G.142), and the DFPT vertex is the screened $g=\epsilon_{\rm e}^{-1}g^{\rm b}$ (§A.3). (ii) EPP keeps the electron–electron interaction explicit; (G.1) has none. (iii) There is no second-order (Debye–Waller) term. (iv) The labels differ: EPP writes $g_{nm}(\bk,\bq)\,c^+_{n\bk}c_{m\bk-\bq}$ where Giustino writes $g_{mn}(\bk,\bq)\,\hat c^\dagger_{m\bk+\bq}\hat c_{n\bk}$, so $g^{\rm EPP}_{nm}(\bk,\bq)=N^{-1/2}g^{\rm G}_{nm}(\bk-\bq,\bq)$, with Giustino's first band index the final state.

Two starting points, and the double-counting rule

Page 21 of EPP makes the argument that shapes the rest of the manuscript. Perturbation theory around (E.109) never double counts: “everyone can interact with everyone” through $v$ or the bare phonon propagator, and nothing is already included in $H_0$. But neither the electron–electron nor the electron–phonon interaction is small, and the bare $\{E^0_{n\bk},\phi^0_{n\bk}\}$ are a poor starting basis: a large part of the electron–electron interaction belongs inside them, and through them inside $\omega^0_\alpha(\bq)$. The practical starting point is DFT, $E^0_{n\bk}\to E_{n\bk}$, $\phi^0_{n\bk}\to\phi_{n\bk}$, $\omega^0_\alpha(\bq)\to\omega_\alpha(\bq)$, with (E.109) otherwise unchanged.

Then the bookkeeping matters. DFT ions already interact adiabatically through the valence electrons, so the static part of the electronic bubble in the phonon self-energy is already inside $\omega_\alpha(\bq)$. Only the dynamic (nonadiabatic) remainder may be added. DFT states inside the RPA bubble, and hence inside $W$, are not double counting. This is Giustino's split $\Pi^{\rm ph}=\Pi^{\rm A}+\Pi^{\rm NA}(\omega)$ (G.125), with $\chi^0(\omega)-\chi^0(0)$ in (G.145) (§A.6).

The second half of the argument concerns range. EPP models DFT force constants as strictly short-ranged,

$$k^{\mathcal S}_{i{\rm a}\mu,j{\rm b}\nu}=\left.\frac{\partial^2V}{\partial R_{i{\rm a}\mu}\,\partial R_{j{\rm b}\nu}}\right|_{\{\bR^0_{i{\rm a}}\}}=0\qquad\text{for }|\bR^0_{i{\rm a}}-\bR^0_{j{\rm b}}|>a,$$

with $\mathcal S$ for short range and $a$ the cell size. It then notes that a displacement in a polar crystal induces a dipole $\bp_{i{\rm a}}=\hat Z^*\bQ_{i{\rm a}}$ whose field reaches far beyond a cell, and that adding it “poses no threat of double counting, in most cases.” The condition hidden in “in most cases” is the rule that governs Part B: only short-range (analytic) force constants may be combined with an explicitly mediated long-range coupling. If the bare phonons already contain the dipole–dipole interaction, photon exchange counts it a second time.

Subtlety: DFPT force constants are not short-ranged

EPP attributes the short range to DFT itself (“neglect of long-range electronic correlations”). That does not hold for density-functional perturbation theory. In polar insulators the DFPT force constants carry a dipole–dipole tail $\propto|\bR|^{-3}$ whose nonanalytic Fourier transform is the LO–TO splitting (Gonze and Lee 1997), and DFPT matrix elements carry the $1/q$ Fröhlich singularity (Giustino §VI.A.3, §A.4). What is true is narrower: a periodic calculation at exactly $\bq=0$ lacks the macroscopic field, which codes add back through $Z^*$ and $\epsilon^\infty$. In practice EPP's bare $\omega_\alpha(\bq)$ should come from the analytic part of the DFPT dynamical matrix, with the dipole–dipole term subtracted; photon exchange then regenerates it (§B.7, §B.9). Van der Waals “long-range correlation” is a separate issue.

IngredientFrom DFT/DFPT?Role in EPP
Bands $E_{n\bk}$, states $\phi_{n\bk}$yesinside the RPA bubbles of the photon self-energy (§B.5)
Short-range (analytic) force constantsyesbare phonons $\omega_\alpha(\bq)$, $\mathbf e_\alpha(\bq)$
Long-range dipole–dipole force constantsno, subtractregenerated by photon exchange: LO–TO splitting (§B.7)

$\epsilon^\infty$inserted by hand in §3regenerated from the electronic photon self-energy (§B.5, §B.8)
Short-range vertex $g^{\mathcal S}$available, as DFPT $g$ minus $g^{\mathcal L}$not used: absent from the Lagrangian (E.134) (§B.2)

Polar coupling from Born charges (EPP §3)

In a polar crystal, displacing atom ${\rm a}$ along $\nu$ changes the dipole of its cell along $\mu$. EPP defines the Born effective charge tensor as that response,

$$Z^*_{{\rm a}\mu\nu}=\frac{\delta p_\mu}{\delta R_{{\rm a}\nu}}=\Omega_{\rm uc}\frac{\delta P_\mu}{\delta R_{{\rm a}\nu}}, \tag{E.110}$$
$$p_{i{\rm a}\mu}=Z^*_{{\rm a}\mu\nu}Q_{i{\rm a}\nu}. \tag{E.111}$$

$Z^*$ is the same in every cell and, in EPP, has the dimension of charge. EPP's Fig. 2 stresses the tensor character: a displacement along $\nu$ can produce a dipole along a different direction $\mu$. The potential of a point dipole $\bp=e\boldsymbol\delta$ (E.112) in a medium with the clamped-ion dielectric tensor $\hat\epsilon^\infty$ follows from Poisson's equation with the bound charge $-\nabla\cdot\bP$, $\bP=\epsilon_0(\hat\epsilon^\infty-\mathbb 1)\bE$ (E.113–E.114). In SI units:

$$\nabla\hat\epsilon^\infty\nabla\phi=-\frac{1}{\epsilon_0}\rho(\br), \tag{E.116}$$
$$\phi(\bq)=-\frac{i}{\epsilon_0}\,\frac{\bp\cdot\bq}{\bq\cdot\hat\epsilon^\infty\cdot\bq}. \tag{E.120}$$
Derivation: from the point dipole (E.112) to (E.120), and the real-space potential

With the convention (E.117), $\phi(\br)=\int\frac{d\bq}{(2\pi)^3}e^{i\bq\br}\phi(\bq)$, the dipole density is $\rho(\br)=e\int\frac{d\bq}{(2\pi)^3}e^{i\bq\br}\big[e^{-i\bq\boldsymbol\delta/2}-e^{i\bq\boldsymbol\delta/2}\big]=-i\int\frac{d\bq}{(2\pi)^3}e^{i\bq\br}\,\bp\cdot\bq$ for $|\boldsymbol\delta|\to0$. On the left of (E.116), $\nabla\cdot\hat\epsilon^\infty\nabla$ acting on $e^{i\bq\br}$ gives $-\bq\cdot\hat\epsilon^\infty\cdot\bq$ (E.118–E.119). Equating Fourier components, $-\bq\cdot\hat\epsilon^\infty\cdot\bq\,\phi(\bq)=(i/\epsilon_0)\,\bp\cdot\bq$, which is (E.120).

Check: for $\hat\epsilon^\infty=\mathbb 1$ this is the transform of $\bp\cdot\br/(4\pi\epsilon_0r^3)$, since the transform of $1/(4\pi\epsilon_0r)$ is $1/(\epsilon_0q^2)$ and $-\bp\cdot\nabla$ brings down $-i\bp\cdot\bq$. In real space the anisotropic result is [derived]

$$\phi(\br)=\frac{\bp\cdot\hat\epsilon^{-1}\cdot\br}{4\pi\epsilon_0\sqrt{\det\hat\epsilon}\,\left(\br\cdot\hat\epsilon^{-1}\cdot\br\right)^{3/2}},$$

so equipotentials are squeezed into ellipsoids and field lines are no longer radial. Gaussian units follow from $\epsilon_0\to1/4\pi$, as EPP notes.

Two properties of (E.120) drive everything that follows. It scales as $1/q$, the Fourier image of a potential that decays as $1/r^2$, and its limit $q\to0$ depends on the direction $\hat\bq$: the expression is nonanalytic at the zone centre. And it vanishes for $\bp\perp\bq$, because only the longitudinal component of a dipole wave produces a scalar potential. EPP calls $\hat\epsilon^\infty$ “the electronic part of screening that we have already calculated so far”, inserts it ad hoc, and announces that it will be removed later to avoid double counting.

Summing the potentials of all displaced atoms and multiplying by the electron charge $-e$ gives $\Delta V^{\mathcal L}_{\rm cr}$ (E.121–E.123), with $\mathcal L$ for long range. EPP then notices that with the definitions

$$V^{\mathcal L}_{\rm a}(\bq)=\frac{e^2}{\epsilon_0\,\bq\cdot\hat\epsilon^\infty\cdot\bq}, \tag{E.124}$$
$$e^{\mathcal L}_{{\rm a}\mu\alpha}(\bk)=-\frac1e\sum_\nu Z^*_{{\rm a}\mu\nu}e_{{\rm a}\nu\alpha}(\bk), \tag{E.127}$$

the result has exactly the form of the rigid-ion potential (E.102):

$$\Delta V^{\mathcal L}_{\rm cr}(\br)=-i\sum_{i{\rm a}\mu}Q^{\mathcal L}_{i{\rm a}\mu}\int\frac{d\bq}{(2\pi)^3}\,q_\mu V^{\mathcal L}_{\rm a}(\bq)\,e^{i\bq(\br-\bR^0_i)}, \tag{E.128}$$

where $Q^{\mathcal L}_{i{\rm a}\mu}=-\frac1e\sum_\nu Z^*_{{\rm a}\mu\nu}Q_{i{\rm a}\nu}$ (E.125). Its phonon expansion (E.126) is (E.83) with $\mathbf e\to\mathbf e^{\mathcal L}$. The polar crystal acts as if every atom carried a point charge $-e$, displaced by $\bQ^{\mathcal L}$, that interacts with the electron through a Coulomb form factor screened by $\hat\epsilon^\infty$. All of §2 then applies unchanged, and the explicit polar vertex, boxed in the source, is

$$\boxed{\begin{aligned}g^{\mathcal L}_{nm\alpha}(\bk,\bq)=\frac{4\pi i}{\Omega_{\rm uc}}\frac{e}{4\pi\epsilon_0}\sum_{\bG}\sum_{{\rm a}\mu\nu}&\sqrt{\frac{\hbar}{2Nm_{\rm a}\omega_\alpha(\bq)}}\;\frac{(q_\mu+G_\mu)\,Z^*_{{\rm a}\mu\nu}\,e_{{\rm a}\nu\alpha}(\bq)}{(\bq+\bG)\cdot\hat\epsilon^\infty\cdot(\bq+\bG)}\\&\times\rho_{n\bk,m\bk-\bq}(-\bG)\end{aligned}} \tag{E.131}$$

The two diagrams summarize the difference. In $g^0$ the phonon shakes the ionic pseudopotential directly. In $g^{\mathcal L}$ the phonon's dipole $\hat Z^*\bQ$ reaches the electron through the Coulomb interaction screened by $\hat\epsilon^\infty$, drawn here as the page's screened-Coulomb line; in §B.4 that line becomes the longitudinal photon. Equation (E.131) is in SI with a charge-dimensioned $Z^*$, so the prefactor $eZ^*_{\rm EPP}/4\pi\epsilon_0$ is Giustino's $e^2Z^*_{\rm G}/4\pi\epsilon_0$. In the Gaussian units of §4 on, $e/4\pi\epsilon_0\to e$. At $\bG=0$ the kernel is $(1/q)\,\hat\bq\cdot\hat Z^*\cdot\mathbf e/(\hat\bq\cdot\hat\epsilon^\infty\cdot\hat\bq)$, a function of the direction $\hat\bq$ alone divided by $q$. The figure plots that function for a uniaxial crystal.

EPP states that (E.131) is “exactly equal to Eq. 4” of Verdi and Giustino (2015), which appears in Giustino's review, in corrected form and SI units, as (G.180), displayed in §A.4 (there $\Omega$ is EPP's $\Omega_{\rm uc}$ and $Z^*_\kappa$ is dimensionless). The structures agree, and the factor $e$ that EPP mentions is the charge inside its $Z^*$. “Exactly” needs qualifiers: the band and momentum labels differ as for $g^0$; Verdi and Giustino exclude $\bG=-\bq$ and in practice damp the $\bG$ sum with $e^{-a|\bq+\bG|^2}$ (Giustino's footnote 7); and (E.131) lacks the basis phase (note below). For a cubic diatomic crystal, keeping $\bG=0$ and intraband terms, both reduce to Fröhlich's vertex (G.7) once the LO–TO splitting is written through $Z^*$ and $\epsilon^\infty$; §A.4 shows how. With literature inputs the Born-charge and Fröhlich forms agree to 6% for GaAs and to better than 1% for MgO; the GaAs gap comes from inputs that are not mutually consistent (§A.4).

Note on the source: basis phase, citation, Born charge

(1) In (E.121)–(E.123) every dipole of cell $i$ sits at the cell origin $\bR^0_i$ rather than at $\bR^0_i+\br^0_{\rm a}$, although §2 kept the phase in $V_{\rm a}(\bq')=e^{-i\bq'\br^0_{\rm a}}v_{\rm a}(\bq')$. The correct (E.131) carries $e^{-i(\bq+\bG)\cdot\br^0_{\rm a}}$ inside the atom sum. The same factor is missing from Eq. (4) of Verdi and Giustino; Giustino's footnote 7 restores it in (G.180), where it “needs to be retained in order to correctly describe the acoustic modes near $\bq=0$.” So EPP's “exactly equal” is true, but both formulas lack it. (2) EPP cites “F. Giustino, Phys. Rev. Lett. 115, 176401 (2015)”; the authors are C. Verdi and F. Giustino. (3) The Born charge must be the derivative at zero macroscopic field (the transverse charge). The text does not say so, but (E.120) adds the $\hat\epsilon^\infty$ screening separately, which only makes sense for that definition. Index and wording slips in EPP §§2–3 are listed in Z.2.

Subtlety: this is electrostatics

(E.120) is the instantaneous Coulomb field of a dipole, valid when the finite speed of light can be ignored. That requires $q\gg q_c=\sqrt{\epsilon^\infty}\,\omega/c$, far outside the light cone; for optical phonons $q_c$ is of order $10^{-4}$ Å⁻¹ (about $2\times10^{-4}$ Å⁻¹ for the hBN-like in-plane mode, $6\times10^{-5}$ Å⁻¹ for GaAs; §X.1). A transverse dipole wave, invisible to (E.120), still produces a transverse electric field, which is a photon field. It matters only near the light cone, where TO phonons and photons mix into polaritons (§B.6). §B.8 derives the electrodynamic vertex whose $c\to\infty$ limit is (E.131) with $\hat\epsilon^\infty\to\hat\epsilon^{\rm e}(\bq,\omega)$.

What carries forward

  • The displacement operator (E.83) and its momentum (E.84) are unchanged in §4 (p. 40). They become the ionic current vertex $j_{\alpha\sigma}=\sum_{{\rm a}\mu}Z^*_{{\rm a}\alpha\mu}e_{{\rm a}\mu\sigma}/\sqrt{m_{\rm a}}$ (E.295) of the ionic photon self-energy (§B.5).
  • The bare phonons $\omega_\alpha(\bq)$ come from short-range force constants only. Photon exchange dresses them into LO and TO modes and polaritons (§B.6, §B.7).
  • The bare vertex $g^0$ does not appear in the Lagrangian (E.134), where electrons see only the frozen $V_{\rm cr}$. From §4 on, EPP's electron–phonon coupling is purely the polar channel; a complete theory would add a screened short-range $g^{\mathcal S}$. EPP also stops short of electron self-energies: it dresses photons and phonons only.
  • The polar vertex $g^{\mathcal L}$ is the electrostatic seed. §B.8 rederives it from photon exchange without inserting $\epsilon^\infty$ by hand, and §B.9 recovers (E.131) as $c\to\infty$.

Next, §B.2 writes the one Lagrangian in which electrons and ionic dipoles couple only through the vector potential.

B.2EPP §4.1 · Eqs. 132–143

One Lagrangian for electrons, ions and fields

EPP puts band electrons, harmonic ions and the full electromagnetic field into one classical Lagrangian. It has no electron–phonon term: electrons and ions interact only by sharing the vector potential. Its Euler–Lagrange equations give the Lorentz force for the electrons and, for the ions, a lattice driven by the electric field through the Born charges.

In §B.1 EPP built two electron–phonon vertices by hand: the bare rigid-ion vertex $g^0$ (E.107) and the electrostatic polar vertex $g^{\mathcal L}$ (E.131). In the second, the dipole field of a displaced ion was screened by an $\hat\epsilon^\infty$ that the author himself calls ad hoc. EPP §4 changes strategy. It no longer computes the potential that a displaced ion produces. Electrons, ions and the electromagnetic field become three dynamical systems in one Lagrangian, and the field carries every interaction between them.

Physical picture

Treat the electromagnetic field as the medium through which everything talks. A moving electron acts on the field through its current. A displaced ion acts on it through the current of its induced dipole. Apart from the frozen crystal potential felt by the electrons and the short-range springs between ions, nothing acts on anything else directly. What Giustino calls the Coulomb interaction is the part of the field that follows the charges instantly (the longitudinal part). The rest is light, which travels at $c$. An electron–phonon interaction is then a two-step process: electron to field, field to ion.

The temporal gauge

EPP §4 opens by setting the scalar potential to zero, $\Phi=0$. Both fields then come from the vector potential alone:

$$\bE=-\frac1c\frac{\partial\bA}{\partial t}, \tag{E.132}$$
$$\bB=\nabla\times\bA. \tag{E.133}$$

This is the temporal (Weyl) gauge. It is convenient for three reasons.

  • One field carries everything. Split $\bA=\bA_l+\bA_t$ into a curl-free part along $\bq$ and a divergence-free part transverse to it (cf. E.218). The longitudinal field $\bE_l=-\frac1c\dot\bA_l$ is the Coulomb field of the charges, and $\bA_t$ carries radiation. Coulomb and light become two polarizations of one object. That is what later allows a single photon propagator, longitudinal plus transverse, $D^0=D^{0l}+D^{0t}$ (§B.6).
  • Electrons and ions couple in the same way. With no scalar potential there is no $\rho\Phi$ term. Every coupling has the form "current times $\bA$". Electronic and ionic currents therefore enter the photon self-energy on an equal footing (§B.5).
  • Coulomb is derived, not postulated. Giustino takes the instantaneous interaction $v(\br-\br')\delta(t-t')$ as given. Here the Coulomb energy comes out of the energy of the longitudinal field. The Coulomb gauge $\nabla\cdot\bA=0$ describes the same physics in a different bookkeeping: $\bA$ is purely transverse, and $\Phi$ has no dynamics of its own, being fixed at every instant by Poisson's equation. The temporal gauge instead keeps the Coulomb field inside $\bA$, next to the photons.

The price is that Gauss's law is not one of the Euler–Lagrange equations. It is a constraint on the initial state that the dynamics preserves. §B.4 deals with it, and that is where $\frac1{8\pi}\int\bE_l^2$ turns into the Coulomb energy.

Conventions. From here on EPP uses Gaussian units, a signed electron charge ($e<0$) and Born charges with the dimension of charge (see the Part B introduction). The PDF writes dot products without a dot ($\mathbf v_e\bA$); we insert them.

The Lagrangian, term by term

For valence electrons at positions $\br_e$ with velocities $\mathbf v_e$, and ions displaced by $Q_{ia\mu}$ (cell $i$, atom $a$, direction $\mu$) from their sites, EPP writes

$$\begin{aligned}L={}&\underbrace{\sum_e\left[\frac{m_e\mathbf v_e^2}{2}-V_{\rm cr}(\br_e)\right]}_{(1)}+\underbrace{\sum_{ia\mu}\frac{m_a\dot Q^2_{ia\mu}}{2}}_{(2)}-\underbrace{\frac12\sum_{ia\mu,jb\nu}k_{ia\mu,jb\nu}Q_{ia\mu}Q_{jb\nu}}_{(3)}\\&+\underbrace{\int\frac{d\br}{8\pi}\left\{\bE^2(\br)-\bB^2(\br)\right\}}_{(4)}+\underbrace{\frac ec\sum_e\mathbf v_e\cdot\bA(\br_e)}_{(5)}+\underbrace{\frac1c\sum_{ia}\dot{\bp}_{ia}\cdot\bA(\bR^0_i)}_{(6)},\end{aligned} \tag{E.134}$$

where the dipole of atom $a$ in cell $i$ and the frozen crystal potential are

$$p_{ia\mu}=\sum_\nu Z^*_{a\mu\nu}Q_{ia\nu}, \tag{E.135}$$
$$V_{\rm cr}(\br)=\sum_{ia}v_a(\br-\bR^0_{ia}). \tag{E.136}$$
TermWhat it describesWhat it becomes (§B.4)
(1)Noninteracting valence electrons in the frozen local pseudopotential $v_a$ (nucleus plus core) at the equilibrium sitesBand states, taken as Kohn–Sham $E_{n\bk}$ in $H_0$ (E.236)
(2)+(3)Harmonic ions with force constants $k$ (E.5)Bare phonons $\hbar\omega_\alpha(\bq)$ from short-range force constants
(4)The free electromagnetic field, all polarizationsTransverse photons $\hbar cq$ (E.214) and the Coulomb energy $\frac1{8\pi}\int\bE_l^2$ (E.235)
(5)The electron current coupled to $\bA$Electron–photon vertices, paramagnetic $\bj_{\rm e}\cdot\bA$ and diamagnetic $A^2$; electron–electron Coulomb
(6)The ionic polarization current $\dot\bp$ coupled to $\bA$Ion–photon vertices $Z^*\pi\cdot\bA$ and $Z^*Z^*AA$; electron–ion and ion–ion Coulomb

EPP reads term (5) as "the electron–electron interaction" and term (6) as "the electron–phonon interaction", and remarks on the symmetry of the two "current times vector potential" bindings. Taken literally, each term couples one kind of matter to the field. They describe interactions between particles only because the same $\bA$ appears in both.

Why the ions couple through their Born dipoles

In this model the static charge of the ions is already inside $V_{\rm cr}$, which acts on the electrons directly. The field does not see an ion at rest at its site. It sees only how the charge distribution changes when the ion moves, and to linear order that change is a dipole per atom, $\bp=\hat Z^*\bQ$ (E.135). Here $Z^*_{a\mu\nu}=\partial p_\mu/\partial R_{a\nu}=\Omega_{\rm uc}\,\partial P_\mu/\partial R_{a\nu}$ is the Born effective charge of EPP §3 (E.110, §B.1). A changing dipole is a current. Summed over the crystal, $\dot\bP(\br)=\sum_{ia}\dot\bp_{ia}\,\delta(\br-\bR^0_i)$ is the polarization current, and term (6) couples it to $\bA$ exactly as term (5) couples the electron current. A displaced ion behaves like a particle that carries a tensor charge $Z^*$. Three consequences follow.

  • Velocity form equals dipole energy. Since $\bA$ is taken at the fixed site $\bR^0_i$, $\frac1c\dot\bp\cdot\bA=\bp\cdot\bE+\frac1c\frac{d}{dt}(\bp\cdot\bA)$. A total time derivative does not change the equations of motion, so term (6) is equivalent to the Lagrangian term $+\bp\cdot\bE$, i.e. to the familiar dipole energy $U=-\bp\cdot\bE$. If you compute optical spectra, this is the same equivalence as between velocity ($\bp\cdot\bA$) and length ($\br\cdot\bE$) gauge optical matrix elements.
  • Acoustic sum rule. $\sum_aZ^*_a=0$, so a rigid translation of a cell carries no dipole. Acoustic modes at $\bq\to0$ do not couple to the field.
  • The Born charge is the right object. $Z^*$ is the response at zero macroscopic field (the transverse charge). It does not include the electronic screening of the dipole's own long-range field. In EPP that screening has to come from the electrons' own coupling to $\bA$, term (5), instead of the $\hat\epsilon^\infty$ put in by hand in §B.1. EPP regenerates it from the electronic photon self-energy (§B.5, §B.9).

There is no electron–phonon term

No term of (E.134) contains both $\br_e$ and $Q_{ia\mu}$. There is no $g$. Electrons and ions interact only by sharing $\bA$, through two channels:

  • Longitudinal. A longitudinal polarization wave carries bound charge $\rho_{\rm ion}=-\nabla\cdot\bP$. The electron charge and the ionic bound charge meet in the energy of $\bA_l$, which §B.4 shows is their instantaneous Coulomb energy (E.235). This is the bare, unscreened Fröhlich coupling, i.e. (E.131) with $\hat\epsilon^\infty\to1$.
  • Transverse. An electron current emits a photon through term (5), and a polarization current absorbs it through term (6). This channel is retarded in EPP's sense of the word (finite $c$) and has no counterpart in Giustino. It matters only near the light cone, $q\lesssim q_c=\sqrt{\epsilon_\infty}\,\omega/c\approx6\times10^{-5}$ Å$^{-1}$ for a GaAs phonon (§X.1).

The same field also carries the electron–electron interaction (term 5 twice) and the ion–ion interaction (term 6 twice). The latter is the dipole–dipole force behind the LO–TO splitting (§B.7). The polar, long-range part of Giustino's vertex $g$ reappears only later, as a composite: electron current, photon dressed by the electrons, ionic current (§B.8).

What the Lagrangian leaves out

  • Short-range coupling. $V_{\rm cr}$ is frozen at the equilibrium sites, so the deformation-potential vertex of EPP §2 (E.107–E.108) is absent. Only the polar, long-range channel is rebuilt from the field. A complete theory would add a screened short-range $g^{\mathcal S}$.
  • Double counting. $k$ must be the short-range (analytic) force constants, because the dipole–dipole part is regenerated through $\bA_l$. The same holds for the electron–electron Coulomb term and the Hartree–xc part already inside DFT bands (discussed in §B.4).
  • Dipole approximation. Every atom's dipole sits at the cell origin, $\bA(\bR^0_i)$, while $V_{\rm cr}$ uses the atomic sites $\bR^0_{ia}$. This drops the basis phase $e^{-i(\bq+\bG)\cdot\br^0_a}$, the factor Giustino restores in the Verdi–Giustino vertex (his footnote 7). It is harmless at photon wave vectors but matters for local fields. Ions also carry no quadrupoles and feel no magnetic force.
  • Model electrons. Nonrelativistic and spinless, with a local pseudopotential.

Electrons: the Lorentz force

EPP §4.1 checks that term (5) is the correct coupling. The Euler–Lagrange equation for electron $e$ is

$$\nabla_eL-\frac{d}{dt}\nabla_{\mathbf v_e}L=0. \tag{E.137}$$

Because $\bA_e\equiv\bA(\br_e,t)$ is evaluated at the moving electron, its total time derivative has a convective part. After a vector identity, the result (unnumbered, EPP p. 27) is the Lorentz equation,

$$m_e\frac{d\mathbf v_e}{dt}=-\nabla_eV_{\rm cr}(\br_e)+e\bE_e+\frac ec\,\mathbf v_e\times\bB_e .$$

In the temporal gauge, $e\bE_e$ contains the Coulomb force of all other charges, through $\bE_l$, as well as the radiation field. The canonical momentum $\partial L/\partial\mathbf v_e=m_e\mathbf v_e+\frac ec\bA_e$ differs from the kinetic one. That difference is the origin of the minimal coupling $(\bp-\frac ec\bA)^2/2m_e$ of §B.4 (E.182).

Derivation: from (E.137) to the Lorentz equation

Inserting (E.134) into (E.137), only terms (1) and (5) depend on $\br_e$ and $\mathbf v_e$:

$$\begin{aligned}\nabla_eL&=-\nabla_eV_{\rm cr}(\br_e)+\frac ec\nabla_e(\mathbf v_e\cdot\bA_e),\\ \frac{d}{dt}\nabla_{\mathbf v_e}L&=m_e\frac{d\mathbf v_e}{dt}+\frac ec\frac{d\bA_e}{dt}.\end{aligned} \tag{E.138}$$

The electron moves, so $\frac{d\bA_e}{dt}=\frac{\partial\bA_e}{\partial t}+(\mathbf v_e\cdot\nabla_e)\bA_e$. Then

$$m_e\frac{d\mathbf v_e}{dt}=-\nabla_eV_{\rm cr}-\frac ec\frac{\partial\bA_e}{\partial t}+\frac ec\Big[\nabla_e(\mathbf v_e\cdot\bA_e)-(\mathbf v_e\cdot\nabla_e)\bA_e\Big].$$

With $\mathbf a\times(\mathbf b\times\mathbf c)=\mathbf b(\mathbf a\cdot\mathbf c)-(\mathbf a\cdot\mathbf b)\mathbf c$, where $\nabla_e$ acts only on $\bA$ and $\mathbf v_e$ is an independent variable, the bracket is $\mathbf v_e\times(\nabla_e\times\bA_e)$. With (E.132)–(E.133), $-\frac1c\partial_t\bA_e=\bE_e$ and $\nabla_e\times\bA_e=\bB_e$, which gives the Lorentz equation.

Ions: a lattice driven by the electric field

For the ions, EPP §4.2 writes

$$\frac{\partial L}{\partial Q_{ia\mu}}-\frac{d}{dt}\frac{\partial L}{\partial\dot Q_{ia\mu}}=0. \tag{E.139}$$

Term (6) depends on $\dot Q$, not on $Q$, so it enters through the canonical momentum. Its time derivative is $\dot\bA$ at a fixed site, which (E.132) turns into an electric force:

$$m_a\ddot Q_{ia\mu}+\sum_{jb\nu}k_{ia\mu,jb\nu}Q_{jb\nu}=\sum_\nu Z^*_{a\nu\mu}E_\nu(\bR^0_i). \tag{E.143}$$

Each ion is a harmonic oscillator driven by the field through its Born charge. In EPP's words, the field "couples to the dipole moment $p_{ia\mu}$ and not to the coordinate $Q_{ia\mu}$". The generalized force $F_{a\mu}=\sum_\nu Z^*_{a\nu\mu}E_\nu$ is the standard alternative definition of the Born charge, $Z^*_{\nu\mu}=\partial F_\mu/\partial E_\nu$. Note the transposed index order relative to (E.135). Since $\bR^0_i$ does not move, there is no convective term and no magnetic force on the ions; the dipole approximation drops forces of order $v/c$.

Derivation: (E.139) to (E.143)

Only term (3) depends on $Q$. With the symmetry $k_{ia\mu,jb\nu}=k_{jb\nu,ia\mu}$,

$$\frac{\partial L}{\partial Q_{ia\mu}}=-\sum_{jb\nu}k_{ia\mu,jb\nu}Q_{jb\nu}. \tag{E.140}$$

Terms (2) and (6) depend on $\dot Q$. Since $\dot p_{ia\nu}=\sum_\mu Z^*_{a\nu\mu}\dot Q_{ia\mu}$, we get $\partial L/\partial\dot Q_{ia\mu}=m_a\dot Q_{ia\mu}+\frac1c\sum_\nu Z^*_{a\nu\mu}A_\nu(\bR^0_i)$, which is the ionic canonical momentum (E.183) of §B.4. Its time derivative at the fixed site is

$$\frac{d}{dt}\frac{\partial L}{\partial\dot Q_{ia\mu}}=m_a\ddot Q_{ia\mu}+\frac1c\sum_\nu Z^*_{a\nu\mu}\dot A_\nu(\bR^0_i), \tag{E.141}$$ $$m_a\ddot Q_{ia\mu}=-\sum_{jb\nu}k_{ia\mu,jb\nu}Q_{jb\nu}-\frac1c\sum_\nu Z^*_{a\nu\mu}\dot A_\nu(\bR^0_i). \tag{E.142}$$

With $-\frac1c\dot A_\nu=E_\nu$ (E.132) this is (E.143).

Take a diatomic cell at $\bq\to0$ with $Z^*_a=-Z^*_b\equiv Z^*$ and the lattice-summed spring $k$ of §B.3. Dividing each of the two equations (E.143) by its mass and subtracting, the relative coordinate $u=Q_a-Q_b$ obeys $M\ddot u+ku=Z^*E$, with reduced mass $M$ and bare optical frequency $\omega_{\rm O}^2=k/M$. Add a phenomenological damping $\gamma$ (anharmonic decay, which E.134 does not contain) and drive with $E(t)=\mathrm{Re}\,E_0e^{-i\omega t}$. Then

$$u(\omega)=\frac{Z^*E_0/M}{\omega_{\rm O}^2-\omega^2-i\gamma\omega},\qquad \dot P=-i\omega\,\frac{Z^*u}{\Omega_{\rm uc}} .$$

Below resonance $u$ follows $E$ in phase. At resonance it lags by $90^\circ$, so the polarization current $\dot P$ is in phase with $E$ and the field does work on the lattice. Above resonance $u$ is in antiphase. In the Lorentz oscillator model, a bound valence electron obeys the same equation with $Z^*\to e$, $M\to m_e$ and a resonance in the eV range (this model is not part of E.134, whose electrons are band electrons). A free carrier has no restoring force at all. The figure compares the three.

Bridge to Giustino

Giustino starts from electrons and nuclei interacting through the instantaneous Coulomb interaction, with no vector potential (G §IV.A, Eqs. 62–67, §A.5). His working Hamiltonian (G Eq. 1, §A.2) has bands, phonons and an explicit vertex $g$ computed by DFPT (G Eq. 38). That $g$ already contains the Coulomb field of the displaced ions, screened by the electrons. EPP's Lagrangian has no $g$. The field is a dynamical variable whose longitudinal part reproduces Giustino's Coulomb interaction (§B.4) and whose transverse part adds retardation in EPP's sense, the finite speed of light. (In Giustino, "retardation" means the frequency dependence of the electronic screening.) Light does appear in Giustino, but only as an external classical field coupled through the electron velocity (G Eq. 200, §A.9). That is the same $\frac ec\mathbf v\cdot\bA$ form as term (5), without the field's own dynamics.

Note on the source

  • "Thus in this way we have plausibly closed the scheme" (p. 26) holds for the polar channel only, since the short-range coupling is absent. The remark on the symmetry of terms (5) and (6) refers to an external "Lecture 9" that is not part of the manuscript.
  • (E.141)–(E.143) carry the transposed charge $Z^*_{a\nu\mu}$, while (E.135) has $Z^*_{a\mu\nu}$. Both are correct.
  • The vector identity printed on p. 27 lacks its parentheses (the derivation above uses the correct form). This slip and the unannounced changes of units and of the sign of $e$ are listed in Z.2.

The ionic equation (E.143) is tested on a diatomic polar crystal in §B.3, where it yields $\epsilon(\omega)$, LO and TO modes and the Lyddane–Sachs–Teller relation. The field's own Euler–Lagrange equations come next, in §B.4: the Ampère–Maxwell law with source $\bj_{\rm e}+\dot\bP$, Gauss's law from continuity, the canonical momenta and the quantized photons.

B.3EPP §4.2 · Eqs. 144–165

The polar crystal as a dielectric

Drive the ions of a diatomic crystal with a uniform field and the Lagrangian of B.2 returns a Lorentz oscillator. Its dielectric function has poles at the TO and zeros at the LO frequency. The Reststrahlen band, the Lyddane–Sachs–Teller relation and the lattice part of the screened interaction $W$ all follow from that one function.

In §B.2 the electron–phonon–photon Lagrangian (E.134) gave every ion a harmonic equation of motion, driven by the electric field through its Born charge: $m_a\ddot Q_{ia\mu}+\sum_{jb\nu}k_{ia\mu,jb\nu}Q_{jb\nu}=\sum_\nu Z^*_{a\nu\mu}E_\nu(\bR_i^0)$ (E.143). Before quantizing anything, EPP §4.2.1 tests this equation on the textbook case: a diatomic polar crystal at long wavelength. EPP §4.2.1 is classical (no $\hbar$) and written in Gaussian units. $Z^*$ carries the dimension of charge, $Z^*_{\rm EPP}=|e|\,Z^*_{\rm G}$. Here $\mathbf D$ is the electric displacement, not the photon propagator $D$ of §B.5–§B.7.

Two masses, one spring, one field

At $|\bq|\ll 1/a$ neighbouring cells move in phase, $Q_{ja\mu}\approx Q_{ia\mu}$. Every short-range spring between the two sublattices then adds into one effective spring $k_\mu$, and the crystal behaves like one diatomic molecule per cell, repeated in lockstep. With diagonal Born charges and force constants (exact for cubic sites) the three Cartesian directions decouple, and the nearest-neighbour equations (E.144)–(E.145) reduce to

$$ m_a\ddot Q_{a\mu}=-k_\mu\left(Q_{a\mu}-Q_{b\mu}\right)+Z^*_{a\mu}E_\mu,\qquad m_b\ddot Q_{b\mu}=-k_\mu\left(Q_{b\mu}-Q_{a\mu}\right)+Z^*_{b\mu}E_\mu . $$

The equal and opposite spring constants come from the acoustic sum rule and the symmetry of the force-constant matrix, applied to the lattice-summed constants. A harmonic drive $[Q_{a\mu},Q_{b\mu}]=[A,B]\,e^{-i\omega t}$ (E.146) turns this into a $2\times2$ linear system with determinant

$$ \det = m_am_b\,\omega^2\left[\omega^2-\omega^2_{\mu{\rm O}}\right]. \tag{E.148}$$

Its zeros are the normal modes. Three acoustic modes have $\omega=0$ and both atoms moving together. Three bare optical modes have $\omega^2_{\mu\rm O}=k_\mu/M$, with $M=m_am_b/(m_a+m_b)$, and the atoms moving against each other with the centre of mass at rest ($A:B=1:-m_a/m_b$). "Bare" is the paper's word: $\omega_{\rm O}$ is set by short-range springs only and has not yet felt the macroscopic field that its own dipoles create.

A Lorentz oscillator with an ionic plasma frequency

The polarization is the dipole per cell over the cell volume, $P_\mu=(Z^*_{a\mu}Q_{a\mu}+Z^*_{b\mu}Q_{b\mu})/\Omega_{\rm uc}$. In a diatomic crystal the two Born charges are equal and opposite, $Z^*_\mu\equiv Z^*_{a\mu}=-Z^*_{b\mu}$, and the driven response becomes

$$ P_\mu=-\frac{\left[Z^*_\mu\right]^2}{\Omega_{\rm uc}M}\,\frac{1}{\omega^2-\omega^2_{\mu\rm O}}\,E_\mu . \tag{E.150}$$

The acoustic pole has dropped out. A rigid translation of a neutral cell carries no dipole, so the field drives only the relative coordinate, and what is left is a Lorentz oscillator resonant at the bare frequency.

The macroscopic $E$ is an average over the cell. A given dipole feels that average plus the field of its near neighbours, which the average smears out. For sites of cubic symmetry this local field is $E_\mu\to E^*_\mu=E_\mu+\frac{4\pi}{3}P_\mu$ (Lorentz, E.151). Inserting it into (E.150) gives

$$ P_\mu=-\frac{\omega^2_{p\mu}}{4\pi}\,\frac{1}{\omega^2-\omega^2_{\mu\rm O}}\left(E_\mu+\frac{4\pi}{3}P_\mu\right), \tag{E.152}$$

where the paper introduces the ionic plasmon frequency

$$ \omega^2_{p\mu}=\frac{4\pi\left[Z^*_\mu\right]^2}{\Omega_{\rm uc}M}. $$

This is exactly a plasma frequency $4\pi ne^2/m$ for a gas of charges $Z^*$ with mass $M$ and density $1/\Omega_{\rm uc}$. In SI units with dimensionless $Z^*$ it reads $\omega_p^2=Z^{*2}e^2/(\varepsilon_0\Omega_{\rm uc}M)$, or $\omega_p^2\,[\mathrm{cm^{-2}}]=4.92\times10^{7}\,Z^{*2}/(\Omega_{\rm uc}[\text{Å}^3]\,M[\mathrm u])$. For NaCl ($Z^*\approx1.12$, $\Omega_{\rm uc}=44.9$ Å$^3$, $M=13.9$ u; literature values, illustrative) this gives $\omega_p\approx314\ \mathrm{cm^{-1}}\approx39$ meV, the same scale as the phonons themselves. Solving (E.152) for $P$ moves the resonance down to $\omega^2_{\mu\rm O}-\frac13\omega^2_{p\mu}$ (E.153): the local field reinforces the displacement and softens the restoring force.

Derivation: from the driven two-mass problem to (E.150)

With $e^{-i\omega t}$ the reduced equations become

$$\begin{bmatrix}k_\mu-\omega^2m_a&-k_\mu\\-k_\mu&k_\mu-\omega^2m_b\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}A\\B\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}Z^*_{a\mu}\\Z^*_{b\mu}\end{bmatrix}E_\mu ,$$

with $\det=(k-\omega^2m_a)(k-\omega^2m_b)-k^2=m_am_b\omega^4-k\omega^2(m_a+m_b)$, which is (E.148). Inverting,

$$\begin{bmatrix}A\\B\end{bmatrix}=\frac{E_\mu}{\det}\begin{bmatrix}(Z^*_{a\mu}+Z^*_{b\mu})k_\mu-m_b\omega^2Z^*_{a\mu}\\(Z^*_{a\mu}+Z^*_{b\mu})k_\mu-m_a\omega^2Z^*_{b\mu}\end{bmatrix}, \tag{E.147}$$ $$P_\mu=\frac{E_\mu}{\Omega_{\rm uc}\det}\left\{\left(Z^*_{a\mu}+Z^*_{b\mu}\right)^2k_\mu-\omega^2\left[m_a\left(Z^*_{b\mu}\right)^2+m_b\left(Z^*_{a\mu}\right)^2\right]\right\}e^{-i\omega t}. \tag{E.149}$$

For $Z^*_{b\mu}=-Z^*_{a\mu}$ the curly bracket is $-\omega^2(m_a+m_b)Z^{*2}_\mu$. Its $\omega^2$ cancels the acoustic factor $\omega^2$ in $\det$, and $(m_a+m_b)/(m_am_b)=1/M$ gives (E.150). If the charges did not sum to zero, a term $(Z^*_a+Z^*_b)^2k/(\Omega_{\rm uc}\det)\propto1/\omega^2$ would survive at low frequency: a free-charge (Drude-like) response that an insulator cannot have. This is why the charge-neutrality sum rule $\sum_\kappa Z^*_\kappa=0$ must hold.

Adding the electrons: $\epsilon(\omega)$

Macroscopic electrodynamics closes the loop. With $P_\mu=\chi_\mu E_\mu$ (E.154) and $D_\mu=\epsilon_\mu(\omega)E_\mu=E_\mu+4\pi P_\mu$ (E.155), the lattice alone gives $\epsilon_\mu(\omega)=1-\omega^2_{p\mu}/(\omega^2-\omega^2_{\mu\rm O}+\frac13\omega^2_{p\mu})$ (E.157). The valence electrons are then added by hand:

$$ \epsilon_\mu(\omega)=\epsilon_\infty-\frac{\omega^2_{p\mu}}{\omega^2-\omega^2_{\mu\rm O}+\frac13\omega^2_{p\mu}} . \tag{E.158}$$

The justification is that independent polarizable subsystems add their susceptibilities, $\epsilon_{12}=\epsilon_1+\epsilon_2-1$. In RPA language, $W=v+v(\chi^0_1+\chi^0_2)W$, so $\epsilon_{12}=1-v(\chi^0_1+\chi^0_2)$. A constant $\epsilon_\infty$ means the electrons follow the ions instantaneously, i.e. no retardation in Giustino's sense (no frequency dependence of the electronic screening on phonon time scales). The paper calls this step ad hoc and promises that the diagrammatic theory will generate $\epsilon_\infty$ from the electronic photon self-energy (§B.5, §B.9). Written with its zero and its pole, (E.158) becomes

$$ \epsilon_\mu(\omega)=\epsilon_\infty\,\frac{\omega^2-\tilde\omega^2_{{\rm LO}\mu}}{\omega^2-\tilde\omega^2_{{\rm TO}\mu}}, \tag{E.159}$$
$$ \begin{aligned} \tilde\omega^2_{{\rm LO}\mu}&=\omega^2_{\mu\rm O}+\left[\frac{1}{\epsilon_\infty}-\frac13\right]\omega^2_{p\mu},\\ \tilde\omega^2_{{\rm TO}\mu}&=\omega^2_{\mu\rm O}-\frac13\,\omega^2_{p\mu}. \end{aligned} \tag{E.160}$$
Derivation: from the local field to (E.157) and the factorized form (E.159)–(E.160)

Multiply (E.152) by $\omega^2-\omega_{\rm O}^2$ and collect $P$: $P\,(\omega^2-\omega_{\rm O}^2+\tfrac13\omega_p^2)=-\tfrac{\omega_p^2}{4\pi}E$, which is (E.153). With $P=(\epsilon-1)E/4\pi$ (E.156) this is $\epsilon-1=-\omega_p^2/(\omega^2-\omega_{\rm O}^2+\tfrac13\omega_p^2)$, i.e. (E.157). Replacing $1\to\epsilon_\infty$ and writing $\tilde\omega_{\rm TO}^2=\omega_{\rm O}^2-\tfrac13\omega_p^2$,

$$\epsilon_\infty-\frac{\omega_p^2}{\omega^2-\tilde\omega_{\rm TO}^2}=\epsilon_\infty\,\frac{\omega^2-\left(\tilde\omega_{\rm TO}^2+\omega_p^2/\epsilon_\infty\right)}{\omega^2-\tilde\omega_{\rm TO}^2},$$

so $\tilde\omega_{\rm LO}^2=\tilde\omega_{\rm TO}^2+\omega_p^2/\epsilon_\infty=\omega_{\rm O}^2+(1/\epsilon_\infty-1/3)\,\omega_p^2$, which is (E.160). The pole of $\epsilon$ is the pole of the oscillator. The zero is where the electronic and ionic polarizations cancel the vacuum term in $\mathbf D$.

Zeros are LO, poles are TO

Picture a longitudinal optical wave first. The ions oscillate along $\bq$, so $\bP\parallel\bq$ and $\nabla\cdot\bP\neq0$. Sheets of bound charge $\rho_{\rm b}=-\nabla\cdot\bP$ form at the nodes of $\bP$ and produce a macroscopic field that opposes the displacement. That field is an extra restoring force, so the longitudinal mode is stiffer. In a transverse wave $\bP\perp\bq$, $\nabla\cdot\bP=0$, no bound charge forms, and in the electrostatic limit there is no macroscopic field at all.

Formally, with no free charge $\nabla\cdot\mathbf D=0$, and in electrostatics $\nabla\times\bE=0$. For a plane wave $e^{i\bq\cdot\br}$ these read $\epsilon\,\bq\cdot\bE=0$ and $\bq\times\bE=0$. A longitudinal field ($\bE\parallel\bq$) survives the first condition only if $\epsilon(\omega)=0$ (E.161), and then

$$ D_\mu=\epsilon_\mu(\omega)E_\mu=E_\mu+4\pi P_\mu=0, \tag{E.163}$$
$$ E_\mu=-4\pi P_\mu . \tag{E.164}$$

The zeros of $\epsilon$ are therefore the dressed LO phonons: longitudinal electromagnetic modes in which the polarization sustains its own field. Once $\epsilon_\infty$ is in, $P$ in (E.163)–(E.164) is the total polarization. The electrons screen the field of the ions, so the ionic part alone gives $E=-4\pi P_{\rm ion}/\epsilon_\infty$. A transverse field must vanish, $\bE=0$, and a finite $\bP$ with $\bE=0$ requires $\epsilon\to\infty$. The poles of $\epsilon$ are the TO phonons, with $\mathbf D=4\pi\bP\neq0$ and $\nabla\cdot\mathbf D=0$ guaranteed by transversality. A mode with $Z^*=0$ has $\omega_p=0$ and is not shifted at all.

Lyddane–Sachs–Teller, and what is model independent

At $\omega\to0$, (E.159) gives the Lyddane–Sachs–Teller (LST) relation

$$ \frac{\epsilon_\mu(0)}{\epsilon_\infty}=\frac{\tilde\omega^2_{{\rm LO}\mu}}{\tilde\omega^2_{{\rm TO}\mu}} . \tag{E.165}$$

The static dielectric constant exceeds the electronic one by the squared ratio of LO to TO frequencies. In NaCl, $\epsilon(0)=2.34\times(264/164)^2=6.06$, close to the measured 5.9 (literature values, illustrative). Subtracting the two lines of (E.160) gives a second exact statement, not written in the paper but immediate:

$$ \tilde\omega^2_{\rm LO}-\tilde\omega^2_{\rm TO}=\frac{\omega_p^2}{\epsilon_\infty}=\frac{4\pi Z^{*2}}{\epsilon_\infty\,\Omega_{\rm uc}M}. $$

The local-field term cancels. This difference of squares is the observable splitting, and it is exactly what the Gonze–Lee non-analytic term adds to the longitudinal mode of a cubic diatomic crystal. The positions of $\tilde\omega_{\rm TO}$ and $\tilde\omega_{\rm LO}$ relative to the bare $\omega_{\rm O}$ depend on the local-field model, and $\omega_{\rm O}$ itself cannot be measured.

The author argues that "LO–TO splitting" is a misnomer and prefers "LO shift": the LO mode is the dipole-active phonon dressed by its own macroscopic field. In (E.160) both frequencies move away from $\omega_{\rm O}$, so the clean form of the argument is this. The TO frequency is the analytic one, which already contains the short-range and local-field physics. The LO frequency is the TO frequency plus the dressing by the macroscopic longitudinal field, $\omega_p^2/\epsilon_\infty$ in $\omega^2$.

Bridge to Giustino: LO–TO splitting

Giustino does not derive the LO–TO splitting. In §VI.A.3 he only notes that his treatment of the long-range vertex is analogous to the way DFPT codes compute the splitting (Gonze and Lee, 1997): a non-analytic term of the dynamical matrix, $\propto(\bq\cdot\bZ^*_\kappa)(\bq\cdot\bZ^*_{\kappa'})/(\bq\cdot\boldsymbol\epsilon^\infty\cdot\bq)$, with the same kernel as the Verdi–Giustino vertex (see §A.4). For an isotropic diatomic crystal that term adds exactly $\omega_p^2/\epsilon_\infty$ to the longitudinal $\omega^2$, the model-independent difference above. In DFPT the analytic part already gives $\omega_{\rm TO}$, so DFPT's "bare" frequency is the TO, not the paper's $\omega_{\rm O}$. EPP re-derives the shift as a photon-mediated phonon self-energy in §B.7 and recovers the Gonze–Lee form for $c\to\infty$ in §B.9.

Subtlety: the local field and the bare frequency

Three warnings about (E.151)–(E.160). All three are built into the lab below.

  • Born charges already contain the local field. EPP takes $Z^*=\Omega_{\rm uc}\,\delta P/\delta R$ (E.110) from DFT, where it is computed at zero macroscopic field and already includes the electronic and local-field response. In a Clausius–Mossotti model the charge that feels the Lorentz field is the Szigeti charge $Z_s=3Z^*/(\epsilon_\infty+2)$, so applying (E.151) with $Z^*$ double counts. The factor $4\pi/3$ also holds only for cubic sites.
  • $\tilde\omega_{\rm LO}<\omega_{\rm O}$ when $\epsilon_\infty>3$. Keeping the vacuum factor $\frac13\omega_p^2$ after inserting $\epsilon_\infty$ makes the bracket in (E.160) negative for GaAs, SiC or hBN, so the "shifted" LO sits below the bare mode. A consistent Clausius–Mossotti treatment (not in the paper), with $\omega_p$ still built from the Born charge, gives $\tilde\omega_{\rm TO}^2=\omega_{\rm O}^2-\omega_p^2/(\epsilon_\infty+2)$ and still $\tilde\omega_{\rm LO}^2=\tilde\omega_{\rm TO}^2+\omega_p^2/\epsilon_\infty$. It keeps $\tilde\omega_{\rm LO}>\omega_{\rm O}$ and reduces to (E.160) at $\epsilon_\infty=1$.
  • Cochran instability. If $\omega_p^2>3\omega_{\rm O}^2$ then $\tilde\omega_{\rm TO}^2<0$. The dipolar local field beats the short-range spring and the lattice polarizes spontaneously, a ferroelectric soft mode (Cochran's picture, not in the paper). Approaching it, $\tilde\omega_{\rm TO}\to0$ and LST sends $\epsilon(0)\to\infty$.

The Dyson-equation route of §B.5–§B.7 has no local field. There, away from the light cone, the TO frequency equals the bare $\omega_\sigma$ of the short-range force constants, and the photon propagator supplies only the macroscopic field. That is the "none" setting of the lab.

The Reststrahlen lab

The lab evaluates (E.158)–(E.160) with a retarded damping, $\omega^2\to\omega^2+i\gamma\omega$. The time dependence is $e^{-i\omega t}$, so ${\rm Im}\,\epsilon>0$ means absorption. Four panels show the same $\epsilon(\omega)$: ${\rm Re}$ and ${\rm Im}\,\epsilon$, the normal-incidence reflectance $R=|(\sqrt\epsilon-1)/(\sqrt\epsilon+1)|^2$, the loss function $-{\rm Im}\,1/\epsilon$, and $W/v=1/\epsilon$ split into electronic and lattice parts (derived below). In spectroscopic mode you set $\omega_{\rm TO}$, $\omega_{\rm LO}$ and $\epsilon_\infty$ directly. In microscopic mode you build them from $Z^*$, $\Omega_{\rm uc}$, $M$, $\omega_{\rm O}$ and a local-field model.

The lattice inside $W$

For a homogeneous polar insulator at long wavelength the screened Coulomb interaction is $W(\omega)=v/\epsilon(\omega)$, with $v=4\pi e^2/q^2$. Splitting off the electronic part with (E.159), and using LST in the last step,

$$ \begin{aligned} \frac{W(\omega)}{v}=\frac{1}{\epsilon(\omega)}&=\underbrace{\frac{1}{\epsilon_\infty}}_{W_{\rm e}/v}+\frac{W_{\rm ph}(\omega)}{v},\\ \frac{W_{\rm ph}(\omega)}{v}&=\frac{1}{\epsilon_\infty}\,\frac{\tilde\omega_{\rm LO}^2-\tilde\omega_{\rm TO}^2}{\omega^2-\tilde\omega_{\rm LO}^2}\\ &=\left(\frac{1}{\epsilon_\infty}-\frac{1}{\epsilon(0)}\right)\frac{\tilde\omega_{\rm LO}^2}{\omega^2-\tilde\omega_{\rm LO}^2}. \end{aligned}$$

The lattice part has its pole at $\tilde\omega_{\rm LO}$, not at $\tilde\omega_{\rm TO}$. $W$ is the longitudinal (Coulomb) propagator, so its poles are the zeros of $\epsilon$, and the TO frequency appears in $W$ only as a zero. At $\omega\to0$ the ions screen too and $W\to v/\epsilon(0)$. Far above $\tilde\omega_{\rm LO}$ the ions cannot follow and $W\to v/\epsilon_\infty$. Panel (d) of the lab draws exactly this decomposition.

Bridge to Giustino: this is his lattice contribution to $W$

The lattice term above is the polar, long-wavelength case of Giustino's $W=W_{\rm e}+W_{\rm ph}$ (G Eqs. 104–105) with $W_{\rm e}=v/\epsilon_\infty$: Fröhlich's $|g|^2$ times the LO propagator, worked out in §A.5 and, in Born-charge form, in §A.4. Giustino also describes the alternative of Botti and Marques (§IX.A.1): skip the split and build $W$ directly from a Lyddane–Sachs–Teller total dielectric function, which is the $1/\epsilon(\omega)$ of panel (d). In EPP the same object returns as the longitudinal sector of the photon propagator, with $\epsilon_\infty$ no longer put in by hand (§B.6, §B.9).

Physical picture: optics sees TO, Coulomb sees LO

A transverse light wave probes the poles of $\epsilon$: infrared absorption peaks at $\omega_{\rm TO}$, and the crystal reflects between TO and LO. Longitudinal probes see the zeros: an electron passing through (EELS), Fröhlich scattering of a carrier and the screening of an exciton all go through $1/\epsilon$, which has its pole at $\omega_{\rm LO}$. For BSE work this is the practical message. When exciton binding energies are comparable to $\hbar\omega_{\rm LO}$, the relevant screening lies between $\epsilon_\infty$ and $\epsilon(0)$, and $W_{\rm ph}$ tells you how much.

Subtlety: this is electrostatics

The L/T classification used $\nabla\times\bE=0$, which holds for $cq\gg\omega$: no retardation in EPP's sense (finite speed of light), i.e. $c\to\infty$. With Faraday's law the transverse modes hybridize with photons through $c^2q^2=\omega^2\epsilon(\omega)$ and become phonon polaritons, confined to $q\lesssim\sqrt{\epsilon(0)}\,\omega_{\rm TO}/c$, the same scale as the light-cone wave vector $q_c=\sqrt{\epsilon_\infty}\,\omega/c$ of §X.1 and $10^{-5}$–$10^{-4}$ of the Brillouin zone. The Lagrangian (E.134) already contains the transverse field. §B.4 quantizes it, §B.6 finds the polaritons, and §B.7 shows that the order of the limits $q\to0$ and $c\to\infty$ matters.

Notes on the source (EPP §4.2.1)

An index typo on p. 30 and several loose statements in EPP §4.2.1 (the range of validity of the Lorentz field, "three LO + TO phonons" from the zeros of $\epsilon$, a TO that "remained where it is" despite (E.160)) are listed in Z.2. One matters here: $Z^*_{a\mu}=-Z^*_{b\mu}$ is not an approximation read off Fig. 5. For a diatomic crystal it is exact, by charge neutrality, and it is what removes the $\omega=0$ pole from (E.149).

B.4EPP §§4.3–4.4 · Eqs. 166–237

Quantized fields: transverse photons, and Coulomb as the longitudinal photon

The Lagrangian of §B.2 becomes a quantum Hamiltonian. Two of the three field polarizations turn into photons with energy $\hbar cq$. The third has no restoring force, and its energy is exactly the instantaneous Coulomb interaction of electrons and ionic bound charges.

In §B.2 one Lagrangian (E.134) coupled band electrons, harmonic ions and the vector potential in the temporal gauge $\Phi=0$ and gave the ionic equation of motion; §B.3 turned that into the dielectric function of a polar crystal. Here the field itself becomes a quantum degree of freedom. The end product is the split $H=H_0+V'$ of (E.236)–(E.237), on which every diagram of Part B is built.

Physical picture

Expand the field in plane waves. For each $\bq$ the amplitude is a 3-vector. The two components perpendicular to $\bq$ have a curl, hence a magnetic field, hence a restoring "spring": they oscillate at $\omega=cq$ and are the photons. The component along $\bq$ has no curl and no spring. Its electric field has a divergence instead, which Gauss's law ties to the charge density at the same instant. So the longitudinal field is not an independent degree of freedom, and its energy is the Coulomb energy of the charges. Giustino postulates that Coulomb interaction (§A.5); EPP derives it.

Conventions. Gaussian units, as in the rest of Part B, with $\bE=-\frac1c\partial_t\bA$ and $\bB=\nabla\times\bA$ in the temporal gauge (to convert to SI, $e^2\to e^2/4\pi\varepsilon_0$ and $4\pi\to1/\varepsilon_0$ in Poisson's equation). Here $\Omega$ is the normalization volume of the whole crystal, not the cell volume $\Omega_{\rm uc}$. We write photon ladder operators as $b_{\bq\alpha}$ and keep $a$ for phonons; the PDF also uses $a$ for photons in Eqs. (208)–(217) and in §4.7.

Maxwell's equations from the field Lagrangian

EPP §4.3 rewrites the point-particle couplings of (E.134) with densities: the electronic current $\bj_{\rm e}(\br)=e\sum_e\mathbf v_e\,\delta(\br-\br_e)$ (E.166) and the ionic polarization of point Born dipoles, $\bP(\br)=\sum_{ia}\mathbf p_{ia}\,\delta(\br-\bR^0_i)$ (E.167), with $\mathbf p_{ia}=\hat Z^*_a\bQ_{ia}$ (E.135). The field part of the Lagrangian is then a local density,

$$\mathcal L_A(\br)=\frac{1}{8\pi c^2}\dot{\bA}^2(\br)-\frac{1}{8\pi}\big[\nabla\times\bA(\br)\big]^2+\frac1c\,\bj_{\rm e}(\br)\cdot\bA(\br)+\frac1c\,\dot{\bP}(\br)\cdot\bA(\br). \tag{E.169}$$

The Euler–Lagrange equation for $A_\mu(\br)$ (E.172–E.173) collects $\partial\mathcal L_A/\partial A_\mu=(j_{{\rm e}\mu}+\dot P_\mu)/c$, $\partial\mathcal L_A/\partial\dot A_\mu=-E_\mu/4\pi c$ and a curl of $\bB$ from the magnetic term. The result is the Ampère–Maxwell law with two sources:

$$\nabla\times\bB=\frac1c\dot{\bE}+\frac{4\pi}{c}\dot{\bP}+\frac{4\pi}{c}\bj_{\rm e}. \tag{E.175}$$

With $\mathbf D=\bE+4\pi\bP$ (E.176) this is the textbook macroscopic law $\nabla\times\bB=\frac1c\dot{\mathbf D}+\frac{4\pi}{c}\bj_{\rm e}$ (E.177). Its divergence, combined with continuity $\nabla\cdot\bj_{\rm e}=-\dot\rho_{\rm e}$, gives $\frac{d}{dt}(\nabla\cdot\mathbf D-4\pi\rho_{\rm e})=0$ (E.179), which EPP integrates to Gauss's law:

$$\nabla\cdot\mathbf D=4\pi\rho_{\rm e}. \tag{E.180}$$

Faraday's law and $\nabla\cdot\bB=0$ are identities of the potentials. Note the division of labour: the ions are a polarizable background $\bP$ (ionic part only), while the valence electrons are free charges and currents whose polarization reappears as the photon self-energy $\Pi^{\rm e}$ in §B.5.

Gauss's law is a constraint, not an equation of motion

In the temporal gauge, varying $\bA$ yields only Ampère's law. Gauss's law is preserved by the dynamics (E.179) and must be imposed on the initial state (EPP silently sets the integration constant to zero). Quantum mechanically, $\nabla\cdot\mathbf D-4\pi\rho_{\rm e}=\nabla\cdot\bE-4\pi(\rho_{\rm e}+\rho_{\rm ion})$ generates the residual gauge transformations $\bA\to\bA+\nabla\chi(\br)$ and annihilates physical states, so using Gauss's law inside $H$, as in (E.234) below, is legitimate on that subspace. The Coulomb gauge reaches the same physics directly.

Legendre transform: four minimal couplings

The canonical momenta of electrons, ions and field are (EPP §4.4)

$$p_{e\mu}=\frac{\partial L}{\partial v_{e\mu}}=m_ev_{e\mu}+\frac ecA_\mu, \tag{E.182}$$
$$\pi_{ia\mu}=\frac{\partial L}{\partial\dot Q_{ia\mu}}=m_a\dot Q_{ia\mu}+\frac1c\sum_\alpha Z^*_{a\alpha\mu}A_\alpha(\bR^0_i), \tag{E.183}$$
$$p_{A_\mu}=\frac{\delta L}{\delta\dot A_\mu}=\frac{\partial\mathcal L_A}{\partial\dot A_\mu}=-\frac{1}{4\pi c}E_\mu. \tag{E.184}$$

Both matter momenta are minimally coupled: a displaced ion behaves as a particle of charge $Z^*$. The field momentum is minus the total electric field over $4\pi c$, transverse plus longitudinal. Inserting the momenta into the Legendre transform

$$H=\sum_e\bp_e\cdot\mathbf v_e+\sum_{ia}\pi_{ia}\cdot\dot\bQ_{ia}+\int d\br\,\bp_A\cdot\dot\bA-L, \tag{E.181}$$

all linear couplings cancel and only energies remain:

$$\begin{aligned}H={}&\sum_e\frac{m_e\mathbf v_e^2}{2}+\sum_eV_{\rm cr}(\br_e)+\sum_{ia\mu}\frac{m_a\dot Q_{ia\mu}^2}{2}\\&+\frac12\sum_{ia\mu,jb\nu}k_{ia\mu,jb\nu}Q_{ia\mu}Q_{jb\nu}+\frac{1}{8\pi}\int d\br\,\big[\bE^2+\bB^2\big].\end{aligned} \tag{E.185}$$

The interaction is hidden in the momenta, and the Coulomb interaction is hidden in $\int E^2$. In canonical variables (EPP p. 39, unnumbered),

$$\begin{aligned}H={}&\sum_e\frac{1}{2m_e}\Big[\bp_e-\frac ec\bA(\br_e)\Big]^2+\sum_eV_{\rm cr}(\br_e)+\sum_{ia\mu}\frac{1}{2m_a}\Big[\pi_{ia\mu}-\frac1c\sum_\alpha Z^*_{a\alpha\mu}A_\alpha(\bR^0_i)\Big]^2\\&+\frac12\sum_{ia\mu,jb\nu}k_{ia\mu,jb\nu}Q_{ia\mu}Q_{jb\nu}+\frac{1}{8\pi}\int d\br\,\big[\bE^2+\bB^2\big].\end{aligned}$$

Expanding the two squares gives $H=H_0'+V$. Here $H_0'$ contains the $\bA$-free kinetic and lattice terms plus the field energy, and the interaction is

$$\begin{aligned}V={}&-\frac{e}{2m_ec}\sum_e\big[\bp_e\cdot\bA(\br_e)+\bA(\br_e)\cdot\bp_e\big]+\frac{e^2}{2m_ec^2}\sum_e\bA^2(\br_e)\\&-\frac1c\sum_{ia\alpha\mu}\frac{1}{m_a}Z^*_{a\alpha\mu}\pi_{ia\mu}A_\alpha(\bR^0_i)+\frac{1}{c^2}\sum_{ia\mu\alpha\beta}\frac{1}{2m_a}Z^*_{a\alpha\mu}Z^*_{a\beta\mu}A_\alpha(\bR^0_i)A_\beta(\bR^0_i).\end{aligned} \tag{E.186}$$
CouplingTerm of (E.186)What it doesBecomes (§B.5)
Electron paramagnetic$-\frac{e}{2m_ec}\sum_e[\bp_e\cdot\bA+\bA\cdot\bp_e]$an electron absorbs or emits one photon$\Pi^{\rm e,para}$: current–current bubble
Electron diamagnetic$\frac{e^2}{2m_ec^2}\sum_e\bA^2(\br_e)$two photons at one point (contact)$\Pi^{\rm e,dia}$: the $-ne^2/m_ec$ (f-sum) term
Ion paramagnetic$-\frac1c\sum\frac{1}{m_a}Z^*_{a\alpha\mu}\pi_{ia\mu}A_\alpha$a phonon turns into a photon, or the reverse ($\pi$ is linear in $a,a^\dagger$)$\Pi^{\rm ion,para}$: one phonon line between Born-charge vertices
Ion diamagnetic$\frac{1}{c^2}\sum\frac{1}{2m_a}Z^*_{a\alpha\mu}Z^*_{a\beta\mu}A_\alpha A_\beta$two photons at an ion site; no phonon operator$\Pi^{\rm ion,dia}$: the ionic f-sum term

Every charged species couples twice, linearly through its current and quadratically through a contact term. For the ions the "charge" is the Born tensor and the current is the polarization current $Z^*\pi/m_a\approx\dot\bP$. The electronic product is symmetrized because $\bp_e$ does not commute with $\bA(\br_e)$ (here $\nabla\cdot\bA\neq0$); $\pi$ and $\bA$ commute.

Quantizing the field in the polarization triad

The free-field part of $H_0'$, written with $\bp_A=-\bE/4\pi c$, and its canonical commutator are

$$H^{0\prime}_{\rm ph}=\int\frac{d\br}{8\pi}\big[\bE^2+\bB^2\big]=\int\frac{d\br}{8\pi}\big\{16\pi^2c^2\bp_A^2+[\nabla\times\bA]^2\big\}, \tag{E.188}$$
$$\big[A_\mu(\br),p_{A\nu}(\br')\big]=\ii\hbar\,\delta(\br-\br')\,\delta_{\mu\nu}. \tag{E.189}$$

The delta function is the ordinary one for all three Cartesian components, a feature of the temporal gauge (the Coulomb gauge would have the transverse delta). With plane waves, $\bA(\br)=\Omega^{-1/2}\sum_\bq\bA_\bq e^{\ii\bq\cdot\br}$ (E.190), each $\bq$ carries a three-component amplitude. This is step 1 of the phonon recipe of §B.1, and EPP repeats steps 2 and 3: a rotation that decouples the Cartesian components, then ladder operators. The rotation is the orthogonal triad of its Fig. 6: $\be_3(\bq)=\hat\bq$, $\be_2=-\hat\bq\times\be_1$ and $\be_1=\hat\bq\times\be_2$ (E.197–E.199). Writing $\bA_\bq=\sum_\alpha\be_\alpha\tilde A_{\alpha\bq}$ and $\bp_{A\bq}=\sum_\alpha\be_\alpha\tilde p_{A\alpha\bq}$ (E.202–E.203), and using $\bq\times\be_3=0$, gives

$$\boxed{H^{0\prime}_{\rm ph}=2\pi c^2\sum_{\bq,\alpha=1,2,3}\tilde p_{A\alpha\bq}\,\tilde p_{A\alpha-\bq}+\sum_{\bq,\alpha=1,2}\frac{q^2}{8\pi}\tilde A_{\alpha\bq}\tilde A_{\alpha-\bq}} \tag{E.204}$$

This is the structural result of the section. The electric ("kinetic") term contains all three polarizations. The magnetic ("spring") term contains only the two transverse ones, because $[\bq\times\be_\alpha]\cdot[\bq\times\be_\beta]=q^2(\delta_{\alpha\beta}-\delta_{\alpha3}\delta_{\beta3})$.

For $\alpha=1,2$, (E.204) describes harmonic oscillators of frequency $cq$ ("mass" $1/4\pi c^2$, spring $q^2/4\pi$). The ladder operators $\tilde A_{\alpha\bq}=\sqrt{2\pi c\hbar/q}\,(b_{\bq\alpha}+b^\dagger_{-\bq\alpha})$ and $\tilde p_{A\alpha\bq}=-\ii\sqrt{\hbar q/8\pi c}\,(b_{\bq\alpha}-b^\dagger_{-\bq\alpha})$ (E.208–E.209) diagonalize them, and the field energy splits as $H^{0\prime}_{\rm ph}=H^0_{\rm Tph}+H^0_{\rm Lph}$ with

$$H^0_{\rm Tph}=\sum_{\bq,\alpha=1,2}\hbar qc\,\Big\{b^\dagger_{\bq\alpha}b_{\bq\alpha}+\frac12\Big\}, \tag{E.214}$$
$$H^0_{\rm Lph}=2\pi c^2\sum_\bq\tilde p_{A3\bq}\,\tilde p_{A3-\bq}. \tag{E.215}$$

Each transverse mode is an oscillator whose energy changes in quanta $\hbar cq$: a photon. The longitudinal term has no $\tilde A_3^2$ partner. Inserting (E.209) into it produces $b_{\bq3}b_{-\bq3}$ and $b^\dagger b^\dagger$ terms, so it is not diagonal, and EPP assigns it to the interaction. The field operator nevertheless keeps all three polarizations:

$$\bA(\br)=\sum_{\bq,\alpha=1,2,3}\sqrt{\frac{2\pi c\hbar}{q\Omega}}\;\be_\alpha(\bq)\,\big\{b_{\bq\alpha}+b^\dagger_{-\bq\alpha}\big\}\,e^{\ii\bq\cdot\br}. \tag{E.216}$$

The reason is the commutator (E.189), which closes only through the completeness relation $\sum_{\alpha=1}^{3}e_{\mu\alpha}e_{\nu\alpha}=\delta_{\mu\nu}$ (EPP p. 45). The transverse projector alone, $\delta_{\mu\nu}-q_\mu q_\nu/q^2$, is nonlocal in real space, with a dipolar $1/r^3$ tail. The longitudinal projector cancels that tail. The same $1/r^3$ tensor will reappear below as the dipole–dipole interaction between ions.

Note on the source: triad conventions

(E.197)–(E.199) define a left-handed set, $\be_1\times\be_2=-\be_3$, as in Fig. 6; this is harmless. (E.200)–(E.201) give $\bq$ and $-\bq$ the same unit vector, so $\be_3(\bq)=\pm\hat\bq$ by half-space; only $e_{3\mu}(\bq)e_{3\nu}(-\bq)=q_\mu q_\nu/q^2$ enters later. "Unitary" in (E.196) means real orthogonal. The $\alpha=3$ ladder operators reuse the scale $cq$, which nothing in (E.215) fixes: they are bookkeeping, not normal modes (EPP §4.7 sets $\omega_{\bq3}=0^+$, E.262).

The longitudinal photon is the Coulomb interaction

What, then, is $H^0_{\rm Lph}$? EPP §4.4.3 inverts the triad and the Fourier transform (E.221–E.226), then uses $\bp_A=-\bE/4\pi c$ and $e_{3\mu}(\bq)=q_\mu/q$:

$$H^0_{\rm Lph}=\frac{1}{8\pi}\sum_{\mu\nu=x,y,z}\int d\br\int d\br'\,E_\mu(\br)\left\{\int\frac{d\bq}{(2\pi)^3}\,\frac{q_\mu q_\nu}{q^2}\,e^{-\ii\bq\cdot(\br-\br')}\right\}E_\nu(\br'). \tag{E.227}$$

The kernel in braces is the longitudinal delta function, the projector onto curl-free fields. So (E.227) is simply $\frac{1}{8\pi}\int\bE_l^2$, the energy of the longitudinal electric field. Since $q_\mu q_\nu/q^2=\frac{1}{4\pi}q_\mu q_\nu\cdot\frac{4\pi}{q^2}$, the kernel is $\frac{1}{4\pi}\partial_\mu\partial'_\nu$ acting on the Coulomb propagator $V(\br-\br')=1/|\br-\br'|$ (E.229).
